people: Casey Harrell, 45 at implant, climate campaigner and father
title: ALS took his voice. A brain implant gave it back — in his own voice.
hook: His daughter couldn't understand him anymore. Then AI learned to read the words straight from his brain.
body: ALS slowly stole Casey Harrell's speech until even his young daughter couldn't make out his words. In July 2023, surgeons at UC Davis placed four tiny electrode arrays in his brain. AI learned to decode the speech he was trying to say — and read it aloud in a recreation of his old, pre-ALS voice, rebuilt from recordings. It worked on day one. He wept. So did everyone in the room.

It wasn't a one-day demo. Published in the New England Journal of Medicine at 97.5% accuracy, the system kept working — by 2026 it was running at roughly 99%, about 56 words a minute, in Casey's own home with no researchers present. He has now spoken over two million words through it: talking with his family, working, telling his daughter he loves her — while looking his wife in the eye.
This is the most accurate speech neuroprosthesis ever reported. And it made the jump skeptics said wouldn't happen: from lab demo to daily household tool, for nearly two years and counting.

stat.l: words Casey has spoken through the implant at home — at up to 99% accuracy

why: Locked-in no longer has to mean silent. A disease that takes a person's voice can now be answered with technology that gives it back — their actual voice.

sources.name: UC Davis Health — Nature Medicine home-use study (Jun 2026)

people: Joseph Coates; Dr. David Fajgenbaum, Every Cure
title: Sent home to die, he was saved by a drug combination an AI found
hook: His partner emailed a doctor with an algorithm. Four months later he was in remission.
body: Joseph Coates was dying of POEMS syndrome, a rare blood disorder. His nerves were failing, his heart was enlarged, his kidneys were shutting down — and he was too sick for the stem-cell transplant that was his only hope. He had been told to prepare for the end.

His partner emailed Dr. David Fajgenbaum at Penn, who runs an AI system that scores every approved drug against every known disease. The AI pointed to an unusual combination of chemotherapy, immunotherapy and steroids that nobody had tried for his case. It worked. About four months later, Coates was strong enough for the transplant. He went into remission.

Fajgenbaum knows the territory personally: as a medical student he nearly died of Castleman disease, and saved his own life by finding a 25-year-old transplant drug nobody had tried. His nonprofit, Every Cure, has now scored some 75 million drug-disease pairs — and in February 2026 won up to $76 million from the US government's health research agency to push 10 candidates into trials.

stat.l: drug-and-disease combinations scanned for cures already sitting on pharmacy shelves

why: There are about 3,000 approved drugs and over 12,000 diseases. No human can check every pair — but the cure for a dying patient may already exist under a different label.

people: Dr. Kristina Lång, Lund University
title: Sweden ran the first real trial of AI cancer screening. It found 29% more cancers with 44% less work.
hook: 105,000 women. Half screened the usual way, half with AI. Then they waited to see who got sick.
body: Sweden put AI mammography screening to the hardest test medicine has: a randomized controlled trial with more than 105,000 women. Half had their mammograms read the usual way, by two radiologists. Half had AI working alongside one doctor.
The AI group had 29% more cancers caught at screening — and the radiologists needed 44% fewer readings. Both at once, which is not supposed to happen.

Then came the part that mattered most. Final results published in The Lancet in January 2026 followed the women forward: the AI group had fewer aggressive and advanced cancers turn up later, including 27% fewer fast-growing subtypes. The tumours were being caught while they were still small. And false positives did not increase.

stat.l: more breast cancers detected — alongside a 44% cut in radiologist workload

why: Catching breast cancer early is the difference between a small operation and a losing battle. This is gold-standard proof, not a press release.

people: Ann Johnson, teacher and coach, stroke at age 30
title: Silent for 18 years, she spoke again — in her wedding-day voice
hook: A brainstem stroke locked her in at 30. AI found her voice exactly where she left it.
body: Ann Johnson was a 30-year-old math teacher and volleyball coach when a brainstem stroke paralyzed her almost completely. For 18 years she could not speak. Then researchers at UCSF and Berkeley laid a thin sheet of electrodes over the speech area of her brain, and an AI learned to turn her attempts to talk into words spoken by a digital avatar.

The detail that breaks people: they trained the voice on a recording of her 15-minute wedding speech. So when the machine speaks for her, it sounds like her. In 2025 an upgrade cut the delay from eight seconds to about one — close enough to real time to hold a conversation.
Ann's plan now is to become a counselor for people in rehab. Her message: disabilities don't need to stop us or slow us down.

stat.l: of silence before she heard her own voice again

why: Even people locked in for decades aren't beyond reach. The brain still holds the speech — AI can now decode it fast enough for real conversation.

people: Ji Woong (Brian) Kim, Juo-Tung Chen, Jeffrey Jopling and Axel Krieger at Johns Hopkins University, with Lucy Xiaoyang Shi and Chelsea Finn at Stanford University
title: A robot completed the riskiest steps of a gallbladder removal by itself, eight times out of eight, on pig gallbladders in a laboratory
hook: Nobody was holding the controls. And the tissue was pig, on a bench, not a patient.
body: A da Vinci surgical robot leaned over a pig's gallbladder on a bench at Johns Hopkins University. Over about five minutes it worked through 17 separate jobs: grab the gallbladder, place six metal clips, make two cuts. The clips and cuts go on the cystic duct and the cystic artery, the small tubes carrying bile and blood. Cut in the wrong place and you injure the main bile duct. That is the injury surgeons fear most in this operation.

The system is called SRT-H, short for hierarchical surgical robot transformer. It is two neural networks stacked together. The top one looks at the camera feed and writes the next instruction in plain English, things like grab the gallbladder head, or move the left gripper closer to me. The bottom one turns that sentence into arm movements. Both learned by copying humans. The team recorded 16,000 example movements, roughly 17 hours of data, across 34 pig gallbladders. Then they ran the trained system on eight gallbladders it had never seen. It finished all 17 jobs on all eight. On average it spotted and fixed its own mistakes about six times per run, without anyone telling it to.

The tissue matters, so be plain about it. These were pig gallbladders already removed from the animal and placed on a bench. No living animal was operated on. No human patient was involved at any point. A person also sat beside the robot. Each time the robot fired a clip it paused and waited for the human to load the next one, and it asked the human to swap tools. The five minute seventeen second average is robot time only. It excludes the clip loading and the tool changes. Gallbladders with unusual plumbing, where the artery crosses over the duct or branches, were kept out of the training data. The authors put that at roughly one in ten, and say the system is not failure-proof on anatomy it has not seen.

A human surgeon still finished the same tasks faster. What is new here is length and recovery. Earlier autonomous surgery demonstrations were short single actions in tidy setups. This was a long chain of steps on soft, floppy, variable tissue, and when the lower network fumbled, the upper one noticed and told it to try again. Axel Krieger's group published the work in Science Robotics on 9 July 2025.

stat.l: removed pig gallbladders on which the robot finished all 17 surgical steps with no human taking over

why: Surgical autonomy has been promised for decades and has mostly meant one stitch at a time. This is the first published case of a machine running a long, multi-step surgical sequence on real soft tissue and correcting its own errors as it went.
caveat: Pig gallbladders on a bench, already removed from the animal. Not a living animal, and not a person. Eight trials is a small number. A human loaded every clip and changed every tool, and that time is excluded from the reported five minutes. A surgeon was still faster. Rare anatomical variants, about one gallbladder in ten, were left out of the training data, and the authors say performance on unfamiliar anatomy is not guaranteed. Bleeding and breathing motion, both unavoidable in a live patient, were absent from the test. The training demonstrations were performed by non-clinical research assistants trained by a surgical resident, not by surgeons.

people: Sarah Ezekiel; her children Aviva and Eric; Simon Poole of Smartbox
title: Her voice was rebuilt from eight seconds of a scratchy VHS tape
hook: Her children had never heard their mother's real voice. They were 28 and 25.
body: Motor neurone disease was diagnosed in April 2000, when Sarah Ezekiel was 34 and pregnant with her second child. After her son Eric was born her speech went quickly. Her children grew up hearing her only through a robotic synthesiser; they had no memory of her real voice.

Twenty-five years later, Smartbox asked her for an hour of old audio. Her family found a 1990s home video — eight seconds of her voice, with a television blaring over it. Simon Poole's reaction was that there was no way to build a voice from audio that bad. ElevenLabs' voice isolator stripped out the television; a second model trained on real voices filled the gaps and predicted her intonation, the rise and fall that makes a voice a person.

'When I first heard it again, I felt like crying. It's a kind of miracle.' She is an eye-gaze artist in north London. The same technology has been given free to others losing their voices, including the rugby player Rob Burrow.

stat.l: of usable audio — 25 years after the disease took her voice

why: A voice is not a convenience, it is a large part of how people know you. This is a technology that can reach back through decades of tape and return one.

place: NewYork-Presbyterian and Columbia University, New York City
people: Dr. Pierre Elias, Dr. Timothy Poterucha and Holly Hartman, with colleagues at Columbia and NewYork-Presbyterian
title: He arrived short of breath with a clean chest X-ray. The AI read his ECG and found a failing heart.
hook: An ECG costs almost nothing. Nobody knew it held this much.
body: Structural heart disease means something wrong with the heart's physical machinery — the valves, the walls, the chambers. It is common, it is treatable, and it gets missed constantly, because the test that finds it is an ultrasound of the heart: costly, slow, and not available everywhere. The cardiologist who led this work puts the gap plainly. We have colonoscopies and we have mammograms, he says, but there is no equivalent screen for most heart disease.

An ECG is the opposite: ten electrodes, a squiggle on paper, done in almost every clinic on earth for the price of nothing. A team at Columbia and NewYork-Presbyterian trained a model called EchoNext on 1.2 million ECGs paired with the ultrasound results from the same patients — 230,018 people across eight hospitals — to learn what a failing heart looks like in a trace a human reads as unremarkable. Then they put it against 13 cardiologists on the same 3,200 ECGs. The cardiologists correctly spotted 64% of the structural disease. EchoNext got 77%.

In July 2026 the team published a single case in Nature Medicine. A 45-year-old man came into an emergency department after four days of worsening breathlessness and a cough, having recently been in wildfire smoke. His chest X-ray was clean. His bloods were normal except for a slightly raised marker of heart injury. EchoNext flagged his ECG. The tests that followed found advanced cardiomyopathy — a badly weakened heart muscle. Drug treatment did not hold him. He needed a temporary mechanical pump, and about six months after diagnosis he received a heart transplant.

The screening result is the part that scales. Among roughly 85,000 patients who had an ECG but had never had a heart ultrasound, EchoNext flagged 9% as high risk. Of those who went on to be scanned, about 73% did have structural heart disease — roughly double the rate that population would otherwise show. It cleared the US Food and Drug Administration in July 2026, the first AI tool cleared to detect six kinds of structural heart disease from a standard 12-lead ECG, and it is being offered to clinicians free.

stat.l: structural heart disease correctly spotted — the AI, then 13 cardiologists reading the same 3,200 ECGs

why: Heart disease has no mammogram. This turns the cheapest and most widespread test in medicine into a way of deciding who needs the expensive one, which is the only shape a heart screen could realistically take for people who would otherwise never be scanned at all.
caveat: The transplant is one patient, written up as a two-page case report by the same people who built the tool. It is not evidence the AI saved him: he walked into an emergency department with symptoms and an abnormal cardiac marker, so he was already being investigated, and nobody can say what would have happened without the flag. We also could not find a primary source for the widely repeated line that this is the 'first documented case' of its kind — treat that as newsletter framing, not a published claim. On the headline comparison: it was done on stored ECGs in a study setting rather than live clinic conditions, and when those same cardiologists were given AI assistance they reached 69%, so the gap narrows when human and model work together. The screening arm carries the adoption problem this bank keeps running into — only 55% of the patients EchoNext flagged actually got a scan. And a 9% flag rate across 85,000 people means over 7,500 extra ultrasound referrals, a real capacity cost somebody has to absorb. Finally, it is cleared, not approved: FDA clearance is a lower bar, and the tool is authorised to say 'scan this person', not to diagnose anyone. The authors disclose patent applications, stock holdings and consulting arrangements; the work was funded in part by the NIH.

people: Bieszczady Mountain Rescue Service (GOPR); Tomasz Niedzielski and colleagues, University of Wroclaw and SARUAV Ltd
title: The thermal camera missed him. A neural network found him in an ordinary drone photo, alive.
hook: He had a stroke the day before, and his family said he could not stand up again if he fell.
body: On the afternoon of 28 June 2021 a 65-year-old man walked out of his house in Cergowa, a village in south-east Poland. He had Alzheimer's disease. He had suffered a stroke the previous day and had trouble walking. At 11:30 that night his family reported that they had not heard from him.

Seventeen mountain rescuers, police, volunteer firefighters, quad bikes and a search dog worked through the night. A drone with a thermal camera went up around 3am and an analyst watched its imagery for hours. It found nothing. The next day the drone flew again with an ordinary colour camera, this time in a survey grid: 910 overlapping photographs covering about 100 hectares of meadow, bushes, deep valleys and forest.

Seven hundred and eighty-two of those photographs, from four of the flights, went into a laptop running SARUAV, a program from the University of Wroclaw built on a convolutional neural network, the same family of image-recognition model that picks faces out of a phone's photo library. It was trained on aerial pictures of people across different seasons, land covers, times of day and clothing colours, including camouflage. It cuts each photo into squares and flags the ones that look like a person. The flight he was actually in held 121 photos. Upload, scan and human checking of the flagged squares took 5 minutes and 48 seconds. He appeared in three photographs and the software caught all three.

The coordinates went out at 18:21. Rescuers set off at 18:25 and reached him at 18:30. He had been outside for more than 24 hours and needed only minor medical help. The authors point out that in a study of people with Alzheimer's who went missing in Virginia, 46% of those still missing after 24 hours were dead when searchers arrived. This was the first time in the scientific literature that an automatic human detector found a missing person in a real search and the person lived.

stat.l: to upload, scan and check the 121 photographs from the flight he turned out to be in

why: Wandering is one of the commonest emergencies in dementia care and the clock is the entire problem. Flying a drone over the search area is easy. Having someone look at every photograph before dark is not.
caveat: This is one case, and two of the authors work for the company that sells the software, which the paper discloses. The authors say plainly that nobody can know how the search would have ended without it. Thermal imaging failed here but often works better, and the software needs daylight, open terrain and specific flight settings. It produces false alarms that a human must sort through, and the developers' own tests put detection at 86% to 100% of people found in at least one photo, not every photo. The second confirmed detection by the system, in South Tyrol in 2024, found someone who had already died.

people: Demis Hassabis, John Jumper, David Baker; John Hopfield, Geoffrey Hinton
title: The week AI won two Nobel Prizes
hook: Chemistry and Physics, two days apart — for teaching machines to understand nature.
body: In October 2024, the Nobel committees honored AI twice in one week. The Chemistry prize went half to David Baker, who designs brand-new proteins by computer, and half to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of Google DeepMind, whose AlphaFold cracked a 50-year-old grand challenge: predicting a protein's 3D shape from its genetic recipe.
The Physics prize went to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for the neural-network discoveries in the 1980s that made modern AI possible.

The citation noted that AlphaFold had already been used by more than two million researchers in 190 countries. The most conservative institution in science looked at AI and judged it not hype, but prize-worthy discovery.

stat.l: Nobel Prizes for AI work in a single week

why: Science's highest honor now recognizes AI as a genuine instrument of human knowledge — the clearest possible signal to every skeptic.

people: Ethan Goh, Robert Gallo and Jonathan H. Chen (Stanford); Adam Rodman and Zahir Kanjee (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center); Andrew Parsons (University of Virginia); commentary by Sumant Ranji (UCSF)
title: A randomised trial found GPT-4 reasoned through hard patient cases better than the doctors who were handed GPT-4 to help them
hook: The model scored 92%. The doctors given the model scored 76%. The doctors without it scored 74%.
body: In late 2023, 50 doctors sat down with written patient cases and a time limit. They were 26 attending physicians and 24 residents in internal medicine, family medicine and emergency medicine, recruited through Stanford, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, and the University of Virginia. Each was given up to six cases built from real patients, using only the information a doctor would have at the first assessment. A coin toss decided who got GPT-4 to use alongside their normal references, and who got the normal references only. Graders then marked the written reasoning against a fixed rubric: list the diagnoses worth considering, give the evidence for and against each one, name your leading diagnosis, and say what you would test next.

The doctors with GPT-4 scored a median 76% of the available rubric points. The doctors without it scored 74%. A two point gap on that rubric is not a real difference, and the trial says so: the confidence interval runs from minus 4 to plus 8 points. The researchers then ran GPT-4 on the same cases with nobody steering it. Alone, it scored a median 92%, sixteen percentage points above the doctors working with conventional resources. They also checked whether the chatbot at least saved time. It did not.

The number worth staring at is 76, not 92. Giving a doctor a tool that scores 92 on its own moved that doctor by two points. In the write-up from Stanford's institute for human-centered AI, the investigators said plainly what happened: many of the physicians in the ChatGPT group did not agree with the model's diagnosis or did not factor it in at all. Nobody had trained them to prompt it, and the trial did not try to. Goh described the missing ingredient as trust, meaning a doctor treating the model's view as a serious possibility rather than noise. Sumant Ranji, writing an invited commentary alongside the paper, drew the same line: access to generative AI on its own will not improve diagnosis, and clinicians will need training to use it.

This trial gets quoted as AI beating doctors. That is a misreading twice over. The two groups of doctors did not differ, and the model's sixteen point edge came with a wide margin of error, from 2 to 30 points. What the trial actually shows is that the handover between a good model and a good clinician was broken. The same group went back and fixed it. In Nature Medicine in 2025 they ran 92 physicians on treatment decisions rather than diagnosis, and this time GPT-4 assistance did help, by 6.5 percentage points. In 2026, in npj Digital Medicine, they rebuilt the interaction so the model wrote its own diagnosis first, then compared it with the clinician's and argued the disagreements out loud. Clinicians using conventional resources scored 75%. With the model as a second opinion, 82%. With it as a first opinion, 85%. The model alone still scored 90%, but the gap had mostly closed.

stat.l: Share of points on the trial's reasoning rubric: GPT-4 working alone, against the doctors who were given GPT-4 to help them.

why: It is one of the few randomised trials where a model out-reasoned trained physicians on the same task, and the same trial shows that handing clinicians the model changes almost nothing. The bottleneck is the handover, not the model.
caveat: These were written case vignettes under a time limit, not real patients in a clinic, and the rubric scores documented reasoning rather than whether anyone got better. Fifty physicians and six cases is small, the score spreads overlap heavily, and the model's 16 point lead over the unaided doctors carried a confidence interval from 2 to 30 points. The model was the GPT-4 of late 2023. The 50 doctors are the whole trial across three institutions, not a Beth Israel subgroup of something larger.

people: Chin-Sheng Lin and Chin Lin, National Defense Medical Center, Taipei
title: An AI read 450,000 ECGs, then cut deaths by 31% in a real trial
hook: Eric Topol: "It's very rare for any medication to produce a 31 per cent reduction in mortality."
body: An ECG is one of the cheapest tests in medicine — a few electrodes, a squiggle on paper. Researchers in Taiwan trained an AI on hundreds of thousands of them, paired with what happened to those patients afterwards, until it could read a risk of dying that no cardiologist could see in the same trace.

Then they did the thing most AI studies skip: a randomised trial, published in Nature Medicine. 15,965 patients across two hospitals. When the AI flagged someone as high risk, it alerted the 39 physicians on duty. Among those high-risk patients, deaths within 90 days fell 31% (hazard ratio 0.69). Deaths specifically from cardiac causes fell from 2.4% to 0.2% — a reduction of more than 90%.

Across all patients, including the low-risk majority, 90-day mortality fell from 4.3% to 3.6%. Cardiologist Eric Topol's comparison puts it in perspective: it is very rare for any drug to deliver a mortality cut like the one seen in the high-risk group. This is software reading a test the hospital was already running.

stat.l: fewer deaths within 90 days among high-risk patients, in a randomised trial

why: The cheapest test in the hospital, already being run on millions of people, turns out to contain a warning nobody could read. That is the pattern to watch.
caveat: The 31% is the high-risk subgroup. Across all 15,965 patients the reduction was smaller — 3.6% versus 4.3% at 90 days, hazard ratio 0.83 — which is what you would expect when most people flagged are not the ones in danger. The 450,000-ECG training figure comes from the researchers' own description, not the paper.

people: Martin De Simone and World Bank co-authors
title: Six weeks with an AI tutor in Nigeria beat 80% of every education programme ever tested
hook: Girls started behind the boys. They gained the most.
body: In June and July 2024, about 800 first-year senior secondary students in Benin City went to free after-school sessions to practise English with an AI chatbot, guided by teachers in school computer labs.

The World Bank ran it as a randomized controlled trial — the gold standard. After six weeks, students who got the AI sessions scored 0.31 standard deviations higher than the control group. By the World Bank's own cost-effectiveness benchmarking, that's equivalent to something like 1.5 to 2 years of ordinary schooling. It outperformed roughly 80% of all rigorously tested education programmes in the developing world.
And the girls, who started out behind the boys, gained the most.

stat.l: test-score gain in six weeks — which the World Bank benchmarks at 1.5–2 years of schooling

why: The cheapest effective schooling interventions ever tested rarely move scores this much this fast. If a chatbot plus a teacher can do this in a low-income setting, the ceiling for poor students just moved.
caveat: Be precise: the measured effect is 0.31 standard deviations. The 'nearly two years of learning' figure is the World Bank's own equivalence calculation, not a literal grade jump. It was 800 students over six weeks, and gains skewed toward girls and toward students who started stronger. No published scale-up results yet — this is a pilot.

people: Syed Mohammad Asad Zaidi of University College London and Community Health Solutions in Karachi; Saira Khowaja of the Indus Health Network; Aamir Khan of Interactive Research and Development; Jacob Creswell of the Stop TB Partnership; Andrew Copas and Hanif Esmail of University College London
title: Software read 1.2 million chest X-rays in Pakistani roadside camps. 7,625 people started TB treatment.
hook: Eleven thousand one-day camps over four years, and not one radiologist. The software was the only reader.
body: A chest camp in Pakistan is a single day's work. A van parks up, loudspeakers announce it, fieldworkers walk the neighbourhood, and for four to six hours anyone who turns up gets a chest X-ray. Between the third quarter of 2017 and the second quarter of 2021, Community Health Solutions, a private organisation working as an implementing partner of Pakistan's National TB Programme, ran 11,327 of these camps across 20 districts. A third of them were in Karachi. Altogether 1,214,289 people were X-rayed.

Two things about how it worked. Nobody was asked about symptoms first: screening was symptom-agnostic by design, so people who felt perfectly well were X-rayed alongside people who were coughing. And no radiologist saw the images. Every one went to CAD4TB, made by Delft Imaging in the Netherlands, which returns a score from 0 to 100. Anyone above the cut-off was asked for a sputum sample. The programme began with a cut-off of 50 to catch as many cases as possible, then raised it to 60 in 2018, after consulting the national programme, because the lower setting was sending too many people for expensive molecular tests.

133,036 people, just under 11 percent of those screened, were flagged as possible TB. 105,976 got a sputum test. 7,625 were diagnosed with tuberculosis and started on treatment. Of those, 3,500, or 45.9 percent, had TB confirmed in a laboratory; the other 4,125 were treated on a doctor's judgement without a positive test. Nationally the camps found 289 lab-confirmed cases for every 100,000 people screened.

The most useful thing in the paper is how unevenly that worked. Depending on the district, yield ran from 70 to 678 lab-confirmed cases per 100,000 people screened. Same vans, same software, same cut-off, and close to a tenfold difference in how many people it found. The authors' conclusion is that programmes should point the vans at the places with the most TB rather than spreading them evenly, and that the empirical-treatment problem has to be fixed alongside any scale-up. They published the underlying dataset openly through University College London.

stat.l: chest X-rays read by software rather than a radiologist in Pakistani screening camps over four years

why: This is AI as the only reader of a medical image, at national-programme scale, for four years of routine work rather than a pilot. 7,625 people started tuberculosis treatment after software looked at their X-ray, and many of them had no symptoms to report.
caveat: A retrospective analysis of aggregate camp-level data with no control group and no human-reader comparison, so it cannot show how many of the 7,625 a radiologist would also have found. The paper makes no claim that these camps raised Pakistan's national TB notifications, and that claim should not be made on its behalf. More than half the people treated, 4,125 of 7,625, never had TB confirmed in a laboratory; the authors flag this as a problem for programmes to fix, not as a win. Yield varied nearly tenfold between districts, so results here do not predict results elsewhere. Children under 15 and pregnant women were excluded under national guidelines. Funding came from the Global Fund and the Stop TB Partnership.

people: Alpha School; Joe Liemandt
title: The same software: 1x learning at home, 2.6x at school
hook: The most useful finding in AI education is an argument against the software.
body: Alpha School's pitch is two hours of AI-personalised academics a day and learning at 2.6 times the normal rate. Then it ran a beta of the same system for homeschoolers — identical apps, identical dashboard, same two hours a day, but no campus, no guides, no incentives.
Result, in the words of a parent who moved his family to Austin for a year to investigate: students in the homeschool pilot were 'advancing at ~1x speed.' The software on its own did nothing special.

Alpha's founder Joe Liemandt says the quiet part out loud: 'Motivation is 90% of the solution. The edtech is 10%.' The AI is necessary and nowhere near sufficient — what does the work is guides, peer culture, incentives, and someone noticing.

stat.l: identical software, at home versus on campus

why: Anyone promising that AI alone will fix education is contradicted by the most enthusiastic AI school in the world, using its own data.
caveat: The 2.6x is Alpha's own internal metric, and the reviewer devotes a section to questioning how it is calculated. Alpha is selective and largely affluent; its gifted-and-talented sibling programme shows around 5x, which the reviewer attributes mostly to selection. The homeschool arm is a beta pilot, not a shipped product.

place: Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Austin, Atlanta
title: 220 million driverless miles later, the crash numbers are hard to argue with
hook: 94% fewer crashes that seriously hurt or killed someone. Same streets, same period, human drivers as the control.
body: Waymo's cars have now driven more than 220 million miles on public roads with nobody behind the wheel. That's a big enough number to do real statistics on.

Compared with human drivers in the same cities over the same period: 94% fewer crashes that seriously injured or killed someone. 82% fewer injury crashes of any kind. 93% fewer injury crashes involving people on foot. 84% fewer involving cyclists.

At over 4 million miles a week, that works out to roughly one serious crash prevented every eight days. Cumulatively: an estimated 47 serious-or-fatal crashes and 707 injury crashes that didn't happen. In Atlanta, across 5.4 million miles, Waymo had zero serious-injury crashes where human drivers would have been expected to cause more than one.
About 40,000 Americans die on the roads every year, and 1.2 million people worldwide. We have quietly accepted this as the price of driving.

stat.l: fewer crashes causing serious or fatal injury, across 220M driverless miles

why: The single largest real-world evidence base that machines are simply better drivers than we are. Road death was never inevitable — it was just unaddressed.
caveat: This is Waymo's own analysis against human benchmarks it selects, though the methodology is published and peer-reviewed, the crash reports are federally mandated, and insurer Swiss Re and the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety both found large reductions independently. Waymo still has minor crashes, and it drives in mapped, mostly mild-weather cities.

people: J.D. Fletcher and John E. Morrison, Institute for Defense Analyses; Ralph Chatham, DARPA; US Navy Center for Information Dominance and Fleet System Engineering Teams
title: A DARPA-funded tutor trained Navy IT recruits in 16 weeks to out-troubleshoot sailors with nine years at sea
hook: The famous number is real. It is attached to the wrong comparison.
body: In March and April 2012 the US Navy ran two week-long test sessions at its San Diego base. Three groups of twelve sailors sat the same exams. One group had spent 16 weeks with a computer program called the Digital Tutor, paid for by DARPA. One group had finished the Navy's own 35-week IT classroom course. The third group were working Fleet technicians with 4 to 15 years of service, averaging about nine and a half years. Their commands had picked them as the best people available in port, the shipboard go-to technicians. The test problems were real faults, pulled from a database of more than 20,000 trouble tickets that ships had sent ashore because nobody on board could fix them.

The Digital Tutor group won most of it. Working in teams of three across two and a half days, they solved 74 percent of the troubleshooting problems they attempted. The experienced Fleet teams solved 51 percent and the classroom teams 38 percent. Only the Digital Tutor teams attempted the problems rated very hard, and they solved three of the five. They also broke less on their way through. The chance that a Digital Tutor team left a harmful change behind in the system was 0.14, against 0.41 for the Fleet teams. The Fleet beat them at one thing. In a four-hour security exercise the Fleet teams found and fixed 69 percent of the planted security holes and the Digital Tutor teams found 44 percent. The evaluators blamed that on the one part of the course where no expert human tutor had been available.

People retelling this story usually say the recruits finished four standard deviations above sailors with ten years of experience. Sometimes they say eight. Both numbers appear in the published evaluation, in the same table. Neither is invented and neither is being quoted properly. In Table 7 of the 2014 report the troubleshooting effect size is 4.19 against the experienced Fleet technicians and 7.98 against the Navy's 35-week classroom course. So eight is not a bigger version of four. It is a different comparison, against a training course rather than against experienced people. Both figures also come from comparing four teams on each side, not individual sailors. The earlier 2012 report scored the identical exercise problem by problem instead of team by team, and reported 0.85 against the Fleet and 1.13 against the classroom course. Same sailors, same week, same answers. The headline number moves about fivefold depending on what the authors chose to count. The authors' own one-line summary of the whole programme was more careful than either version in circulation: effect sizes often well above two standard deviations.

The Digital Tutor was not machine learning and shared nothing with today's chatbots. Its evaluators describe the back end as classic knowledge engineering, meaning feature extraction, ontologies and an inference engine, hand-coded by expert programmers. It read typed answers using natural language processing but, the report states plainly, it did not attempt full natural language understanding. A component called the Recommender decided when to go and fetch a human mentor. Roughly half the programme's money went on finding 24 human experts and having them tutor the first intake one-to-one, so that their teaching could be recorded and copied into software. The claim that DARPA buried the result is false. The 2014 report is stamped approved for public release, distribution unlimited, and has sat in the Pentagon's own technical library since 2015.

stat.l: share of real ship faults solved — Digital Tutor teams, then hand-picked Fleet technicians averaging 9.6 years at sea

why: It is the best evidence anyone has that deep technical skill can be built in months rather than years, and it was done with 2000s-era symbolic AI, not modern models. It is also a lesson in how a real finding gets distorted: the number survived the retelling but the comparison group did not.
caveat: Small and fragile. Twelve people per group, and the headline troubleshooting effect sizes rest on four teams per side, six degrees of freedom. Scoring the same data per problem gives 0.85 rather than 4.19 against the Fleet group. Blinding was partial. The review board could not tell Digital Tutor graduates from classroom graduates, but the Fleet veterans were obvious from their age and rank, and the hands-on scoring was not blinded. The Fleet group was hand-picked for being unusually good, which makes the win harder to explain away, but they were tested on material the tutor was purpose-built to teach, drawn from the same trouble-ticket database used to design it. IDA described itself as an impartial third party, and for the 2012 report it was working under contract to DARPA, the programme's own sponsor. The Fleet group's mean experience is given as 9.1 years in one report and 9.6 in the other, so ten years is rounded up. The tutor was never scaled. Its evaluators noted it was expensive to build and to run, that content had to be coded by expert programmers rather than teachers, and that further funding would have to come from outside research budgets. The widely repeated claim that ten years of experience reduces to about 40 scenarios appears nowhere in these reports. The only 40 in them is the roughly 40 candidate training domains DARPA surveyed before choosing Navy IT.

people: Dr. Ajit Goenka, Sovanlal Mukherjee and colleagues, Mayo Clinic, with Dr. Suresh Chari, MD Anderson
title: AI found pancreatic cancer on scans doctors had already read as normal — up to 3 years early
hook: The deadliest common cancer, visible in scans nobody knew to look at twice.
body: Pancreatic cancer is usually found too late to cure. By the time it causes symptoms, it has often spread.

Mayo Clinic built a model called REDMOD that measures hundreds of tiny texture and structure features on ordinary abdominal CT scans — the kind millions of people get every year for unrelated reasons. It was trained on 969 scans and then tested on a separate set of 493, of which 63 came from people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer 3 to 36 months later. Its specificity was checked again on two more outside collections of 539 and 80 scans.

Then two board-certified abdominal radiologists read the same 493 scans, blind. They were not told which scans were which, and they were not even told how many cancers were in the pile. REDMOD flagged 73% of the pre-diagnosis cancers. The radiologists flagged 38.9%. What 73% sensitivity means for a patient: out of 100 people already carrying an invisible pancreatic cancer, it would catch 73 and miss 27. On scans taken more than two years before diagnosis the gap widened to 68% against 23%. The median warning was 475 days, about 16 months.
'This AI can now identify the signature of cancer from a normal-appearing pancreas,' said Dr. Ajit Goenka.

stat.l: of hidden pancreatic cancers caught on scans already read as normal — two radiologists reading those same scans caught 38.9%

why: Caught before the tumour is even visible, pancreatic cancer can sometimes still be cured by surgery. This is warning time on one of the deadliest cancers there is — from scans that already exist.
caveat: The comparison is genuinely head-to-head on identical images, blinded, which is rare and strong. But it was a study, not a clinic: only two radiologists took part, both three years out of residency, and they had no clinical history, no referral reason and no prior scans — all things a radiologist normally has. They were also told to hunt specifically for early pancreatic cancer, which nobody does in routine reading. And the test set was loaded to about one cancer in every six scans; in the real population pancreatic cancer is far rarer than that, so false alarms would be much more frequent in practice. Mayo says prospective validation in high-risk groups is the next step. Not in routine use.

people: Sofia Schierbeck and Andreas Claesson, Karolinska Institutet; Region Västra Götaland; the 112 call-takers at SOS Alarm; drone operator Everdrone
title: Drones carrying defibrillators reached Swedish cardiac arrest patients before the ambulance in 37 of 55 cases, and one patient shocked by a drone-delivered defibrillator was alive 30 days later.
hook: The defibrillator arrived from the sky first. The ambulance was still three minutes away.
body: When a heart stops outside a hospital, the thing that helps most is a shock from a defibrillator, and it helps most in the first few minutes. Ambulances cannot always be that fast. So between 21 April 2021 and 31 May 2022, a team led by Sofia Schierbeck and Andreas Claesson of Karolinska Institutet parked five drones, each carrying an automated external defibrillator, inside two blocks of controlled airspace in western Sweden covering about 200,000 people. When a 112 caller described what sounded like a cardiac arrest, the call-taker at SOS Alarm sent the ambulance and launched a drone at the same time.

Over that period 211 calls were flagged as a suspected cardiac arrest. A drone actually flew for only 72 of them. It got the defibrillator down in 58. In 55 cases the researchers had a recorded arrival time for both the drone and the ambulance, and the drone won 37 of those, or 67 percent. Where it won, the median head start was 3 minutes and 14 seconds. The defibrillator was dropped within 15 metres of the patient or the building 91 percent of the time.

Then the numbers get small, and this is the part worth reading slowly. Of those 37 head starts, 18 turned out to be genuine cardiac arrests. In 6 of those 18, the people on the scene actually attached the defibrillator. In 2, the machine detected a shockable rhythm and delivered a shock before the ambulance arrived. One of those two people was alive 30 days later. That is one documented survivor, not a pile of lives saved, and the researchers do not claim otherwise. No adverse events occurred.

Two things get misreported about this study. The first is the timing: it is often written up as the drone being faster by "up to three minutes," which actually undersells it. 3 minutes 14 seconds was the median, so in half of those 37 cases the head start was longer than that. The second is the technology. Everdrone's aircraft flew themselves from take-off to landing and used onboard stereo cameras to spot obstacles and to find a landing marker where GPS was unreliable, watched by a remote operator. But no machine-learning model made any decision here. A human call-taker decided to launch. And the "automated" in automated external defibrillator is heart-rhythm analysis software of a kind that has been in these boxes since the 1990s. This is autonomous flight and machine perception doing something useful, not artificial intelligence practising medicine.

stat.l: the median head start the drone had over the ambulance, in the cases where it arrived first

why: It is one of the few times an uncrewed aircraft has been shown, in a real emergency and in a peer-reviewed prospective study rather than a simulation, to put a working treatment into a bystander's hands before the ambulance could.
caveat: One 30-day survivor is not evidence that drones save lives; the study was never designed or statistically powered to measure survival. The funnel is severe and should always be quoted in full: 211 alerts, 72 launches, 58 deliveries, 55 comparable cases, 18 confirmed arrests, 6 defibrillators actually attached, 2 shocks, 1 survivor. The "two-thirds faster" figure describes only the 55 cases where a drone flew and both arrival times were logged, not cardiac arrest calls in general, because a drone flew for just 34 percent of alerts. Flights were cancelled for darkness, bad weather, no-delivery zones and air traffic control refusal, so this is a fair-weather daytime result. Children under 8, trauma cases and arrests witnessed by ambulance crews were excluded. The service covered about 200,000 people in two pre-approved airspaces, which is a long way from national coverage.

people: Tyto Care; Nader Shaikh and Alejandro Hoberman, University of Pittsburgh
title: A parent can now check a child's ear at 2am better than a paediatrician can
hook: The regulator let them sell it over the counter. No prescription, no clinic.
body: Ear infections are the single most common reason a small child is prescribed antibiotics. The diagnosis turns on one thing a doctor looks for down an otoscope: is the eardrum bulging? A bulging drum means pressure behind it, which means infection. A flat one usually means a miserable cold and nothing to prescribe for.

It is a genuinely hard call. In February 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration reviewed an AI trained to make it, tested on 857 ear recordings where the answer had been settled by a majority vote of three ear, nose and throat specialists. The comparison was not against those specialists. It was against three ordinary US clinicians — two paediatricians and a GP — the people who actually see the child.

The AI spotted 92% of the bulging eardrums; the clinicians spotted 72%. On healthy ears the AI was right 95% of the time; the clinicians, 73%. Both gaps are about 20 percentage points, both were targets set in advance rather than found afterwards, and both were cleared. The FDA authorised it in March 2026 for sale over the counter — no prescription — as the first device of its kind, which required writing a new regulation for it.

The independent check matters here. A separate University of Pittsburgh team built their own version and published it in JAMA Pediatrics in 2024, testing on 1,151 videos from 635 children, most under three. They got 94% sensitivity and 94% specificity. Two groups, two devices, same answer: this is a task software does reliably well and tired humans do not.

stat.l: share of bulging eardrums correctly spotted — the AI, then paediatricians and a GP

why: Roughly 5 in 6 children get at least one ear infection, and both over-prescribing antibiotics and missing a real infection do damage. This is the rare AI result that lands in a parent's hand at 2am, when the alternative is guessing or driving to an emergency room.
caveat: Read the two directions differently. When it says the ear is clear it is very trustworthy — a negative is wrong about 1 time in 140. When it flags a bulge it is much weaker: at real-world rates roughly 4 in 10 flags are false alarms. So this is a tool for ruling infection out, not for ruling it in, and the FDA is explicit that it is not authorised to diagnose anything. The validation data are the company's own, drawn from its own telehealth recordings, and no outside group has independently tested this specific algorithm — the Pittsburgh confirmation is of a different device doing the same task. The company's marketing cites a database of 1.6 million ear images; the set actually used to train the model was 3,102 recordings. And FDA authorisation is not itself proof of good numbers: in the same batch of AI device approvals, two devices missed the performance targets their own makers had set in advance and were authorised anyway on a broader benefit-versus-risk judgement.

place: UMC Utrecht, Princess Máxima Center and Amsterdam UMC, Netherlands
people: Jeroen de Ridder, Bastiaan Tops and Eelco Hoving
title: Surgeons waited a week to learn what the tumour was. Now they know before they close.
hook: And when it isn't sure, it says so instead of guessing.
body: In brain surgery the right move depends on exactly which tumour it is. For one type you cut aggressively; for another you stop early and spare healthy tissue. The problem is that the precise molecular answer took about a week — arriving long after the patient was sewn up — and the fast alternative of freezing a slice and reading it in twenty minutes is often unreliable.

A Dutch team built a neural network called Sturgeon that reads the thin, patchy DNA data a portable sequencer can produce inside the operating theatre, and runs on a laptop. On 50 stored samples it returned a correct answer within 40 minutes for 45 of them, and declined to guess on the rest.

Then they used it live during 25 real operations, with results in under 90 minutes. Eighteen times it gave an answer, and all eighteen were right. Seven times it said it was not confident enough — and stayed quiet. A children's cancer centre now uses it when a child's operation depends on the answer.

stat.l: from biopsy to knowing the tumour type, mid-operation — it used to take a week

why: A child's whole life can turn on whether a surgeon removes two more millimetres, and until now that call was made blind. The model also knows when to shut up, which is exactly what you want from AI in an operating theatre.
caveat: Only 18 of the 25 live cases produced an answer at all; in the other seven the surgeon got nothing and fell back on the old methods. Small numbers, a handful of Dutch hospitals, and no study yet showing patients live longer or better. Pathologists still review every slide.

people: Microsoft Research (MAI-DxO)
title: Five virtual doctors argued about the case. They out-diagnosed 21 real ones.
hook: 85.5% against 19.9% — on cases the New England Journal publishes because they defeat specialists.
body: The New England Journal of Medicine publishes diagnostic puzzles precisely because they beat clinicians. Microsoft ran 304 of them past a system that works unusually: instead of one model answering, it convenes a panel of five virtual physicians with fixed jobs — one forms hypotheses, one picks tests, one plays devil's advocate, one watches spending, one runs the checklist — and makes them argue.
The panel got 85.5% right. Twenty-one physicians with a median twelve years' experience, working the same 304 cases, averaged 19.9%.

Two things must be said for that number to mean anything. The physicians were deliberately stripped of their normal tools: no colleagues, no textbooks, no search engines, no AI. Microsoft says so itself. And the 85.5% configuration was expensive — about $7,184 of tests per case against the doctors' $2,963 average. A cheaper setting reached 79.9% while spending about 20% less than the physicians did. Accuracy and thrift came from different settings, not the same one.

stat.l: versus 19.9% for 21 experienced physicians on NEJM's hardest cases

why: The structure is the lesson: not one cleverer answer, but several perspectives forced to disagree before committing.
caveat: Three real limits. These are written case vignettes, not live patients. The physicians were barred from colleagues, textbooks, search and AI — so this is not a like-for-like contest. And the top-accuracy configuration ordered roughly 2.4x more testing than the doctors, which in a real hospital is a harm, not a saving. It is also still a preprint, not peer-reviewed.

people: Gert-Jan Oskam, paralyzed in a 2011 cycling accident
title: Told he'd never walk again. An AI 'digital bridge' had other plans.
hook: One implant reads his brain, another fires his spine, and AI translates between them.
body: In 2011, a cycling accident in China left Gert-Jan Oskam's legs paralyzed. Twelve years later, Swiss researchers gave him two implants: one that reads his brain's intention to move, and one that stimulates his spinal cord. An AI sits between them, translating thought into step — a 'digital bridge' across the injury.

He can now stand at a bar with his friends, climb stairs, and walk up to 450 feet at a time. Walking is slow and it's hard work — this is honest progress, not a miracle cure. But something remarkable happened along the way: some movement returned even with the system switched off. The training appears to help his own nerves rewire.

By 2025, five people had received the bridge, and the trial (run by Onward Medical) is expanding toward real-world approval. The most severely injured recipient, a triathlete, took steps without a harness after six months.

stat.l: how far he can walk, 12+ years after being told he never would

why: Walking after paralysis was science fiction a decade ago. The AI decoder is the piece that made the bridge possible — and it's now in a growing clinical trial.

place: Nine countries, from Nigeria to Cambodia to Brazil
people: Mark Schiffman and Brian Befano of the US National Cancer Institute; Kayode Ajenifuja at Obafemi Awolowo University Teaching Hospital, Nigeria; Karen Yeates and Bariki Mchome at Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Centre, Tanzania; Miriam Cremer and Karla Alfaro of Basic Health International in El Salvador; Amna Haider of Epicentre and Henry Phiri of Malawi's Ministry of Health; the HPV-Automated Visual Evaluation (PAVE) Consortium
title: Cervical cancer needs a pathologist to catch. Software did it from one photograph, in nine countries.
hook: A nurse takes one photo. The software says who needs treating before she leaves.
body: Cervical cancer is almost entirely preventable, and it still killed around 280,000 women in 2024. Nearly 90 percent of those deaths happen in low- and middle-income countries. The reason is not that the disease is mysterious. It is that catching it needs a lab, or a doctor with a colposcope, or both, and most of the world has neither.

The usual workaround is called VIA. A nurse swabs the cervix with vinegar, waits, and looks for a white patch. It is cheap and it can be done in a village clinic. It is also a judgement call made by eye, and it is often wrong. So the US National Cancer Institute assembled a consortium to try replacing the eye with a camera and a neural network. Women take their own swab for an HPV test. If the swab is positive, a nurse photographs the cervix with a handheld camera, and a network called DenseNet-121 grades the picture as normal, indeterminate or severe.

The first results, published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute in 2025, cover 27,654 women screened in Brazil, Cambodia, the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Eswatini, Honduras, Malawi, Nigeria and Tanzania. Of those, 6,866 tested HPV-positive, and the first 1,832 to finish the whole process were analysed. Among that group, 138 turned out to have CIN3+, the grade of precancer that needs treating. The photograph sorted them well. Where the software said normal, 3 of 285 women had precancer, or 1.1 percent. Where it said severe, 85 of 618 did, or 13.8 percent. Combine the picture with which HPV type the woman carried, and the spread widened: no precancer at all in 128 women with a low-risk HPV type and a normal-looking photo, against 29 of 100 women who had HPV-16 and a severe-looking photo. In this first phase the grading was done afterwards on research servers, not live in the room.

The point is not that the software is clever. It is that a nurse in a clinic with no pathologist can now separate the woman who should be treated this morning from the woman who can safely be told to come back in a few years. That is the whole game in cervical cancer, and until now it needed a hospital.

stat.l: share of HPV-positive women who had precancer, from the lowest-risk group to the highest

why: Cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers there is, and the women dying of it are dying of a missing pathologist rather than a missing cure. This is a way to make the decision without one.
caveat: In this first phase the algorithm did not actually run in the clinic. Images were shipped to graphics servers and graded afterwards, so nobody's treatment was decided by it in real time. The authors say the model cannot yet be moved to a different camera without retraining. Only 1,832 of the 6,866 HPV-positive women had completed the protocol at the data freeze, and the number with high-grade disease is expected to more than quadruple by the end of the study, so all these percentages will move. Roughly a tenth of the high-grade cases were actual cancers, so this measures precancer detection, not lives saved. And the field's own history here is a warning: a celebrated 2019 paper from this same NCI group reported near-perfect accuracy for this idea, and in December 2025 its senior author, Mark Schiffman, published a letter in the same journal saying those results came from overfitting and urging readers to ignore them.

people: Nick Wray, living with ALS
title: "I microwaved my own chicken nuggets and fed myself!"
hook: The list he wrote is better than any specification sheet.
body: Nick Wray has ALS and is the eighth person to receive a Neuralink implant. Using it to control a robotic arm over three eight-hour working days, he wrote down what he had done, and the list is more persuasive than any technical claim:

'I put on my own hat for the first time in years! I microwaved my own chicken nuggets and fed myself! I learned how to open my fridge and how to remove and replace lids on jars! I even got to try driving my wheelchair with it slowly inside. I did really well!'
He also set study records on the dexterity tests — 39 cylinders moved across a table in five minutes. But the hat and the nuggets are the point. Independence is made of small things.

stat.l: cylinders moved in five minutes, by thought, with a robotic arm

why: Ask anyone who has lost the use of their hands what they miss and they rarely say 'dexterity.' They say feeding themselves.

people: NICE's diagnostics advisory committee, with patient and clinical experts; the four permitted products are Rayvolve (AZmed), TechCare Alert, BoneView (Gleamer) and RBfracture (Radiobotics)
title: England's health watchdog let four fracture-spotting AI programmes into the NHS, on condition they keep proving themselves
hook: A broken bone missed in a busy emergency department is one of the most common mistakes in medicine.
body: When you arrive at urgent care with a wrist that might be broken, the X-ray is often read on the spot by an emergency doctor or a nurse practitioner rather than by a radiologist. The specialist report can take hours or days. So fractures get missed. The patient goes home in a bandage, the bone shifts, and what would have been a cast turns into surgery.

On 14 January 2025 NICE, the body that judges which technologies the NHS in England should use, published its verdict on five AI programmes that mark up suspected fractures on X-rays. Four were allowed into the NHS: Rayvolve and TechCare Alert for patients of any age, BoneView and RBfracture for patients aged two and over. The fifth, qMSK, was confined to research, because the reviewers could not find a single study comparing X-ray reading with and without it.

Sixteen studies met the review's criteria. In the study NICE leaned on most heavily for BoneView, emergency physicians' sensitivity rose from 61% to 74% with the software. Sensitivity here means the share of X-rays that genuinely did show a fracture and were correctly identified, so roughly four in ten real fractures were being missed unassisted, and closer to two and a half in ten with help. Other products showed similar movement: 74% to 83% for RBfracture, 79% to 94% for Rayvolve. Just as important, NICE found no study in which specificity dropped, meaning the extra fractures did not appear to come at the price of raising false alarms on healthy bones.

What NICE authorised is narrow and conditional, and worth stating plainly. This is an early value assessment, which permits use only while the companies actively gather real-world evidence, only alongside a human reading the same X-ray, and only once a product has passed NHS England's Digital Technology Assessment Criteria. UK radiation rules already require a trained person to evaluate an X-ray, so the software cannot legally read alone. The companies must report to NICE every year, and submit evidence after two years, when NICE will decide whether any of this becomes routine. NICE states it may withdraw the guidance if the conditions are not met.

stat.l: share of genuinely fractured X-rays that emergency physicians correctly spotted, before and after AI help, in the study NICE relied on most

why: Missed fractures are among the most common diagnostic errors in emergency medicine, and the people reading those X-rays are usually not radiologists. The mechanism is also worth noting: rather than a simple yes or no, the regulator said yes provisionally, named the exact products, named the one that failed, and made continued permission depend on evidence actually turning up.
caveat: NICE's own committee was blunt about how thin the evidence is. Most of the 16 studies were retrospective case-control studies. None was done in a UK urgent care setting. In many, the readers were radiologists rather than the emergency staff who would actually use the software, and they judged X-rays in isolation without the patient or their history in front of them, so their unassisted scores were probably worse than in real practice. NICE said this "could overestimate" the benefit of the AI. A clinical expert flagged that some studies had folded the AI's own output into the reference standard used to grade it, which is circular. Only two studies reported accuracy in children, and there is very little evidence for children under two. Nothing here demonstrates that patients ended up healthier. That is precisely what the two-year evidence period is meant to establish, and NICE has not yet said it can be adopted routinely.

people: Prof. Zuojun Xu, Peking Union Medical College Hospital; Insilico Medicine
title: The first drug where AI chose the target AND drew the molecule is now in final trials
hook: Untreated, this lung disease kills in two to four years. Patients on the AI drug gained lung capacity.
body: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis scars the lungs until breathing fails. Untreated, patients typically live two to four years after diagnosis.

Insilico Medicine used AI twice over: once to pick a brand-new target protein called TNIK — a biological hypothesis no human had pursued — and again to design the molecule that hits it. In a 71-patient trial in China, patients on the highest dose gained 98.4 mL of lung capacity over 12 weeks. The placebo group lost 20.3 mL. Nature Medicine published the results in 2025.

On 7 July 2026, the Phase 3 trial began: 320 patients across 47 centres, the trial that decides approval. For years the objection was that AI could only speed up chemistry humans had already imagined. This molecule's target and structure both came from machines.

stat.l: lung capacity gained in 12 weeks — while the placebo group lost 20.3 mL

why: The first fully AI-originated medicine to reach the trial that decides whether patients can have it. The proof-of-concept era is ending.
caveat: No AI-designed drug has full regulatory approval anywhere yet. The Phase 2 trial was small (71 patients), China-only, and primarily a safety study; some patients dropped out due to liver effects and diarrhea.

people: Ceribell, Inc.; Prof. Geraldine Boylan and Dr. Andreea Pavel, University College Cork (the ANSeR trial)
title: A newborn having a seizure often looks completely calm. Software now catches them down to 25 weeks.
hook: No twitching, no crying, nothing to see. The only evidence is in the brainwaves.
body: Seizures are common in sick newborns and they are dangerous, because a brain seizing for a long time gets damaged. The cruel part is that most newborn seizures are invisible. In an adult you would see convulsions. In a newborn there is often nothing at all — the baby lies there looking settled while the storm happens inside.

The only way to see it is an EEG, a set of electrodes reading brainwaves. But newborn EEG is one of the hardest things in the whole field to read, the squiggles look nothing like an adult's, and very few hospitals have someone who can read it at three in the morning. So a machine that reads it instead is not competing with an expert. It is competing with nobody being there.

In November 2025 the US Food and Drug Administration cleared software to do exactly this, and the age range is the striking part: preterm babies from 25 weeks, which is around the edge of survival, right through to infants under one. Three specialist paediatric neurologists set the right answers, and they were fully blinded. The test data had never been used to train the model. Across 713 babies it caught 91% of the seizure episodes, at about one false alarm every five hours.

Now the honest half. In 2020 an Irish-led team ran a proper randomised trial of a different newborn seizure AI across eight hospitals. Giving clinicians the algorithm did not help them identify which babies were having seizures — on that measure it was slightly worse, 81% against 89%. What it did improve was catching the hours in which seizures were happening: 66% against 45%. The tool was better at finding seizure time than at finding seizure patients, and the trial changed no treatment decisions.

stat.l: how premature a baby can be and still have this software watch their brainwaves for seizures

why: Newborn seizures are both common and largely invisible, and the expertise to read a newborn EEG is scarce everywhere and absent overnight in most hospitals. This is the kind of gap where software does not replace a specialist so much as stand in for an empty chair.
caveat: Nobody has shown a single baby did better because of this. It is a validation result — the FDA's own instructions say the software 'does not provide any diagnostic conclusion.' The marketing says real time; the FDA-cleared label says delays of up to several minutes can occur between a seizure starting and the alert appearing. The 91% also is not what it sounds like: it counts seizure episodes that were already frequent enough to cross a clinical threshold, not every brief isolated seizure, and the highest-burden group rested on only 34 episodes. The company's 'first and only' claim needs care too — a rival product has had a cleared newborn indication since December 2022, though only for term babies and with no public performance figures at all. And the randomised trial described above is the only trial of its kind on this class of tool, part-funded by an EEG manufacturer, and its result on the main measure was unflattering. Worth holding both facts at once: the technical validation here is unusually clean, and the clinical benefit is unproven.

people: Paul Conyngham; UNSW RNA Institute; University of Queensland
title: An engineer with no medical training got a cancer vaccine designed, approved and made
hook: Four AIs, a hundred-page ethics application, and a dog called Rosie.
body: Paul Conyngham is an engineer with no medical or biology training. His rescue dog Rosie had a mast-cell cancer that had been dismissed for close to a year as warts and then a rash, by which point she had a tumour the size of a tennis ball.

So he set out to build her a personalised mRNA vaccine. ChatGPT mapped the plan and pointed him to a genome sequencing centre. Gemini did much of the analysis. AlphaFold modelled her mutated c-KIT protein. Grok produced the final vaccine construct. UNSW's RNA Institute synthesised the mRNA in under two months, and a veterinary pathologist at the University of Queensland shepherded a hundred-page ethics application he wrote in two-hour sessions after work over three months.

Rosie's largest tumour shrank by around three quarters within a month. But she was also given a checkpoint inhibitor and chemotherapy drugs at the same time, and those are the more probable explanation. A Stanford-trained chemical biologist reviewing the case said there is no evidence the AI work did anything. Conyngham does not claim a cure.

stat.l: used by one engineer with no medical training to get a vaccine designed and made

why: The remarkable part is not the outcome, it is the access: the design, approval and manufacture of a personalised mRNA therapy is now within reach of one determined person's evenings.
caveat: This is not evidence that the vaccine worked. Rosie received a PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor and chemotherapy alongside it, so the tumour response cannot be attributed to the AI-designed vaccine — and an independent scientist says there is zero evidence it did anything. Nothing here is peer-reviewed, some of her tumours did not respond, and sources disagree on the treatment dates. We include it as a story about who can now attempt this, not about what it achieved.

place: Memphis, Tennessee, with Heidelberg and Vienna
people: Kyle Smith, Katie Han, Tom Fischer and Paul Northcott at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, with the Hopp Children's Cancer Center in Heidelberg and the Medical University of Vienna
title: A neural network named a child's brain tumour type from half a nanogram of DNA floating in spinal fluid
hook: The tumour is in the brain. The answer was in the fluid around it.
body: Treating a child's brain tumour depends on knowing exactly which tumour it is. Two growths that look the same on a scan can need different chemotherapy, different radiation and carry completely different odds. Getting that answer normally means getting a piece of the tumour. For growths sitting deep in the brain or in the brainstem, that can mean dangerous surgery, and sometimes surgery nobody is willing to do.

Tumours shed DNA. Some of it drifts into cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid around the brain and spine, which is drawn with a needle in the lower back. Children with brain tumours often have this done anyway, to check whether the cancer has spread. The problem is how little DNA is in there. Fractions of a nanogram, which is a billionth of a gram.

A team led by Paul Northcott at St. Jude, with groups in Heidelberg, Vienna, Tampere, Amsterdam and Kiel, built a deep neural network called M-PACT. It ignores mutations. Instead it reads DNA methylation, the chemical tags that mark which genes a cell has switched on and off, and which differ sharply from one tumour type to another. It was trained on 5,014 methylation profiles covering roughly 100 kinds of central nervous system tumour, plus blood and immune cells so it can separate tumour signal from background noise. Given real spinal fluid from 79 children with embryonal brain tumours, the family that includes medulloblastoma and ATRT, it named the correct tumour type 92% of the time, working from a median of half a nanogram of DNA. On a separate set of 58 samples from 48 children it was right 88% of the time.

The paper also shows it doing things a one-off tissue biopsy cannot. Because the fluid can be sampled again, the same test can track whether a tumour is responding during treatment. And it can tell a relapse of the original cancer apart from a brand new second tumour, which is a distinction that changes what doctors do next.

stat.l: of 79 children's spinal-fluid samples, how often the network named the correct brain tumour type

why: A lumbar puncture is not nothing, but it is not brain surgery. If this holds up, some children could get a precise diagnosis, and repeated checks during treatment, without anyone opening the skull.
caveat: This is a validation study, not clinical care. The authors write that validation in prospective clinical trials is warranted before it guides decisions. The headline accuracy numbers cover embryonal tumours specifically, not all childhood brain tumours; other types are shown but on smaller numbers. The method needs a sample where roughly 5 to 10% of the DNA came from the tumour, so it fails on tumours that shed little. It cannot see gene-level mutations, which some treatment choices depend on. The authors call their own intraoperative spinal-fluid numbers modest. No child's treatment has yet been changed by it in a trial.

people: Brent Seales, Nat Friedman, Luke Farritor, Youssef Nader, Julian Schilliger, Marcel Roth, Micha Nowak
title: A scroll buried by Vesuvius in AD 79 has been read — without opening it
hook: Every attempt to unroll them for 250 years destroyed them. AI read one from the inside.
body: The eruption that buried Pompeii also carbonized a library of about 800 papyrus scrolls at Herculaneum — the only library from the ancient world that survived in place. They're too fragile to open; every attempt for 250 years ended in fragments.

So the Vesuvius Challenge offered prize money to anyone who could read them from CT scans, using AI to detect ink invisible to the human eye. In 2023 a college student, Luke Farritor, found the first word: 'purple.' In 2024 his team read 15 columns and won $700,000. In May 2025 came the first title recovered from a sealed scroll — 'On Vices' by the philosopher Philodemus. And in 2026, the landmark: scroll PHerc. 1667 became the first Herculaneum scroll ever read from beginning to end.
Two thousand years of silence, ended by a neural network and a few thousand obsessed volunteers.

stat.l: the scrolls sat unreadable — until AI read one end to end in 2026

why: Hundreds more scrolls — possibly lost works of Greek and Latin literature — are now readable in principle. AI just handed humanity a key to its own past.

people: The European Medicines Agency's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) and its Scientific Advice Working Party; PathAI of Boston, which built the tool
title: Europe's medicines regulator agreed that an AI's reading of liver biopsies counts as valid evidence in drug trials
hook: Three pathologists look at the same sliver of liver and often disagree. That disagreement has been quietly wrecking drug trials.
body: MASH is a liver disease where fat builds up, the liver becomes inflamed, and scar tissue spreads. To test a drug against it, doctors take a needle biopsy and a pathologist scores what they see under the microscope: how much fat, how much inflammation, how much swelling of liver cells, how much scarring. Those scores decide who gets into the trial and whether the drug worked. The problem is that the scoring is a judgement call. Pathologists disagree with each other, and with their own earlier readings. When the measuring stick wobbles, a drug that works can look like a drug that failed.

On 27 February 2025 the EMA's human medicines committee adopted a qualification opinion on a tool called AIM-NASH. The tool is a stack of neural networks: one set marks up the features on the scanned slide pixel by pixel, another turns those maps into scores. A qualification opinion is the regulator agreeing in advance that data produced this way is scientifically sound enough to support an application to license a medicine. It is not approval of a medicine, and it is not approval of a medical device.

The evidence behind it is unusually well documented, because EMA published all 71 pages of its reasoning. The main study used 1,501 biopsy cases drawn from three real drug trials, including the phase 3 REGENERATE trial of obeticholic acid and a phase 2 semaglutide study. Ground truth for each case was set by a panel of two expert liver pathologists, with a third breaking ties. Eight pathologists then scored slides the ordinary way, at least three reads per case, while six other pathologists scored them with the AI's suggestions in front of them. Measured by how closely each matched the expert panel, the AI-assisted readings were clearly better for two features: inflammation scored 0.42 against 0.30, and cell swelling 0.56 against 0.41, on a scale where 1.0 is perfect agreement. The tool was also consistent with itself, giving the same answer on 93% to 96% of slides rescanned on three different days.

EMA was equally clear about the limits. A qualified pathologist must review every output and accept or reject each score, and EMA wrote that the tool "is not a substitute". The model is frozen: retrain it substantially and the qualification may not hold. It is tied to one specific brand of slide scanner. And EMA noted its opinion does not override Europe's medical device rules or the AI Act. Notably, Europe got there first. The US FDA qualified the same tool on 8 December 2025, more than nine months later.

stat.l: how closely pathologists matched an expert panel when scoring liver inflammation, with the AI's help versus without it

why: Liver drug trials have partly been failing because the ruler used to measure success bends. A regulator accepting an AI-steadied measurement means fewer wasted trials and fewer patients enrolled in studies that could never have produced a clear answer. It is also the first time EMA accepted data generated with an AI's help as valid support for licensing a medicine.
caveat: Even with the AI, agreement is far from perfect: 0.42 on a scale to 1.0 still means a great deal of residual disagreement between readers. On two of the four features the AI added nothing at all, and EMA said so bluntly, writing that there was "literally no net gain" for fat and scarring, where the scores were 0.677 versus 0.674 and 0.653 versus 0.645. The test set barely contained mild disease, with under 1% of cases having no scarring and under 1% no inflammation, so performance at the early end of the disease is largely untested. When the same slides were rescanned at three different sites, agreement dropped to between 85% and 91%, and was worst for early-stage scarring. Most importantly, this is qualified only for running clinical trials. It is not cleared to diagnose a patient in a clinic, and it is not a licence to sell the software as a medical device.
