place: Osmo, Google Research and Monell Chemical Senses Center
people: Alex Wiltschko, Osmo
title: AI taught computers to smell — then teleported the scent of a plum
hook: Colour needs three dimensions. Smell needed about 300.
body: Sight and sound were digitised decades ago. Smell was not, because it has no simple axes: colour needs three dimensions, and the map these researchers built to organise odour needs 256.

Their model predicts how a molecule will smell from its structure alone. In a prospective test on 400 odorants it had never seen, published in Science in 2023, it matched a trained human sensory panel better than the median panellist did — outperforming that median on 53% of the molecules in the final validation set.

Then things got stranger. They captured a fresh summer plum on a mass spectrometer, turned it into data, and had a formulation robot reprint it — releasing 100 numbered vials of 'Plum 1.0'. The same odour maps, applied to roughly 19,000 digitised historical repellency measurements, produced more than ten candidate molecules that repel mosquitoes as well as or better than the most widely used repellents. And at StockX, a probe in a shoebox thumbhole distinguishes a real sneaker from a fake in about 20 seconds.

stat.l: unseen odorants where the AI beat the median trained human nose

why: A whole human sense became computable. Mosquito-borne disease kills hundreds of thousands of people a year, and repellents are now searchable rather than stumbled upon.

sources.name: Science (Aug 2023) — 'A Principal Odor Map Unifies Diverse Tasks in Olfactory Perception' (full text via PMC)

caveat: Two peer-reviewed results here (the odour map in Science, the repellent screen in Chemical Senses); the plum reprint and the sneaker authentication are company demonstrations with no published accuracy data. 'Better than the median panellist' is an aggregate — it won on 53% of molecules, not all of them. The repellents are candidate molecules, not products.

place: Royal Berkshire Hospital, Reading — and 26 NHS sites across England
people: Dr. Kiruba Nagaratnam; Prof. David Hargroves, NHS national clinical director for stroke
title: Stroke patients walking out independent tripled after AI started reading the brain scans
hook: In a stroke, two million brain cells die every minute. The AI reads the scan in about one.
body: In a stroke, roughly two million brain cells die every minute. The decisions that save someone — is there a clot, can it be removed, should this patient be moved to a specialist centre — used to take up to an hour.

The e-Stroke AI, from an Oxford spinout, reads the brain scan in about a minute and pings every relevant doctor's phone at once. At Royal Berkshire Hospital, the share of stroke patients recovering to functional independence — able to live their own life afterwards — tripled from 16% to 48%.

A UK government-commissioned evaluation across 26 hospitals and more than 83,000 patients found AI sites more than doubled their rate of clot-removal procedures and cut hospital-transfer delays by 49 minutes. In September 2025 the NHS's own stroke director called it revolutionizing.

stat.l: stroke patients recovering to functional independence at Royal Berkshire Hospital

why: Stroke is a race against a clock nobody can pause. AI didn't replace the doctors — it stopped them losing the race to paperwork and phone calls.
caveat: The tripling figure is one hospital's before-and-after comparison, not a randomized trial. The 26-hospital evaluation is the broader evidence.

place: Stanford Center for Inherited Cardiovascular Disease, California
people: Stanford University and Google (AMIE)
title: AI halved serious clinical errors in a randomised cardiology trial
hook: Not exam questions — real ECGs, echoes, cardiac MRIs and genetic results.
body: Nine general cardiologists at Stanford assessed 107 consecutive real patients referred for suspected inherited heart muscle disease. Each patient was assessed twice, by two different cardiologists — one randomly assigned an AI assistant, one working alone. Crucially they were reading actual clinical material: ECGs, echocardiograms, Holter monitors, exercise tests, cardiac MRI, genomics.

Blinded subspecialists then judged the written assessments without knowing which was which. They preferred the AI-assisted version 46.7% of the time against 32.7% for the unaided cardiologist, with 20.6% ties. Clinically significant errors nearly halved, from 24.3% to 13.1%. Missing content fell from 37.4% to 17.8%.

The system was not a bespoke cardiology model. It was Gemini with no domain-specific fine-tuning, adapted to the subspecialty using web search and self-critique — which makes the result easier to reproduce elsewhere, not harder.

stat.l: rate of clinically significant errors, with AI assistance

why: Subspecialist judgment is rationed by geography. This is a way of putting some of it in the room with a general cardiologist.

caveat: The outcome is subspecialist preference and rated errors on written assessments — not what happened to patients. These were referral-enriched cases at a specialist centre, not routine cardiology. And Google co-authored the study of its own system.

people: Mike Stopper, Armand Latreille and Brian Rocco at Hadrian; Oren Cass and Bruno V. Manno of American Compass; the US Department of Labor Office of Apprenticeship; the IAM/Boeing Joint Apprenticeship Committee
title: A machining factory in Los Angeles puts people with no factory background on the production floor after 30 days of training
hook: The traditional route into this job takes about four years. Mike Stopper has 30 days.
body: Mike Stopper used to teach marksmanship to recruits in the US Marine Corps. He now runs training at Hadrian, a factory in Los Angeles that machines precision metal parts for rockets and aircraft. His job is to take people who have mostly never worked in a factory and get them onto the production floor in 30 days. In 2025 the company hired 45 technicians out of 893 applicants. Everyone starts between $18 and $20 an hour, whatever they did before. One technician, Brian Rocco, came from construction.

The normal route into this work is an apprenticeship, and the real numbers are on the public record. US Department of Labor national guidelines set a machinist apprenticeship at four years and 8,000 hours of on-the-job learning. The registered machinist apprenticeship run jointly by Boeing and the machinists' union in Washington State is 7,360 hours, rising to 8,000 for programmes approved in 2026. So the honest comparison is 30 days against roughly three and a half to four years. You will often see this described as replacing a ten-year apprenticeship. No registered American programme is that long, and repeating the ten-year figure makes a real achievement look like a tall tale.

What buys the short version is that the factory does not need each worker to be a full journeyman machinist. Hadrian's software, called Opus, reads the engineering drawings, including old hand-drawn ones, and generates the machining and inspection steps. Valerie Insinna reported that capability for Breaking Defense in 2024. A journeyman machinist plans the job, writes the program and designs the fixturing. At Hadrian the software has already done much of that, so the person on the floor runs cells that are largely set up for them.

The most interesting thing about the evidence is what it does not say. Oren Cass and Bruno V. Manno documented Hadrian's training programme for American Compass in March 2026, interviewing staff on the record, and their account never mentions the software once. What it describes is eleven full-time trainers, half of them former teachers and several from the military and fast food; new hires rotating through every station in the factory; and classroom sessions on reading blueprints and measuring. Armand Latreille, a senior director, says the gap he sees in new hires is not machining ability but their understanding of a workplace as somewhere you learn. Stopper says he cares more about soft skills, because "I know we can teach you to be an effective operator." On the published evidence, the 30 days is bought at least as much by a serious training department as by artificial intelligence.

stat.l: training before a new Hadrian technician moves onto a production team, against the 7,360 to 8,000 hours set for a registered US machinist apprenticeship

why: Rebuilding industrial capacity is usually said to be limited by a shortage of skilled tradespeople who take years to train. If software can absorb enough of the craft knowledge, the binding constraint shifts to buildings and machines, and factory work reopens to people without a trade background.
caveat: Almost everything here traces back to Hadrian. The 30-day figure and the training programme are documented independently by American Compass, a think tank, with named employees on the record, but that account is still built from interviews inside the company, and no outside body has audited what a 30-day technician can actually do unsupervised. The often-quoted claim that roughly 90% of Hadrian's staff had never set foot in a machine shop is the company's own number; the independent case study says only that many hires arrive with little or no prior experience. The 30 days and the four-year apprenticeship are also not like-for-like, because a qualified machinist is trained to plan, program and set up jobs that Hadrian's software handles centrally. A second widely repeated claim did not survive checking at all: that Hadrian's machines cut metal 79-80% of the time against an industry norm of 20-30%. Hadrian publishes no such percentage, the Breaking Defense account offers only a company assertion of four times the uptime with no baseline given, and the main published benchmark for the trade, Modern Machine Shop's Top Shops survey of 277 shops, put median self-reported spindle utilisation at 75% for leading shops and 65% for the rest. That 20-30% baseline should not be repeated.

place: 150+ countries — Bangladesh, India, Brazil, most of Africa
title: Two billion people now get flood warnings up to seven days early, free
hook: Most flood deaths happen where there are no river gauges and no warning system at all.
body: Most flood deaths happen in places with no river gauges, no models and no warning system. The forecasting infrastructure rich countries take for granted simply doesn't exist there.

Google trained an AI on decades of weather and river data so it can forecast floods even on rivers that have never been instrumented — inferring what the water will do without a single sensor in it. Flood Hub now covers more than 150 countries and 2 billion people, sending free warnings up to seven days ahead through Search, Maps and Android alerts.

The science was published in Nature in 2024: the AI matched or beat the best Western forecasting systems, five days further out, in basins with no gauges. A poor farmer in Bangladesh now gets flood warnings roughly as good as a homeowner in Germany, for free, on a cheap phone.

stat.l: people covered by free AI flood forecasts, up to 7 days ahead

why: Early warning is the cheapest way to save lives in a disaster. This closed a gap between rich and poor countries that had stood for a century.
caveat: Coverage means forecasts are available, not that every person receives or acts on an alert. Accuracy varies by river basin.

place: Los Angeles, USA and Gronau, Germany
people: Dani Kiyasseh and Anima Anandkumar at Caltech, Andrew J. Hung and Runzhuo Ma at the University of Southern California, Christian Wagner at St Antonius-Hospital in Gronau, Germany, and Brian Miles at Houston Methodist Hospital
title: An AI graded surgeons' hands from operating-room video, and the grade lined up with whether patients regained bladder control
hook: Same operation, same hospital, different surgeon. Some patients stay dry and some do not.
body: Robot-assisted prostate removal leaves some men incontinent for months afterwards. Surgeons have long suspected the difference lies in the hands, especially during one step, sewing the bladder back onto the urethra. Nobody could measure that at scale, because measuring surgical skill meant another surgeon sitting down and watching the video. Dani Kiyasseh, working with Andrew Hung at the University of Southern California and Anima Anandkumar at Caltech, built a system called SAIS that watches the video itself.

SAIS is a vision transformer, the same family of model behind modern image AI. It takes the raw surgical video plus the frame-to-frame motion, and grades two specific things: how the surgeon handles the needle, and how the surgeon drives it through tissue. It was tested on video from three hospitals on two continents, including St Antonius-Hospital in Gronau, Germany and Houston Methodist in Texas. At USC and at Gronau it separated high-skill from low-skill activity with area-under-the-curve scores of 0.82 to 0.88. An AUC of 0.5 is a coin flip and 1.0 is perfect.

The part that matters is the link to patients. When SAIS graded a piece of needle driving as high skill, that patient was 1.31 times more likely to recover urinary continence, confidence interval 1.08 to 1.58, p equals 0.005. Earlier work from Hung's lab pointed the same way using instrument motion data rather than video. His team ranked eight surgeons on machine-measured metrics such as tool velocity and wrist articulation. Of the patients operated on by the top four surgeons, 47.5% were continent at three months, against 36.7% of the patients operated on by the other four, p equals 0.034. At six months it was 68.3% against 59.2%, p equals 0.047. A later prospective study across two institutions, 193 operations by 20 surgeons, found those motion metrics still predicted continence after adjusting for each patient's own clinical risk factors.

Feedback is the point of all this. In a small randomised pilot at USC, 42 people with no robotic surgery experience practised suturing on a da Vinci simulator. Half received SAIS-generated feedback between rounds. Their needle handling score rose by 0.30 while the control group's fell by 0.02, p equals 0.018. The gain was largest among the people who started out worst. Needle driving also improved but not significantly, p equals 0.074.

stat.l: higher odds a patient regained bladder control when the AI graded the surgeon's needle driving as high skill

why: If a machine can grade surgical technique from routine video, and the grade predicts how the patient recovers, then surgical skill becomes something you can measure, feed back and improve. That is a lever no drug or device gives you.
caveat: These are associations, not proof that better technique causes better recovery. The 1.31 times figure holds for individual video clips. When the researchers pooled clips up to whole cases the direction held but significance was lost, odds ratio 1.89, confidence interval 0.95 to 3.76, p equals 0.071. The eight-surgeon continence comparison came from a historical cohort at a single centre, and the published abstract does not give the number of patients in each group. The feedback trial was 42 novices on a simulator in a single one-hour session, not surgeons operating on patients, and only one of its two skill measures improved significantly. Everything here is one operation, prostate removal, and one outcome, continence.

people: Jacob Abernethy and Eric Schwartz, University of Michigan
title: Flint switched off the model that found its lead pipes. Nine in ten digs went wrong.
hook: The same city, the same crews. The algorithm off, then on again.
body: After Flint's water was poisoned, the city had to dig up and replace the pipe running to every house. But its records were a box of old index cards, so nobody knew which homes had lead. Every dig at a house that turns out to have safe copper is thousands of dollars not spent removing lead somewhere else.

Two university researchers built a model using each home's age, value, size and location to rank which houses most likely had lead, updating itself after every dig. In 2017 crews followed it: of 8,833 homes inspected, 6,228 had lead pipes — about 70%, and above 80% at its best.

In 2018 the city handed the work to a large contractor and stopped following the model, digging whole blocks instead so that no street felt skipped. Of 10,531 properties explored, just 1,567 had lead. Fifteen percent — worse than choosing houses at random.

A federal court settlement in 2019 required Flint to go back to the model. The hit rate on model-picked homes recovered to 64%. The method has since spread; the US Environmental Protection Agency now publishes guidance on predictive modelling for lead pipe inventories, against a 2037 deadline covering as many as 10 million pipes.

stat.l: digs that actually found lead — with the model guiding crews, versus the year it was ignored

why: Almost no AI story contains its own control group. This one does: the model was switched off and back on in the same city, and the cost of switching it off was measured in wasted digs and lead left in the ground.
caveat: The model was abandoned for a defensible reason, not a stupid one. Residents on skipped streets felt cheated, and the mayor chose visible fairness over efficiency — a real tension worth keeping rather than flattening into 'politicians ignored the science.' Note also the conflicts: the original work had a $150,000 Google grant, and the two researchers went on to found a company selling this service, so its widely quoted claim that Detroit saved $380 million is vendor-reported and unaudited. Accuracy depends on the city doing enough random verification digs to keep the model honest.

people: India's Ministry of Agriculture; researchers at Chicago, Berkeley, Bombay and Bangalore
title: India sent AI monsoon forecasts to 38 million farmers
hook: The monsoon stalled for 20 days. Only the AI saw it coming.
body: For a smallholder farmer the monsoon decides the year, and the decision it forces — when to plant — has to be made in advance. Conventional forecasting gives useful skill about four to five days out and essentially none at three to four weeks.

India's Ministry of Agriculture, working with the Human-Centered Weather Forecasts Initiative, sent weekly AI monsoon forecasts to 38 million farmers across 13 states, with useful lead times up to four weeks. The system blends Google's NeuralGCM and the European centre's AI model with more than a century of Indian rainfall records. At one week ahead it achieves roughly the skill conventional models manage at four to five days, and it keeps positive skill out to four weeks where they have almost none.

It was tested by a strange season. The monsoon reached mainland India on 24 May 2025, eight days early, then stalled for more than two weeks from 29 May. The AI blend called the onset better than the alternatives — and nearly a million more farmers were reached through Odisha's voice-message platform.

stat.l: farmers receiving AI monsoon forecasts, with lead times up to four weeks

why: Forecasting used to be a luxury good priced in supercomputers. This is what happens when it stops being one.

caveat: The technical paper is a preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, and the reach figures come from the implementing organisations. One agricultural scientist argues the messages should pair rainfall with soil-moisture and crop-stage data to be fully useful.

people: Gregory Kestin and colleagues
title: Harvard students learned twice as much from an AI tutor as from a live class
hook: The control group wasn't a boring lecture. It was Harvard's best evidence-based teaching.
body: Harvard physicist Greg Kestin built a custom AI tutor with careful teaching rules baked in — it doesn't just hand over answers, it does what a good tutor does.

In a crossover trial, 194 introductory physics students learned one topic from the AI at home and another in a well-run, actively taught class. On the post-tests, the AI week produced roughly double the learning gains. Students also finished faster — a median of 49 minutes versus a 60-minute class — and reported feeling more engaged and more motivated.
The crucial detail: the comparison group wasn't a dull lecture hall. It was Harvard's best evidence-based active teaching. The AI beat that.

stat.l: the learning gains of an actively taught in-person class — in less time

why: Benjamin Bloom found in the 1980s that one-to-one tutoring lifts average students two standard deviations. It was simply too expensive to give everyone. That constraint is dissolving.
caveat: Two lessons in one elite course, measured with short-term tests. And the tutor was purpose-built with teaching guardrails — this is not a claim about handing kids a raw chatbot.

people: Maj. Michael Caddigan and the 36th Engineer Brigade, III Armored Corps; Stuart Young, DARPA programme manager; Overland AI; Carnegie Robotics
title: Two soldiers two and a half kilometres away sent a driverless twelve ton tracked vehicle to blow a lane through a minefield
hook: Clearing a lane through mines normally puts fifteen to twenty soldiers at the most dangerous spot on a battlefield.
body: Breaching is the job nobody wants. To get vehicles through a minefield you have to drive up to the edge of it, push a trailer of explosive out into the mines, and set it off. The explosive is a line charge: a long rope of explosive fired out by a rocket, which detonates and clears a path wide enough to drive through. Doing it the normal way, Maj. Michael Caddigan of the 36th Engineer Brigade said, takes fifteen to twenty soldiers standing at exactly the place an enemy is aiming at.

On 30 October 2025 at Fort Hood, Texas, DARPA and the 36th Engineer Brigade did it with two. The vehicle was DARPA's RACER Heavy Platform, a Textron M5 Ripsaw chassis turned into a robot by Carnegie Robotics: twelve tons, twenty feet long, tracked, no cab for anybody to sit in. It ran autonomy software from Overland AI, a company that came out of the University of Washington's robot learning lab through this same DARPA programme. The vehicle drove itself over broken ground to the edge of the minefield towing the trailer with the line charge. One soldier ran the drive on a ruggedised laptop. The second commanded the weapon that fired the charge. They were two and a half kilometres back.

The point of the autonomy is not the driving. It is that the driving does not need a person inside, or a person watching a map. DARPA's programme manager, Stuart Young, framed the whole programme around cutting the vehicle's dependence on GPS and on routes planned in advance, so that it still works where satellite signals are jammed and where nobody has surveyed the ground. Getting combat engineers away from the point of breach, Caddigan said, was the real significance of the demonstration.

Two things get told wrong about this event. It was not the closing act of DARPA's RACER programme. DARPA's own account, published on 14 January 2026, puts the programme's eighth and final experiment at the Fort Irwin National Training Center in California, describes a separate November 2025 force-on-force exercise with the 11th Armored Cavalry Regiment, and treats the Fort Hood breach as one demonstration among several. The programme wound up in 2026, not November 2025, with the Army due to take possession of four of the modified M5 vehicles for further testing. Back at Fort Hood in March 2026 the same brigade ran breaching drills with sixteen new technologies, and the soldier at the controls of the RACER vehicle, Spc. James Clubb, was driving it with a laptop and a modified video game controller.

stat.l: Soldiers needed to breach the minefield in this demonstration, against the fifteen to twenty a conventional breach takes.

why: Breaching is among the most lethal tasks in ground combat, and the same machine and the same problem show up in civilian mine clearance. Removing the crew from the vehicle that has to drive into the mines removes the people from the place where the casualties happen.
caveat: This was a demonstration on a US training range against a prepared obstacle, not combat, and the Army's own video record calls the vehicle semi-autonomous. Soldiers still started the run, supervised it and fired the charge; a human commanded the weapon. DARPA describes the autonomy as reducing reliance on GPS and pre-planned routes, not as working with no GPS at all, and we found no official statement that the vehicle ran with no operator link. The frequently quoted figure of a roughly 100 metre cleared lane is the general specification of the M58 line charge rather than a measurement DARPA or the Army published for this event, so we have left it out. One trade report calls this the programme's final experiment, which conflicts with DARPA's own account.

people: Hamsa Bastani, Osbert Bastani, Alp Sungu and colleagues, University of Pennsylvania
title: A tutor with guardrails lifted scores 127%. Plain ChatGPT made them worse.
hook: Same students, same subject, same model underneath. Opposite results.
body: Researchers ran nearly a thousand Turkish high school maths students through three conditions: textbook and notes only, a standard ChatGPT interface, and a purpose-built 'GPT Tutor' engineered to give incremental hints instead of answers.
During practice, standard ChatGPT lifted grades 48% and the guardrailed tutor lifted them 127%. Both looked like triumphs.

Then the AI was taken away for a closed-book exam. The standard-ChatGPT group scored 17% WORSE than students who had never used AI at all — they had been using it as a crutch. The guardrailed tutor largely mitigated that damage. Same underlying model; the entire difference was whether it was designed to make students think or to make them comfortable. Published in PNAS.

stat.l: guardrailed tutor on practice, versus plain ChatGPT on the real exam

why: This is the most important result in AI education, and it cuts both ways: the technology is not the intervention. The design is.

sources.name: PNAS (Jun 2025) — 'Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning'
Knowledge at Wharton — 'Without Guardrails, Generative AI Can Harm Education'

caveat: The guardrails 'largely mitigated' the harm rather than erasing it entirely — PNAS's own wording. One country, one subject, one school system.

place: Feinstein Institutes / Northwell Health, New York
people: Keith Thomas, 48, paralyzed in a 2020 diving accident
title: He felt his sister hold his hand again — three years after doctors said recovery was over
hook: An AI bypass didn't just route around his broken spine. It helped repair it.
body: A dive into a pool in 2020 broke Keith Thomas's neck. He lost the use of his hands and most feeling below his chest. Researchers at the Feinstein Institutes implanted microchips in his brain and used AI to decode his intent to move — routing the signals around the injury to electrodes on his spine and forearms, while touch sensors fed feeling back into his brain.

First he moved his arm by thought. Then came the moment that made headlines: he felt his sister hold his hand, for the first time in years. Over 35 weeks his right arm grew 86% stronger. Sensation returned to skin that had felt nothing. He can now feed himself and drink from a cup.

In July 2026, the trial made the cover of Nature Medicine — with evidence that the gains persist even when the machines are switched off. The bypass isn't just substituting for his spinal cord. It's helping rewire it.

stat.l: increase in arm strength over 35 weeks — years after his recovery had 'plateaued'

why: First evidence that an AI neural bypass can help the body heal itself — not just work around the damage, but push real recovery.

sources.name: Feinstein Institutes / Northwell — Nature Medicine cover (Jul 2026)

people: Julie Verlinden; Onward Medical
title: She was researching euthanasia. Now she's back doing her PhD.
hook: Fainting ten times a day, from a problem nobody talks about.
body: The paralysis story people know is about walking. The one they don't is about blood pressure. After a spinal cord injury the body can lose the ability to regulate it, so standing up means fainting. Julie Verlinden, a Belgian archaeologist injured in a crash in Serbia, was passing out around ten times a day and could spend hours simply trying to get out of bed. She had begun researching Belgium's legal euthanasia process.

An implant placed in Lausanne in 2022 stimulates a precise region of her spinal cord — what the researchers call the haemodynamic hotspot, dense in the neurons that regulate blood pressure. The regulation came back. She has returned to the PhD she was pursuing when she was injured, hand bikes, and travels.

Roughly fourteen patients have received the stimulator in the trial run with NeuroRestore in Lausanne. The same group has begun pairing spinal implants with brain implants, so an intention becomes a spinally executed movement.

stat.l: fainting episodes, before the implant — now back at her PhD

why: The disabilities that ruin lives are often not the famous ones. Fixing the unglamorous problem gave someone their future back.

people: Tiarnan Keenan and Emily Chew, National Eye Institute; Kester Nahen, Notal Vision; the AREDS2 study participants
title: Retina specialists found fewer than half the eyes leaking fluid. The software found 82%.
hook: Then they gave it to 77-year-olds to run on themselves, at home, before breakfast.
body: Wet age-related macular degeneration blinds people by leaking fluid under the retina. It is treatable — an injection into the eye dries it up — but only if someone notices the leak in time. Noticing means a scan called an OCT, and someone qualified reading it.

In a study of 1,127 eyes from the long-running AREDS2 research programme, retina specialists read those scans against a reference standard set by a specialist grading centre. The specialists were right 80% of the time overall. But on the specific question that matters — is there fluid in this eye? — they spotted only 47% of the eyes that had it. The software caught 82%. It was wrong more often in the other direction, flagging fluid that was not there in about 14% of clear eyes, which is the trade every screening tool makes.

Read that 47% carefully, because it is not a story about lazy doctors. These were specialists reading a scan cold, without the patient in front of them and without the clinical history they would normally have. It is a story about a task that punishes human attention: small grey smudges, thousands of near-identical slices, no coffee break.

So they put the machine where the patient is. In May 2024 the US Food and Drug Administration authorised the first at-home retinal OCT, a device a patient sits at and operates alone while the AI measures what it sees. It needed a brand-new regulatory category because nothing like it had legally existed. In the trial, 87% of participants — average age around 77 — set the thing up by themselves, and 96% went on to scan themselves successfully, producing more than 9,000 usable scans in five weeks.

stat.l: share of fluid-filled eyes correctly spotted — retina specialists, then the AI, on the same 1,127 eyes

why: Wet AMD is one of the leading causes of blindness in older people, and the whole game is catching a leak early enough to inject. A patient who can check their own eyes every morning is checking roughly 200 times more often than someone seen quarterly.
caveat: Be careful in both directions. The 47%-versus-82% comparison was done on ordinary clinic scans, not on the home device, and two of the eight authors worked for the company that makes the AI. On the home device itself, the FDA's own words are that it has not been demonstrated whether the benefits 'will result in improved visual outcomes' — and the agency explicitly forbade using it to delay or stretch clinic appointments. The regulator also refused to let the company call what it measures 'retinal fluid', insisting on 'hypo-reflective spaces', because the two are not the same thing. Its measurements get unreliable exactly where they would matter most: for the smallest amounts of fluid, repeat scans of the same eye varied by more than 400%. The only study that actually changed treatment covered 15 patients, was run by the company, and found injection intervals roughly doubled with vision statistically unchanged, not improved. More than two years after approval the company says it is 'not currently widely available', insurers still class the category as experimental, and there is no Medicare coverage decision. The trial that will settle it is a properly randomised 603-patient study run independently by the DRCR Retina Network, and it reports around mid-2027.

place: University of Washington, Seattle & Technical University of Denmark
people: David Baker (Nobel laureate), Timothy Patrick Jenkins, Susana Vazquez Torres
title: AI invented proteins that stop cobra venom from killing
hook: Antivenom is still made by injecting horses with venom. AI designed something better in a handful of tries.
body: Snakebite kills around 100,000 people a year — mostly poor farmers — and permanently disables three times as many. The antivenom we use is made by injecting horses or sheep with venom and harvesting their blood. It's slow, expensive, needs refrigeration, and works poorly against the nerve toxins in cobra venom.

David Baker's lab used deep learning to design brand-new proteins — nothing like them exists in nature — shaped precisely to grab those toxins. They tested only a handful of designs. The good ones saved mice given lethal doses, with 80–100% survival.

The reason this matters beyond the mice: these proteins can be brewed in bacteria instead of harvested from animals. That points to antivenom that is cheap, stable without a fridge, and actually reachable in a rural clinic — which is where nearly all the deaths happen.

stat.l: survival in mice given a lethal dose of cobra nerve toxin

why: The people who die of snakebite die because the treatment is expensive, fragile and hard to deliver. AI-designed proteins fix all three problems at once.
caveat: Mice only — no human trials yet. This is preclinical work.

people: Prof. Matt Might, University of Alabama at Birmingham
title: They asked an AI about nausea. It saved a teenager who had failed 25 drugs.
hook: She weighed 75 pounds. The answer was an alcohol wipe.
body: A 19-year-old woman was vomiting so persistently that she had dropped to 75 pounds. She had already failed more than 25 different drugs.

Prof. Matt Might asked his drug-repurposing AI a deliberately sweeping question: show every treatment ever proposed, in the history of medicine, for nausea. The system surfaced three papers pointing to something almost nobody reaches for — inhaled isopropyl alcohol. Sniffing an alcohol pad.

Within six months she was back to 125 pounds and living a normal life. Might builds these tools for a personal reason: his own son has an ultra-rare disease. His summary of the method is unromantic — comb through enough drugs and you eventually find the side effect you are looking for.

stat.l: drugs that had already failed her, before the AI suggested an alcohol wipe

why: Medicine's own literature is too large for any doctor to hold in mind. Searching it properly is a medical act.

Forbes (Aug 2025) — 'Medicines Reimagined: Repurposing Drugs For New Indications'

caveat: A single case, reported in the press rather than written up as a peer-reviewed case report. We removed a widely-repeated 'it worked instantly' quote because we could not source it.

people: Demis Hassabis, John Jumper
title: Every protein known to science, mapped and given away free
hook: 60 years of lab work solved 200,000 protein structures. AlphaFold predicted 200 million — and charged nothing.
body: Before AlphaFold, working out a single protein's 3D shape could take a PhD student years. In six decades, science had solved about 200,000 of them. AlphaFold predicted the structures of over 200 million — essentially every catalogued protein on Earth — and DeepMind put them all in a free public database with Europe's bioinformatics institute.

As of late 2025, more than 3 million researchers in over 190 countries use it — including over a million in low- and middle-income countries. The method paper has been cited more than 40,000 times, and the database keeps growing: in March 2026 it added millions of predicted protein-pair interactions.
It's scientific infrastructure on the scale of the Human Genome Project — built in a few years, given away free, quietly accelerating thousands of labs working on enzymes, crops, and disease.

stat.l: protein structures, free to every scientist on Earth

why: When you make the hardest step in biology nearly free, everything downstream — drugs, vaccines, materials — speeds up.

people: Ken Ono, University of Virginia; Elliot Glazer, Epoch AI
title: Thirty mathematicians met in secret to stump an AI. They found ten questions.
hook: They used Signal, so no email could leak into the training data.
body: Thirty of the world's leading mathematicians met quietly in Berkeley, communicating only over Signal so that nothing they wrote could contaminate a training set. Their task was to invent problems that would defeat an OpenAI reasoning model, with a $7,500 bounty for each one that held.

Ken Ono of the University of Virginia posed what he considered a solid PhD-level open question in number theory. Over the next ten minutes he watched the model master the relevant literature, solve a simpler toy version first to orient itself, then produce a correct answer — signing off with a flourish: 'No citation necessary because the mystery number was computed by me!'
With thirty experts trying and money on the table, they managed to find ten questions it could not solve.

stat.l: problems thirty leading mathematicians could find that stumped it

why: Mathematicians are the hardest audience for an AI claim, because in their field wrong answers cannot hide. They came away rattled.

sources.name: Scientific American (Jun 2025) — 'Inside the Secret Meeting Where Mathematicians Struggled to Outsmart AI'

caveat: The problems came from Epoch AI's FrontierMath benchmark, and Ken Ono — a judge at the meeting — also consults for Epoch AI. Worth knowing when weighing the result.

people: Graham Lederer, US Geological Survey research geologist and lead for the DARPA collaboration; Erica Briscoe, DARPA Information Innovation Office programme manager; competition teams from Uncharted, Jataware, the University of Southern California's Information Sciences Institute and the University of Minnesota
title: A US critical-mineral assessment that normally takes two years was run start to finish in two and a half days.
hook: Nine out of every ten geological maps America owns are just pictures of paper.
body: The US Geological Survey holds a catalogue of more than 100,000 geologic maps. Only about one in ten exists as a georeferenced digital image, and only half of those are fully digitised. Everything else, roughly 90% of the archive, is a scan of a paper map. A scan is a picture. A computer cannot look up what is in it. So a geologist trying to work out whether a particular valley might hold cobalt has had to open those pictures one at a time and read them.

DARPA and the USGS ran a joint programme to fix that, called CriticalMAAS, short for Critical Mineral Assessments with AI Support. It began in August 2023 and finished in February 2025. It was organised around four jobs: pull the information out of maps, pull mineral occurrences out of old reports and databases, build models that predict where deposits are likely to be, and wrap all of it in software a geologist can drive without writing code. The map problem was set as a public competition. One challenge asked software to find the map inside a scanned image and line it up with real-world coordinates. Another asked it to extract the features named in the map's legend. Uncharted, Jataware and a team from MIT, the University of Arizona and Penn State placed in the first. USC's Information Sciences Institute with the University of Minnesota won the second.

The time figures come from two named officials, and both agencies published them. Graham Lederer, the USGS research geologist who led the collaboration, said a typical mineral resource assessment takes the survey two years start to finish, "and that's just for one deposit type, which may contain one mineral commodity in one area of the country." Erica Briscoe, the DARPA programme manager, said the hackathons "demonstrated the AI tools' ability to reduce the critical mineral assessment workflow to two and half days, start to finish." DARPA and the USGS each carried those exact quotes in their own January 2025 write-ups of the same workshop.

From February 2024 the programme ran about a dozen pilot assessments. National-scale work covered zinc, copper and nickel. Regional work covered Mississippi Valley Type zinc, magmatic cobalt and nickel in the upper Midwest, lithium in old lake beds, tungsten skarn in Alaska, rare earth elements and porphyry copper. One detail worth being precise about, because it is often dropped: neither agency attaches the two-and-a-half-day figure to a single named commodity or a single patch of ground. Both describe it as the workflow, run inside the hackathons.

stat.l: to run a critical-mineral assessment workflow that normally takes the USGS about two years

why: The United States imports most of the minerals its batteries, magnets and chips depend on, and it cannot decide what to dig until it knows what is down there. Reading the map archive it already owns is the cheapest possible place to start.
caveat: The 2.5 days is a hackathon result, a timed demonstration at a collaborative workshop with the tool developers taking part, not the survey's day-to-day speed. DARPA's own account notes the outputs still need USGS scientific review and peer approval before they can be used operationally. The two-year baseline covers one deposit type in one area, not a nationwide survey, and neither agency ties the fast run to a specific commodity. DARPA now lists the programme as complete, so the open question is how much of it the USGS folds into routine practice.

people: Fil Aronshtein, co-founder and CEO of Dirac; Matt Grimm, co-founder and COO of Anduril; Cy Sack, head of business systems at Anduril
title: Anduril chose a startup's software to write the assembly instructions for its factories and reported that a twelve hour job now takes ninety minutes
hook: More than a hundred of Anduril's manufacturing engineers were spending about half their time writing instructions for other people to follow.
body: A work instruction is the document a factory worker actually follows. Fit this bracket here. Torque this bolt to this number. Check this before you move on. Every time an engineer changes the design, someone has to rewrite the document, re-photograph the steps and get it back onto the floor. Anduril, which builds drones and weapons systems, says it had over 100 manufacturing engineers spending roughly half their working time doing exactly that. In January 2026 it named Dirac, a New York company, as its core partner for generating those documents, and put Dirac's software into an Anduril-hosted secure cloud.

Dirac's product is called BuildOS. It reads the 3D CAD model of a product and, in Dirac's description, reasons over the geometry, infers the assembly steps, works out which parts depend on which, and then pushes engineering changes through the production plans automatically. The instructions come out of the model rather than out of a person's head. Anduril reported an average 87.5% cut in the time it takes to author one set of work instructions, from 12 business hours down to 90 minutes.

Every one of those numbers comes from Dirac's own announcement. That matters, so read them as the vendor's claim. What is independently on the record is that two named Anduril executives put their names to the partnership. Matt Grimm, Anduril's co-founder and chief operating officer, said Dirac was the only team that understood the problem from first principles. Cy Sack, who runs business systems there, called work instructions the atomic unit of information in a factory. Neither of them is quoted attesting to the 87.5% figure, and Anduril has published nothing of its own about it.

The reason this is a story about captured knowledge rather than paperwork is the part the software cannot do. Dirac's own writing on the problem lists what lives only in experienced heads: which fastener is easy to cross-thread, which orientation looks correct but causes a fit problem three steps later, which inspection point catches a defect before the part becomes scrap, which tool setting only works when the fixture is slightly worn. A CAD file does not contain any of that. Someone has to type it in once, and then it stops being tribal and starts being written down.

stat.l: Anduril-reported time to write one set of factory work instructions, before and after Dirac's software. Reported by the vendor, not independently checked.

why: Manufacturing knowledge normally leaves when the engineer who holds it leaves. Deriving the routine 3D steps from the model turns the scarce human input into the small residue of hard-won judgement, and forces someone to write that residue down.
caveat: Every figure here comes from Dirac's own press release of 19 January 2026, not from Anduril and not from any independent source. Anduril's COO and head of business systems are quoted endorsing the partnership, but neither states the 87.5% number. 'Initial deployments' is not defined, no baseline methodology is given, and there is no way to check what a 12 hour authoring job looked like. The claim that BuildOS simulates pulling a product apart to derive assembly order does not appear in any source we could verify; Dirac says only that it reasons over geometry, structure and dependencies. Nor could we verify the often repeated claim that it automates 80 to 90% of a document, leaving 10 to 20% as human tribal knowledge.

people: Alex, then 4 years old, and his mother Courtney
title: 17 doctors couldn't explain a boy's pain. His mother typed the notes into ChatGPT.
hook: Three years. Seventeen specialists. No answer. Then a mother did her own search.
body: Alex's pain started when he was four. He chewed on things constantly, dragged his right foot, stopped growing normally, couldn't sit cross-legged. Over three years his mother Courtney took him to 17 doctors — dentists, paediatricians, specialists. Each looked at their piece. Nobody saw the whole.

Exhausted, she typed his symptoms and his MRI notes, line by line, into ChatGPT. It suggested tethered cord syndrome — a hidden spinal condition where the spinal cord is anchored and stretched as a child grows.
A neurosurgeon looked at the same MRI, confirmed the AI was right, and operated. Alex is recovering.

The lesson isn't that AI is a better doctor. It's that no single specialist ever sees the whole picture — and a machine that reads everything at once can spot the pattern that's spread across 17 sets of notes.

stat.l: doctors seen over three years before an AI suggested the right answer

why: Rare diseases take years to diagnose because the information is scattered across specialists who never compare notes. This is the fix — and it put it in a parent's hands.
caveat: This is a single family's account, reported by TODAY.com. The diagnosis itself was confirmed and operated on by a neurosurgeon.

place: 35 GP practices in Ipswich and East Suffolk, England
people: Dr. Bea Bakshi, C the Signs
title: An AI reading GP notes lifted cancer detection from 58.7% to 66%
hook: The signs were already in the record. Nobody had ten minutes to connect them.
body: Cancer hides in general practice records as a scatter of unremarkable things: a symptom here, a blood result there, a risk factor mentioned two years ago. No GP with a ten-minute appointment can hold all of it at once.

C the Signs reads the record and flags the pattern. An independent evaluation led by Anglia Ruskin University looked at 35 GP practices covering almost 420,000 people, comparing the year before the tool arrived with the year after. The cancer detection rate rose from 58.7% to 66.0%.
The company reports the tool is now in around 1,500 GP practices, having run more than 500,000 risk assessments. Its chief executive, Dr. Bea Bakshi, still works as a GP.

stat.l: cancer detection rate across 35 GP practices, before and after

why: Earlier detection is the single biggest lever in cancer survival, and this one required no new test, no new scan and no new appointment.

sources.name: Journal of Clinical Oncology — ASCO 2024 abstract 1560
Health Innovation East — the independent evaluation

caveat: Be precise about what was measured: this result comes from 35 practices, not the full national deployment, and was published as an ASCO conference abstract rather than a full peer-reviewed paper. Practice counts, assessment totals and the company's much larger 'cancers detected' figures are company-reported and stated inconsistently across its own pages.

place: Miami and London; landfall in Jamaica
people: Google DeepMind with the US National Hurricane Center and the UK Met Office
title: An AI called a Category 5 four days early. The hurricane forecasters' own report says it nailed it.
hook: Melissa was still a weak tropical storm when the model said: this hits Jamaica as a monster.
body: In October 2025, Hurricane Melissa was a 40-knot tropical storm south of Jamaica — unremarkable. The US National Hurricane Center, testing Google DeepMind's new cyclone AI, warned roughly four days before landfall that it would rapidly intensify into something catastrophic.

It did. Melissa hit Jamaica at 185 mph, one of the strongest Atlantic landfalls ever recorded. The NHC's official post-storm report states the DeepMind model 'performed very well in forecasting both intensity and rapid intensification.' Jamaica got days, not hours.

Rapid intensification — storms that jump two categories overnight — is the deadliest surprise in weather forecasting. In August 2026 the model was published in Nature: its three-day forecast is as accurate as the best previous models managed at two days. DeepMind calls that roughly a decade of meteorological progress at once. It now runs 1,000 scenarios per storm, and the code and weights have been released publicly.

stat.l: advance warning of a Category 5 landfall, while the storm was still weak

why: In a hurricane, warning time is the whole game — it's how many people board up and get off the coast. And it's now open-source, so poor countries in storm paths get the same forecast as rich ones.
caveat: Human forecasters made the call using many tools; the AI was one input. Melissa still killed dozens of people and caused around $8.8 billion of damage in Jamaica. The win is warning time, not prevention.

sources.name: NOAA National Hurricane Center — official Tropical Cyclone Report

people: Evans and colleagues, with Madagascar's National Malaria Control Programme
title: Village-level malaria forecasts cut drug shortages by more than half
hook: Not a 99% claim. A five-fold improvement, honestly reported, actually used.
body: Malaria drugs run out in the places that need them because nobody knows how many cases a village will have next quarter. Order too few and people go untreated; order too many and the stock expires.

A project called SMALLER built three-month malaria forecasts at village level in Madagascar, developed with the country's own National Malaria Control Programme rather than around it. It was validated the hard way — held out across both space and time, so the model had to predict places and periods it had never seen.

Health workers used the forecasts to order medicine. Under-ordering fell from 33.8% to 14.2%. The researchers report the model beating a null baseline by roughly five times, and they say so plainly rather than reaching for a bigger number.

We include this partly as a corrective. We investigated a widely shared claim that AI had cut malaria forecasting error by 99.7% and rejected it: the figure came from a press release, the underlying item was a one-page conference abstract, and no baseline was ever published. This is the version that holds up.

stat.l: fall in under-ordering of malaria drugs where forecasts were used

why: The useful version of AI in global health almost never arrives with a 99% attached. It arrives as a five-fold improvement that a health worker actually acts on.
caveat: A single country, and the outcome measured is ordering behaviour rather than cases or deaths averted. The honest framing is the project's own: better than a null model by about five times, not by five hundred.

sources.name: PLOS Global Public Health — scoping review: only 2 of 30 malaria early-warning systems reached routine practice

people: Arizona Public Service; Pano AI
title: An AI camera caught a wildfire when it was smaller than a garden
hook: The Brady Fire was under one acre when the software saw the smoke.
body: Arizona Public Service put more than 30 AI-equipped 360-degree cameras across Flagstaff, Payson, Prescott, Sedona, north Phoenix and southeastern Arizona. The software evaluates smoke within about a ten-mile radius, and — the hard part — is trained not to raise the alarm for fog, dust or cloud shadow.

In February 2025 a camera in Prescott National Forest detected the Brady Fire when it was less than one acre. In December 2024 a Payson camera caught the Horton Fire, at a time of year when wildfire risk is normally treated as low.

Early detection is not the same as early containment: the Brady Fire went on to burn around 400 acres and force evacuations. But the imagery also flows to a staffed operations centre and to fire agencies, which is how a smudge on a horizon becomes a dispatched crew.

stat.l: the size of the Brady Fire when AI spotted the smoke

why: Every megafire was once a small fire that nobody saw. The whole game is the first fifteen minutes.

sources.name: Arizona Public Service (Mar 2025) — 'Extra Eyes: APS, Firefighters Team Up with New AI Smoke-Detection Cameras'
T&D World — Portland General's parallel wildfire programme

caveat: These are the utility's and the vendor's own accounts; there is no independent audit of detection performance. And humans remain in the loop — camera imagery is reviewed by analysts, not acted on automatically.

place: Fortune 500 software firm — agents in the Philippines and US
people: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey Raymond
title: AI made the newest workers 34% more productive. The veterans barely changed.
hook: The exact opposite of what everyone fears — and it's in a top economics journal.
body: Economists tracked 5,179 customer-support agents as their company rolled out an AI assistant that suggested responses during live chats. Productivity — problems actually resolved per hour — rose about 14% on average.

The stunner was in the distribution. Novice and low-skilled agents improved around 34%. The most experienced agents barely changed at all. The AI had learned the moves of the best workers and handed them to everyone else.
Customer satisfaction went up. New workers quit less. Published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 2025 — one of the most rigorous journals in the field.

stat.l: productivity gain for the newest, least-skilled workers (vs ~14% average)

why: This is the opposite of the fear. Measured in a real workplace and peer-reviewed at the highest level: AI compressed the gap between rookies and veterans rather than widening it.

people: Geoffrey Hinton's 2016 prediction
title: Hinton said stop training radiologists. It became the best-paid job in medicine.
hook: The most famous AI job prediction ever made, checked against the payroll.
body: In 2016 Geoffrey Hinton — a Nobel laureate and one of the people most responsible for modern AI — said that 'people should stop training radiologists now.' It became the most-quoted prediction of AI-driven job loss ever made.

In 2025, American diagnostic radiology residency programmes offered a record 1,208 positions, a 4% increase on 2024. Radiology was the second-highest-paid medical specialty in the country, at an average income of $520,000 — more than 48% higher than in 2015.

There was a rehearsal for this, and nobody cites it. When hospitals went filmless in the early 2000s, Vancouver General found the switch boosted radiologist productivity 27% for plain radiography and 98% for CT within a year of going digital. No radiologists were laid off. Demand for imaging simply rose to absorb the new capacity.

stat.l: average radiologist income in 2025 — up 48% since 2015

why: This is the single most useful fact in the AI jobs debate: the most confident, most specific, most expert prediction of displacement was tested by reality and was wrong.
caveat: Stephen's notes also credit the Mayo Clinic with a 55% radiology staff increase. We could not verify that figure in the source, so we have left it out rather than repeat it.

sources.name: Works in Progress — 'The algorithm will see you now'

place: University of Miami Health System, Florida
people: Audrey Crews, 39; Noland Arbaugh, 30
title: Paralyzed at 16, she wrote her name again at 39 — with her mind
hook: "I tried writing my name for the first time in 20 years. I'm working on it. Lol."
body: Audrey Crews lost the use of her body at 16. In July 2025 she became the first woman to receive a Neuralink brain implant — a coin-sized chip that reads the movement signals in her motor cortex. Days after surgery, she posted a shaky signature written by thought alone, with a caption that went around the world: 'I tried writing my name for the first time in 20 years. I'm working on it. Lol.'
She's clear-eyed about what it does: it gives her 'telepathy' over a computer, not movement. But control of a computer is control of modern life — writing, drawing, messaging, work.

The first-ever recipient, Noland Arbaugh — paralyzed in a swimming accident — was still using his implant about ten hours a day, 28 months after surgery: playing chess, studying, living. By early 2026, more than 20 people worldwide had the device.

stat.l: since Audrey last wrote her own name

why: Thought-controlled computers have left the lab and become a production pipeline — measured in years of daily use, not one-off demos.

people: Jules Rodriguez and his wife Maria Fernandez
title: ALS took his voice. He does stand-up comedy in it now.
hook: His wife on the cloned voice versus the robotic one: "like night and day."
body: Jules Rodriguez was diagnosed with ALS in 2020. In October 2024 a tracheostomy saved his life and ended his ability to speak. He and his wife Maria Fernandez fed old recordings into ElevenLabs' voice cloning tool and generated a copy of the voice he used to have.

He types with an eye-tracking device and speaks in it — and he has performed stand-up comedy sets on stage with it. Comedy is the hardest possible test of a synthetic voice: timing, emphasis, the deadpan pause. Fernandez says the difference between the clone and the old robotic synthesiser is 'like night and day.'

More than a thousand people with speech difficulties have used the tool since it was made free to them. A speech therapist working with motor neurone disease patients put it plainly: 'This is genuinely AI for good.'

stat.l: people with speech loss using free AI voice cloning

why: Restoring speech is not just about being understood. It is about being funny, being sarcastic, being recognisably yourself.

sources.name: MIT Technology Review (Feb 2025) — 'Motor neuron diseases took their voices. AI is bringing them back.'

caveat: The thousand-plus user figure is ElevenLabs' own, reported by MIT Technology Review rather than independently audited.

people: Moderna and Merck research teams
title: A cancer vaccine built fresh for each patient — still working five years on
hook: Your tumour's mutations, ranked by algorithm, turned into a shot made only for you.
body: After melanoma surgery, doctors sequenced each patient's tumour. Software then ranked that individual's specific mutations and selected up to 34 of them to teach the immune system to hunt — and a custom mRNA shot was manufactured for that one person.

Combined with the immunotherapy Keytruda, it beat Keytruda alone. In June 2026, five-year results were presented at the world's biggest cancer conference: a 49% lower risk of the cancer returning or the patient dying, and a 59% lower risk of it spreading to distant organs.

Every dose is different, because every tumour is different. Picking the right targets from thousands of mutations is a computing problem no human could do by hand — Merck's own language is that the targets are 'algorithmically derived.'

stat.l: lower risk of the cancer returning or the patient dying, at five years

why: Personalised cancer vaccines were a beautiful theory until the algorithms got good enough to pick targets. Now they have five-year data.
caveat: This is a mid-stage (Phase 2b) trial of 157 patients. The larger Phase 3 trials are fully enrolled but haven't reported yet.

place: University of Cambridge and DIOSynVax, UK
people: Prof. Jonathan Heeney, University of Cambridge and DIOSynVax
title: A vaccine designed entirely by computer has now been tested in people
hook: Aimed not at one coronavirus, but at the whole family — including the ones that haven't reached us yet.
body: Vaccines are normally built against a virus that is already circulating, which is why a pandemic costs a year while we catch up. Cambridge researchers, with the university spinout DIOSynVax, tried the reverse: they took genetic codes from coronaviruses collected by surveillance programmes worldwide and had computers design a single antigen intended to train the immune system against the entire sarbecovirus family — known variants, and animal viruses that have not yet jumped to humans.

In their own careful words, it is 'the first time that a vaccine whose active component was designed entirely by computer simulations has been tested in humans.' The Phase 1 trial has finished and been published: 39 healthy volunteers aged 18 to 50, given a DNA vaccine through a needle-free jet of fluid.
Heeney's framing of what changes: 'We've converted vaccine development from being reactive to being future proof.'

stat.l: volunteers in the first human trial of a computer-designed vaccine antigen

why: The expensive part of a pandemic is the year spent designing the response. A vaccine aimed at a whole viral family is a way of arriving before the virus does.

sources.name: University of Cambridge (Jun 2026) — 'New universal vaccine technology could protect us from future virus outbreaks'
Journal of Infection (Jun 2026) — the Phase 1 trial

caveat: This is a Phase 1 safety and immune-response study in 39 people. It is not evidence that the vaccine protects anybody, and a Phase 2 is planned rather than running. Reports indicate it produced cross-reactive binding across sarbecoviruses without yet demonstrating broad neutralising protection.

people: Prof. José R. Penadés and team
title: AI proposed in 2 days the superbug theory that took scientists 10 years
hook: The team's answer was unpublished — the AI couldn't have looked it up anywhere.
body: Professor José Penadés' team spent about a decade working out how certain 'pirate' genetic elements help bacteria jump between species — a key clue to how superbugs spread antibiotic resistance. The answer: the elements steal tails from different viruses, letting them infect new hosts.

Crucially, the discovery was still unpublished — it existed nowhere the AI could look it up. When the team gave Google's 'AI co-scientist' the same research question, its top-ranked hypothesis matched their secret answer in two days. It also suggested four other plausible ideas, including one the team had never considered.

The human work — with the AI episode — was peer-reviewed and published in Cell in November 2025. Penadés' verdict: starting from the AI's hypothesis would have saved his team years. The AI didn't do the decade of lab work. It did the part that took the decade of guessing.

stat.l: for AI to reach the hypothesis that took a human team ~10 years

why: The cleanest evidence yet that AI can generate genuinely new scientific ideas — not just summarize old ones.

people: Vahe Tshitoyan, Anubhav Jain, Kristin Persson and Gerbrand Ceder
title: They hid the future from an AI. It predicted the discoveries anyway.
hook: Trained on nothing but the words of 3.3 million abstracts. No chemistry taught.
body: A Berkeley Lab team trained a model on nothing but the text of 3.3 million materials-science abstracts — no structures, no measurements, no physics. Just the language researchers use.

Then they ran the cleanest test available: they retrained it on literature published only up to 2008, and asked it to name promising thermoelectric materials, which turn heat into electricity. Three of its top five picks were compounds that human scientists only established were thermoelectric in the years afterwards. The model could not have known; the knowledge was latent in how chemists wrote about neighbouring materials.

Its top ten present-day candidates, drawn from 7,663 compounds never mentioned anywhere near the word thermoelectric, all scored above the average of known thermoelectrics on computed performance. Published in Nature in 2019 — years before the chatbot era.

stat.l: predictions from a model frozen in 2008 that humans later confirmed

why: Scientific literature holds knowledge nobody has assembled, because nobody can read all of it. This is the proof.

sources.name: Nature (Jul 2019) — 'Unsupervised word embeddings capture latent knowledge from materials science literature'
Berkeley Lab — 'Machine learning algorithms can uncover hidden scientific knowledge'

caveat: Correcting a claim that circulates widely, including in our own first draft: those ten candidates were validated computationally, not in a laboratory, and their computed performance was only slightly above the average of known thermoelectrics. The striking result is the 2008 time-travel test, not a lab sweep.

people: Researchers at Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard, with OpenAI
title: They reopened 376 medical mysteries with an AI. Eighteen children finally got an answer.
hook: Every one of these families had already been told: we don't know what this is.
body: Hundreds of children had been through genetic testing and specialist after specialist with no answer. Their files were closed as unsolved.

In 2026, doctors fed 376 of these dead-end cases — de-identified records and genome data — to an AI research model and asked what had been missed. The AI produced hypotheses. Human physicians then checked, retested, and confirmed.

Eighteen children got a real diagnosis. Ten of them came from a group of 100 with neurodevelopmental disorders. The AI diagnosed nobody by itself; every case was confirmed by clinicians. What it did was reread files nobody had time to reread.
Roughly 300 million people live with a rare disease, and the hunt for a name routinely takes five years or more. Published in NEJM AI in June 2026.

stat.l: children who got a diagnosis after every other route had failed

why: There are answers already sitting in files that no human has time to reread. That's a solvable problem now.
caveat: We could not open a primary source for this one — the journal and press pages block automated access. The figures are consistent across four independent news outlets. Treat as well-reported rather than primary-verified.

people: Dartmouth College researchers
title: The first clinical trial of AI therapy: depression scores fell by half
hook: More than half of US counties have no psychiatrist at all.
body: Therapy chatbots have been oversold for a decade, which is exactly why this one counts: Dartmouth ran an actual randomised trial and published it in NEJM AI. 210 people, half given four weeks with Therabot — trained on curated therapeutic conversations rather than general internet text — and half put on a waitlist.

Therabot users' depression scores fell 51% from their own starting point, with anxiety down 31% and eating-disorder concerns down 19%, measured at eight weeks. Those are within-person changes rather than the gap to the control group, but the improvement was significantly larger than the waitlist group's.
Why scale matters as much as effect size: more than half of American counties do not contain a single psychiatrist. The realistic alternative to an imperfect tool is frequently nothing at all.

stat.l: fall in depression scores from baseline, in the first trial of AI therapy

why: Mental health care fails on supply, not knowledge. Something that helps and scales beats something better that isn't available where you live.
caveat: Read the number carefully: 51% is the change from each user's own baseline, not the margin over the control — and the control was a waitlist, which tends to flatter results. Outcomes were self-reported, the study ran eight weeks, and the lead researcher personally reviewed every participant message for safety, a layer that would not exist in a consumer product. NEJM AI published a critical letter alongside it.

sources.name: NEJM AI (Mar 2025) — 'Randomized Trial of a Generative AI Chatbot for Mental Health Treatment'
Dartmouth (Mar 2025) — 'First Therapy Chatbot Trial Yields Mental Health Benefits'

place: European Molecular Biology Laboratory & University of Copenhagen
title: One AI that predicts your risk across a thousand diseases at once
hook: Trained on 400,000 Britons. Then tested, untouched, on 1.9 million Danes.
body: Almost every risk calculator in medicine does one disease at a time — one for heart attack, another for diabetes. Delphi-2M does more than a thousand at once, from ordinary health-record events plus age, sex and lifestyle, sometimes decades ahead.

It was trained on 402,799 UK Biobank participants. Then the researchers did the hard test: they ran it, unchanged, on 1.93 million people in Denmark — a different country, a different health system, data it had never seen. It still matched or beat the existing single-disease tools.

Because it is generative, it does something other risk models cannot: it can sample plausible future health trajectories from a person's history, like weather forecasts for a life. The team is careful about the timeline — they put clinical use five to ten years away.

stat.l: diseases predicted by a single model, validated across two countries

why: Prevention fails because we only look for what we already suspect. A model that watches every direction at once changes what a check-up can be.
caveat: Not in clinical use — the authors estimate five to ten years away. Average accuracy across all diseases (AUC ~0.76 internally, ~0.67 on the Danish data) is good for a thousand-disease model but varies a lot by condition.

place: Stanford University, California, with Danish collaborators
people: Rahul Thapa, Magnus Ruud Kjaer, Emmanuel Mignot and James Zou
title: One night of sleep, read by AI, carries a warning about 130 diseases
hook: 585,000 hours of overnight recordings. Nobody could read them. Something could.
body: A Stanford team trained a model on more than 585,000 hours of overnight sleep studies from about 65,000 people — full clinical recordings, with wires measuring brain waves, eye movement, muscle activity, heart rhythm and breathing.

Then they asked something nobody had: can a single night say anything about diseases a person has not yet been diagnosed with? They tested it against 1,041 conditions drawn from patients' later medical records. For 130 of them, the model sorted people into higher and lower risk clearly better than chance.

What a score of 0.85 for dementia actually means is worth being precise about. Hand the model two patients and ask which will develop dementia first, and it picks correctly about 85 times in 100. It does not mean 85% of its predictions are right, and it certainly does not mean 85 of every 100 people it flags will get dementia — because dementia is rare, most people it flags never will. Sleep carries a faint signature of illness that doctors were not reading, because no human can hold 585,000 hours of squiggly lines in their head.

stat.l: diseases where one night's sleep predicted risk better than chance, out of 1,041 tested

why: Sleep is one of the few things about the body we already measure all night long, and those recordings have been going into filing cabinets. If the signal survives on cheaper sensors, an ordinary night could become a routine health check.
caveat: Three things the popular version gets wrong. It needs a full in-lab sleep study with scalp electrodes and around 23 sensor channels — not a smartwatch, Oura ring or WHOOP. The model is also fed the patient's age and sex, and age and sex alone already reach about 0.78 for predicting death, so a meaningful part of the headline is the AI knowing how old you are; sleep adds real but modest lift. And 130 is what survived a 1,041-condition screen, so 911 did not clear the bar. Retrospective, in patients already referred to a sleep clinic, with no prospective trial and no clinical use.

title: The money arrived before the flood did — and food insecurity fell from 97% to 7%
hook: Aid normally arrives after everything is lost. An AI forecast let it arrive first.
body: Disaster aid almost always arrives after the water has gone down and everything is already lost. In 2024, the charity GiveDirectly tried the opposite.

They watched Google's AI flood forecasts for one of Nigeria's most flood-prone districts. When the model showed a village would flood, payments triggered automatically: $105, then $210, sent by mobile money to more than 4,600 people — weeks before the water peaked in October.

Families used it to build bamboo rafts to lift their food stores, move children and grandparents to high ground, and stockpile medicine. Afterwards, the charity's surveys found food insecurity among recipients had dropped from 97% to 7%, and weekly incomes had doubled.
The reason it works: before the flood, a dollar buys prevention. After the flood, the same dollar buys replacement. The forecast is what moves the money to the cheap side.

stat.l: share of households facing food insecurity, before vs after pre-flood cash

why: AI forecasting flips the economics of humanitarian aid — money that lands before the disaster protects ten times as much.
caveat: The outcome figures come from GiveDirectly's own post-programme surveys, not an independent randomized trial.

sources.name: GiveDirectly — AI flood forecast cash transfers

people: Beewise
title: An AI has saved 200 million honeybees
hook: US beekeepers lost more than half their colonies in twelve months.
body: Beekeeping is a race against problems you cannot see until the hive has already collapsed. Independent national surveys found American beekeepers lost 55.1% of their managed colonies in the year to April 2024 — more than half, gone.

Beewise houses hives in climate-controlled boxes watched by computer vision. When the software detects disease or distress it dispatches a robotic arm installed at the hives to feed or treat the bees, without pesticides and without waiting for someone to drive out and lift the lid. The company says the approach cuts colony loss by about 70% against conventional hives.
By its own count it had saved more than 200 million bees by the end of 2023, a figure it now puts above 300 million.

stat.l: of US honeybee colonies lost in a single year — the problem this attacks

why: A third of what we eat depends on pollination. This is conservation that works by watching constantly rather than caring intensely.
caveat: The colony-loss figure is independent, from the national Apiary Inspectors of America survey. Every 'bees saved' number is Beewise's own modelling, not a third-party count.

sources.name: Apiary Inspectors of America — 2023-24 US Beekeeping Survey results

people: Substrate's engineering team, the company founded in 2022 by brothers James and Oliver Proud; Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve, built by a team including Matej Balog and Alexander Novikov
title: Google's AlphaEvolve spent a month rewriting a chip startup's simulation code, and the startup says its compute bill fell 97 percent.
hook: The number comes from the company that benefited. Google's own blog will not repeat it.
body: Before a factory prints a layer of a chip, it simulates it. Software models how light lands on the sensitive coating covering the wafer, then works backwards to design a mask that will produce the shape you actually wanted. This is computational lithography, and it is one of the largest compute bills in chipmaking, because the simulations are enormous and they never stop running. Substrate, a San Francisco company founded in 2022 by the brothers James and Oliver Proud, is building an X-ray printing tool meant to compete with ASML's machines, and it lives on those simulations.

Substrate pointed the problem at AlphaEvolve, a Google DeepMind system that writes code, scores each version against a test, keeps what wins and mutates it again. Substrate's own technical post, published in April 2026, gives the sequence plainly. After one week, compute costs halved. After a month of AlphaEvolve "co-designing algorithms with our team," compute costs for the same optimisation were down 97%, memory use was 74% lower, and "runtime speed was improved by 680%."

That last figure has travelled badly. It is widely retold as "6.8 times faster," and read strictly a 680% improvement is 7.8 times, not 6.8. Substrate published a percentage, not a multiple, so the honest version quotes the percentage and stops. It is also worth knowing what Google said. DeepMind's official blog a month later confirms Substrate applied AlphaEvolve to its computational lithography framework and reports "a multi-fold increase in runtime speed." It publishes none of the three numbers.

Substrate also shows electron-microscope images of a chip's metal one layer, the dense wiring level directly above the transistors and the hardest layer in the whole process to print, patterned at a 24 nanometre pitch with a single mask and a single exposure. That is a genuine print rather than a plan. But the credit is worth getting right: Substrate attributes the single-exposure printing to its X-ray tool, not to AlphaEvolve. AlphaEvolve's contribution was making the simulation cheap enough to run. And a pattern in photoresist is not a working chip. Substrate has not manufactured chips. It is aiming for production in 2028.

stat.l: the drop in Substrate's compute cost for the same lithography optimisation, as Substrate itself reports it

why: How good a chip you can design is partly a question of how much simulation you can afford. If an AI agent can cut that cost by an order of magnitude, problems that were priced only for the very largest companies come within reach of small ones.
caveat: Every figure here is Substrate's own, published on Substrate's website with no paper, no peer review and no independent audit. Google DeepMind confirms the collaboration but declines to repeat the numbers, saying only "a multi-fold increase in runtime speed." The commonly quoted "6.8x" is a secondary reading of Substrate's published "680%."
