The single-exposure 24nm metal one print is credited by Substrate to its X-ray hardware rather than to AlphaEvolve, and it is a pattern in resist on silicon viewed under an electron microscope, not a functioning device. Substrate is pre-production and pre-revenue, targeting 2028.

sources.name: Substrate (April 2026) — the company's own technical post and the sole published origin of the 97%, 74% and 680% figures; company-reported, not independently verified
Google DeepMind (May 2026) — official blog confirming Substrate applied AlphaEvolve to computational lithography, reporting only a "multi-fold" runtime gain and no figures
Google DeepMind (May 2025) — the original AlphaEvolve announcement and accompanying white paper explaining how the system searches for algorithms
TechSpot (October 2025) — Skye Jacobs's report on Substrate's $100M round, its particle-accelerator X-ray approach and its 2028 production target

people: Owen Henkel and co-authors; built by Rising Academies
title: A $5 WhatsApp maths tutor gave Ghanaian kids roughly an extra year of learning
hook: No laptops. No broadband. Just WhatsApp on a shared basic phone.
body: Most of the world's students don't have laptops or broadband, which makes most education technology irrelevant to them. Rori is an AI maths tutor that runs on WhatsApp, so it works on cheap phones and weak networks.

In a year-long randomized study, about 1,000 students in grades 3 to 9 used Rori for two 30-minute sessions a week on top of their normal classes. After eight months their maths growth was 0.37 standard deviations ahead of the control schools — a large effect, roughly an extra year of learning.
The marginal cost per student: about $5.

stat.l: marginal cost per student, for roughly an extra year of maths learning

why: A tutor that works over WhatsApp on a shared phone is a realistic path to the students who have been unreachable — not in a decade, now.
caveat: Randomization was at the school level with only 11 schools, and the authors themselves urge caution. This is first-year evidence; a larger trial is underway.

place: U.S. House of Representatives, Washington, D.C.
people: Rep. Jennifer Wexton of Virginia
title: A disease stole a congresswoman's voice. AI returned it to the House floor.
hook: The first AI-voiced speech in the 235-year history of Congress — and she cried tears of joy hearing it.
body: Progressive supranuclear palsy — a rare, Parkinson's-like disease — took Rep. Jennifer Wexton's clear speech within about a year of diagnosis. Text-to-speech apps made her sound like a robot. So ElevenLabs trained an AI on recordings of her old floor speeches and gave her back her own voice.

On July 25, 2024, she became the first person ever to address the U.S. House of Representatives through an AI recreation of her voice. 'It was the most beautiful thing I had ever heard, and I cried tears of joy,' she said.

The same technology is now given away free to people losing their voices to ALS — thousands of licenses through the Bridging Voice program, which can even rebuild a voice from old voicemails after the disease has already taken it.

stat.l: AI-voiced speech in the 235-year history of Congress

why: The most public demonstration possible that a cloned voice isn't a gimmick — it's dignity. And it's being handed out free, at scale.

sources.name: Bridging Voice — free ALS voice program

people: Matt de Jonge, Igor Lovchinsky, Andrew Casper and Cole Morris, Fortell
title: He watched four grandparents lose their hearing. So he built an AI ear.
hook: "This was so incredible that I burst into tears."
body: Hearing aids amplify, which is their problem: in a noisy room they amplify the noise too. People with hearing loss stop going to restaurants and drift out of conversations. Hearing loss is also an established dementia risk factor in the wider medical literature.

Matt de Jonge watched his grandparents retreat into that isolation because their hearing aids failed them. 'I had given up on them,' he said. 'I feel like I have blood on my hands.' His company built a custom chip that runs a neural network to separate speech from noise fast enough that the brain never registers the processing — WIRED reports a design ceiling of about ten milliseconds.

The device launched in December 2025 at $6,800 a pair, on roughly $150 million of funding. Its own submitted studies claim a 9.2 decibel improvement in speech-in-noise against 3.1 for a control device.

stat.l: to separate speech from noise — fast enough that the brain doesn't notice

why: Hearing loss is not just isolating, it is a dementia risk factor. Making conversation possible again in a loud room is a bigger medical intervention than it sounds.
caveat: Fortell's clinical evidence has been submitted for publication but is not yet peer-reviewed, and the latency figure comes from WIRED's reporting rather than a published company specification. The dementia link is from the outside literature — the company has not demonstrated an effect on it.

place: MIT and the Broad Institute, Cambridge, Massachusetts
people: James Collins, Aarti Krishnan, Melis Anahtar
title: AI drew 36 million molecules that never existed. Two of them beat superbugs.
hook: No genuinely new class of antibiotic has reached patients in decades. The pipeline was empty because it isn't profitable.
body: Drug-resistant infections already kill millions of people a year, and the antibiotic pipeline has been close to empty — not because the science is impossible, but because new antibiotics don't make money.

James Collins' MIT lab used generative AI to invent more than 36 million molecules that had never existed, then computationally screened them for the ability to kill bacteria without harming human cells. Two winners emerged: NG1 for drug-resistant gonorrhoea, DN1 for MRSA. Both cleared infections in mice. Both attack bacteria in ways no existing antibiotic does.
That last part is the point. Bacteria have evolved defences against our whole arsenal. These compounds hit targets they've never had to defend.

stat.l: novel molecules designed and screened — none had ever existed before

why: AI makes the search cheap enough to run even when the economics don't justify it. That changes which diseases get medicines at all.
caveat: Both compounds are preclinical — mice and lab dishes, no human trials yet. The lab's earlier famous AI antibiotics, halicin (2020) and abaucin (2023), also have not entered human trials.

people: Sam Rodriques and Andrew White, FutureHouse
title: An AI picked the hypothesis, the experiments and the analysis. Humans held the pipettes.
hook: Ten weeks from building the system to a named drug candidate for a leading cause of blindness.
body: Dry age-related macular degeneration blinds people and has almost nothing to offer them. FutureHouse pointed a multi-agent system called Robin at it, and Robin did something broader than answering a question: it generated the hypotheses, chose which experiments to run, analysed the results and drew the figures in the paper.

It proposed boosting a specific clean-up process in the retina, then identified ripasudil — a drug already approved in Japan for other eye conditions and never previously proposed for dry AMD. In cell assays the effect was large, raising that clean-up activity around sevenfold. Robin then designed the follow-up experiment that flagged a second, novel target, a lipid pump called ABCA1.
Nature published it in May 2026 and describes the approach as semi-autonomous, which is the honest word: every wet-lab experiment was performed by human scientists.

stat.l: an approved Japanese eye drug, newly proposed for a blinding disease by AI

why: Most AI-in-science claims cover one step. This covered hypothesis, experimental design and analysis — the part that usually consumes years of a career.
caveat: Two corrections to how this gets retold. The AI did not run the experiments; humans did. And the widely-quoted '2.5 months' covers building Robin and submitting the paper, not ten weeks of drug discovery. Ripasudil is a preclinical candidate validated in cell assays, not a treatment. One neuroscientist has questioned whether the hypothesis was obvious in hindsight.

sources.name: Nature (May 2026) — 'A multi-agent system for automating scientific discovery'
FutureHouse — 'Demonstrating end-to-end scientific discovery with Robin'
The Scientist — 'An AI-Powered Scientist Proposes a Treatment for Blindness'

people: Google DeepMind Gemini Deep Think team; IMO graders
title: From silver to gold in one year: AI conquered the world's hardest math exam
hook: Math is the one arena where answers can't be faked. A proof is right, or it isn't.
body: The International Mathematical Olympiad is the world championship of high-school mathematics — problems so hard most professional mathematicians can't solve them in the time allowed. In 2024, DeepMind's AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry reached silver-medal standard. In July 2025, an advanced version of Gemini became the first AI officially graded gold by IMO judges: 35 of 42 points, five of six problems solved, in plain natural language, within the same 4.5-hour limit as the students. OpenAI reported the same score on its own grading.

At the 2026 olympiad in Shanghai, AI systems from two Chinese labs were reported to have posted perfect 42/42 scores — a feat matched by just 7 of the 666 human contestants. (Those 2026 results are press-reported; the 2025 gold is IMO-certified.)
Silver to gold to reported perfection, in 36 months.

stat.l: officially graded by IMO judges in 2025 — silver was just one year earlier

why: Mathematical reasoning was supposed to be the human moat. The moat is now a benchmark — and the same reasoning engines are being aimed at real scientific problems.

place: University of Cambridge and University of Manchester
people: Katherine Roper, Ross D. King and colleagues; the robot scientist 'Eve'
title: A robot checked the cancer literature. Less than a third held up.
hook: Nobody ever built a career repeating someone else's experiment. So a machine did it.
body: Science has a replication crisis for a mundane reason: no grant, paper or promotion was ever won by checking somebody else's result. So the checking does not happen.

Researchers pointed a semi-automated robot scientist named Eve at 12,260 breast cancer papers, extracted 74 specific claims about how gene expression changes after drug treatment, and tested them in two cell lines using two independent teams.

43 of the 74 could be repeated under identical conditions. But only 22 — under a third — held up as reproducible when different scientists tried them under merely similar conditions. That is an uncomfortable finding, and it is still a good-news story: a machine did the unglamorous work science's incentives guarantee humans will skip, and turned up two accidental discoveries on the way.

stat.l: cancer-biology claims that proved reproducible when others tried them

why: If AI does nothing else for science than make replication cheap enough to actually happen, it will have addressed the field's deepest structural flaw.

sources.name: Journal of the Royal Society Interface (Apr 2022) — 'Testing the reproducibility and robustness of the cancer biology literature by robot'
University of Cambridge — 'Robot scientist Eve finds that less than one third of scientific results are reproducible'

caveat: We first told this as a replication success. It is closer to the opposite: the researchers' own headline was that less than a third of results were reproducible. The value is that a machine measured it at all.

place: Johns Hopkins and four other hospitals, Maryland and Washington D.C.
people: Prof. Suchi Saria, Johns Hopkins
title: An AI watches for sepsis around the clock. Patients it flagged were 19% less likely to die.
hook: Sepsis kills more hospital patients than almost anything. Every hour of delay raises the odds.
body: Sepsis is the body's runaway response to infection, and it kills more hospital patients than almost anything else. Every hour of delay in treatment raises the risk of death — and the early signs are subtle enough that busy clinicians miss them.

Johns Hopkins built an AI called TREWS that watches every patient's vital signs and lab results continuously. In a study of 590,736 patient visits across five hospitals, published in Nature Medicine, it spotted sepsis a median of nearly six hours before doctors would have. When clinicians confirmed the alert within three hours, patients were 18.7% less likely to die in hospital.
The other number that matters: 89% of doctors actually used it. In a field where alert systems are famous for being ignored into uselessness, that's the harder achievement.

stat.l: lower risk of dying in hospital when the AI's alert was confirmed within 3 hours

why: One of the first AI systems proven to save lives in ordinary hospital care — not in a trial, in the wards. It's now running in dozens of US hospitals.
caveat: Worth knowing the contrast: a different, widely-used commercial sepsis model was found in 2021 to miss most cases while flooding staff with false alarms. TREWS is the one that published prospective outcome data.

people: Samuel Andrade, pharmacist
title: One pharmacist, one Amazonian town, fifty caught errors
hook: He arrives at 8am to hundreds of prescriptions. There is nobody else.
body: Caracaraí is a municipality of 22,000 people in the Brazilian Amazon with one pharmacist, Samuel Andrade. He arrives at eight in the morning to hundreds of prescriptions from free government clinics, and frequently cannot get through them — sometimes losing hours cross-checking drug interaction databases by hand.
In April he started using NoHarm, an open-source assistant trained on thousands of real prescriptions, drug combinations, dosage errors and adverse interactions.

It quadrupled how many prescriptions he can clear, and in the following months it caught more than fifty errors. Fifty prescriptions that would have gone out wrong, in a town with no second pharmacist to notice.

stat.l: prescription errors caught in a town with a single pharmacist

why: Most of the world's healthcare is delivered by someone working alone with too much to do. This is what AI looks like there — not a robot doctor, a second pair of eyes.

sources.name: Rest of World (Jun 2025) — 'In Brazil's Amazon, AI is making healthcare safer'

caveat: Both the fourfold capacity gain and the fifty-plus errors are Samuel Andrade's own account to the reporter — one user's experience, not an audited measurement.

people: Richard Allen, UC Berkeley seismologist
title: 2.5 billion phones became the world's largest earthquake warning network
hook: It failed badly in Turkey in 2023. Google admitted it, rebuilt it, and it worked in Istanbul.
body: Every Android phone has a motion sensor that can feel an earthquake. Google links them together: when thousands of phones shake at once, people farther away get a warning seconds before the shaking reaches them. Seconds are enough to get under a table, stop a train, or halt a surgery.
A 2025 paper in Science reported the system has detected over 18,000 quakes and sent 790 million alerts across 98 countries — most of which had never had any warning system.

Then the honest part. It failed badly in Turkey in 2023, drastically underestimating the magnitude-7.8 quake that killed tens of thousands; only a few hundred top-level alerts went out. Google admitted it after BBC reporting and rebuilt the algorithm, halving its magnitude error. When a 6.2 quake struck Istanbul in April 2025, more than 11 million warnings went out, starting about eight seconds after the shaking began.
Earthquake warning networks used to cost hundreds of millions of dollars, so only rich countries had them.

stat.l: people now covered by earthquake early warning — a tenfold increase in about five years

why: This is what a working technology looks like: it failed publicly, the failure was admitted, it was fixed, and then it delivered. That's more trustworthy than a flawless press release.

people: Jake Loosararian, Gecko Robotics; the US Navy
title: Robots that climb are cutting the Navy's ship-inspection backlog
hook: Somebody used to do this dangling off a fifty-foot boiler wall.
body: Inspecting a ship hull, a power-plant boiler or a mine shaft means sending a person somewhere they should not be — up a fifty-foot vertical wall, into a confined space, often with the facility shut down to make it survivable.

Gecko Robotics builds robots that climb, fly and swim, mapping corrosion and cracks with cameras and sensors. In March 2026 it won a five-year Navy contract with a $71 million ceiling and an initial award of up to $54 million, covering 18 vessels in the US Pacific Fleet — destroyers, amphibious warships and littoral combat ships. CNBC reported that the robots condense a three-month process to as little as two days.

Roughly 40% of the Navy's fleet is unavailable at any moment because of maintenance cycles. Across power plants and mines, Gecko's own data claims reactive maintenance down about 80% and asset life doubled; a separate deal with NAES, signed in February 2025, exceeds $100 million and targets the American power grid.

stat.l: in the US Pacific Fleet, inspected by climbing robots instead of people

why: Infrastructure fails because inspecting it is dangerous, slow and expensive. Fix the inspection and you fix the maintenance.

sources.name: Gecko Robotics (Mar 2026) — '$71M Deal to Slash U.S. Navy Maintenance Delays'
TechCrunch (Mar 2026) — 'Gecko Robotics lands the largest U.S. Navy robotics deal yet'
Gecko Robotics / NAES (Feb 2025) — the $100M grid deal

caveat: The $71 million is a contract ceiling, not an award. The performance figures are the company's own: '3 months to 2 days' is CNBC's paraphrase, while Gecko's own release describes eliminating three months of potential maintenance delay rather than compressing an inspection. No Navy-published performance data exists yet.

place: United States — virtual tutoring for under-served districts
people: Rose Wang, Susanna Loeb, Dora Demszky and Stanford colleagues
title: An AI coaching tutors in real time lifted the weakest tutors most — for $20 a year
hook: Expert tutors are scarce and expensive. Mediocre ones are everywhere.
body: Expert tutors are scarce and expensive. Mediocre ones are plentiful. So Stanford researchers built Tutor CoPilot, an AI that listens to a live tutoring session and suggests expert teaching moves in the moment — ask a guiding question here, don't just give the answer away.

They ran the first randomized trial of a human-AI tutoring system: 900 tutors and 1,800 K-12 students from historically under-served communities. Students whose tutors had the AI were 4 percentage points more likely to master their maths topic.

But the striking result was distributional: students of the lowest-rated tutors gained 9 points, nearly closing the gap with students of the best tutors. Analysis of 550,000 messages showed the coached tutors asked more probing questions and offered less empty praise. Cost: about $20 per tutor per year.

stat.l: topic-mastery gain for students of the lowest-rated tutors, at ~$20 per tutor per year

why: You can't conjure thousands of expert tutors. You can upgrade the ones already in the room — which is the fastest realistic path to quality help for poor kids.
caveat: Working-paper stage, not yet a peer-reviewed journal article.

people: Gallup and the Walton Family Foundation
title: Teachers using AI weekly get six weeks of their year back
hook: 5.9 hours a week, and most of them are teaching themselves how.
body: Gallup surveyed 2,232 American public school teachers with the Walton Family Foundation and found those who use AI weekly save an average of 5.9 hours a week. Across a 37-week school year that is roughly six weeks of time returned.

What they spend it on is the interesting part: more detailed student feedback, individualised lessons, emails to parents, and getting home at a reasonable hour. The tasks that got automated were the boilerplate; the tasks that expanded were the human ones.

The gap in the system is the other finding. 60% of teachers had used an AI tool that school year, but only 19% said their school had any AI policy, 68% had received no training from their school or district at all, and 52% had simply taught themselves.

stat.l: saved per week by weekly AI users — about six weeks a school year

why: Teacher burnout is a paperwork problem before it is anything else. This is the largest measured intervention against it.

sources.name: Gallup and Walton Family Foundation (Jun 2025) — 'Teaching for Tomorrow' (full report PDF)
Gallup — 'Three in 10 Teachers Use AI Weekly, Saving Six Weeks a Year'

caveat: Self-estimated hours, from the roughly three in ten teachers who use AI at least weekly. Monthly users estimate 2.9 hours. Margin of error ±2.5 points.

people: Brad Smith, father of three, living with advanced ALS
title: He can only move his eyes. He edits YouTube videos narrated in his own lost voice.
hook: A brain implant for control. A voice clone for identity. An AI assistant for speed.
body: ALS left Brad Smith unable to speak or move anything but his eyes. A breathing tube keeps him alive. In 2024 he became the third person — and the first non-verbal person — to receive a Neuralink implant, letting him steer a cursor with his thoughts, even outdoors where his old eye-tracking rig failed in bright light.

Then ElevenLabs built an AI clone of his voice from recordings made before the disease took it. In 2025, Brad edited and narrated a YouTube video about his life — in his own voice. He uses AI chat tools to draft replies faster to his wife and kids, and he's direct about the division of labor: the AI gives him speed; he stays responsible for every word.
Three separate AIs, stacked into one life: control, identity, speed.

stat.l: stacked into one life — implant, voice clone, assistant

why: A preview of how much agency technology can hand back to the most locked-in people alive today.

place: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (company based in New York)
people: Tim Fisher, 63; Dr. Benjamin Rapoport, Precision Neuroscience
title: A film thinner than a hair, and a Parkinson's patient moving a robot arm
hook: 1,024 electrodes on something the size of a postage stamp.
body: Tim Fisher is 63, works in retail in West Chester, Pennsylvania, and has Parkinson's. The tremors make typing or opening a jar close to impossible. In a Philadelphia operating room, surgeons laid a film thinner than a human hair and roughly an inch square — carrying 1,024 electrodes — onto the surface of his brain.

After brief training, when Fisher thought about moving his left hand, a nearby robotic arm moved with it. 'It was an amazing experience,' he said. He described developing a kind of friendship with the arm.

Precision Neuroscience's array has now been used in at least 37 patients across several US medical centres, and in March 2025 the FDA cleared it for recording, monitoring and stimulating cortical activity for up to 30 days. Its co-founder Benjamin Rapoport helped found Neuralink, then left over safety concerns — he wanted a device that rests on the brain rather than penetrating it.

stat.l: electrodes on a film thinner than a hair, used in 37+ patients

why: Not every brain interface has to go deep. A device that rests on the surface is easier to place, easier to remove, and easier to approve.

sources.name: Bloomberg (Apr 2025) — 'Neuralink Rival Precision Neuroscience Receives FDA Clearance on Brain Device'
OODA Loop — reprint of the Bloomberg report

caveat: Correcting our first draft: the FDA clearance covers a wired array for up to 30 days of use, not a wireless brain-reading device. The company describes it as the first full clearance for a company developing a next-generation wireless interface — a claim about its path, not about a cleared wireless product.

people: Ali Madani, Profluent
title: An AI wrote a gene editor from scratch — and it was safer than nature's
hook: Trained on CRISPR proteins the way ChatGPT is trained on text. Then asked to write new ones.
body: CRISPR gene editors are proteins bacteria evolved over billions of years. Profluent trained a language model on hundreds of thousands of them — the way ChatGPT is trained on text — then asked it to write new ones.

The model generated four million candidate sequences. The team built 48 and tested them in human cells. One, OpenCRISPR-1, edited human DNA slightly better than the standard Cas9 while making 95% fewer unintended cuts elsewhere in the genome. It sits 403 mutations away from anything in nature.

Off-target cuts are the main safety fear in gene therapy — the reason treatments stay in trials. An AI produced a safer editor than four billion years of evolution, and Profluent released it free for research and commercial use. The work was peer-reviewed in Nature in 2025.

stat.l: fewer off-target edits than standard Cas9 — while editing the target slightly better

why: Safety is what stands between gene editing and the millions of people with genetic disease. AI just moved that line, and gave the result away.
caveat: No patient has been treated with OpenCRISPR-1 yet. It's in use in labs and commercial cell-line services.

place: Google Research, Google DeepMind and Yale University
people: Google Research and Google DeepMind with Yale University
title: An AI invented a cancer hypothesis. Then Yale proved it right in the lab.
hook: Not a summary of known biology — a new conditional prediction, tested in living cells.
body: The standing objection to AI in science is that these systems only recombine what is already written down. This is the cleanest counter-example so far.

A 27-billion-parameter model built on Google's open Gemma line, trained on the behaviour of individual cells, predicted something nobody had reported: that the drug silmitasertib would boost a tumour's visibility to the immune system — but only in a particular immune setting, where interferon signalling is low. A conditional amplifier, not a general effect. Google is explicit that inhibiting this target had never been reported to enhance antigen presentation.
Yale then tested it in human cell models the AI had never seen, and the prediction held: combining the drug with low-dose interferon raised antigen presentation by roughly 50%.

stat.l: increase in tumour visibility to the immune system, predicted then confirmed

why: Making tumours visible to the immune system is a central problem in oncology, and an AI just contributed a real, testable idea to it.

sources.name: Google (Oct 2025) — 'Gemma AI model helps discover new potential cancer therapy pathway'
bioRxiv — 'Scaling Large Language Models for Next-Generation Single-Cell Analysis'

caveat: Preclinical and in vitro — human cell models, no animals and no patients. And the finding is a novel combination of known biology rather than new biology from nothing, which is what a sceptic would press on.

title: An AI broke a 56-year-old math record — and pays its own compute bill
hook: Strassen's 1969 algorithm stood unbeaten for 56 years. An AI that evolves its own code found a better one.
body: In 1969, mathematician Volker Strassen found a famous shortcut for multiplying matrices — the operation at the heart of all computing. For certain cases, nobody beat it for 56 years. In 2025, DeepMind's AlphaEvolve — an AI agent that writes, tests, and evolves its own code — found a way to do 4x4 complex matrix multiplication in 48 steps instead of 49.

It wasn't a one-off. Tested against more than 50 open math problems, it matched the best known human results in about 75% of cases and beat them in 20%. Third parties independently verified the headline result.

And it's already practical: one AlphaEvolve-discovered scheduling trick has run in Google's data centers for over a year, continuously recovering 0.7% of Google's entire worldwide computing capacity. The AI that discovers new algorithms already pays for itself.

stat.l: of Google's global compute recovered by one AI-discovered algorithm

why: Improving on decades-old human algorithms is discovery, not autocomplete — and it's running in production, not a paper.

place: University of Toronto and KAIST, South Korea
people: Peter Serles and Tobin Filleter (Toronto); Seunghwa Ryu and Jinwook Yeo (KAIST)
title: AI designed a material with five times titanium's strength-to-weight ratio
hook: Strong as steel, light as foam — and more than double the best previous designs.
body: Researchers combined machine learning with nano-scale 3D printing to design lattice materials that had never existed. The algorithm learned which shape changes worked and which failed, then proposed entirely new geometries.

The result reached 2.03 megapascals per cubic metre per kilogram of density — roughly five times titanium's strength-to-weight ratio, and more than double the strength of existing designs. That is a specific-strength figure: it is not five times as strong as titanium in absolute terms, it is five times as strong for its weight.

The projected payoff, from the team at Toronto working with collaborators at KAIST in South Korea: replacing titanium components in aircraft could save around 80 litres of fuel per year for every kilogram of material substituted. Published in Advanced Materials in January 2025.

stat.l: titanium's strength-to-weight ratio, from an AI-designed lattice

why: Almost everything we build is limited by strength-to-weight. Move that ratio and you move aircraft, vehicles, buildings and rockets at once.

sources.name: University of Toronto Engineering (Jan 2025) — 'Strong as steel, light as foam'
ScienceDaily (Jan 2025) — syndication of the same release

caveat: Correcting a common misstatement, including our own first draft: the five-times figure is strength-to-weight, not absolute strength. The fuel saving is an annual per-kilogram projection, not a measured result, and we removed a quote we could not verify word-for-word.

people: Dr. Gerald Lip, NHS Grampian, and Prof. Lesley Anderson, University of Aberdeen (GEMINI); Dr. Clarisse de Vries, University of Glasgow; Dr. Hutan Ashrafian and Lord Ara Darzi, Imperial College London
title: AI found more breast cancers while calling back 39% fewer healthy women
hook: False alarms put healthy women through weeks of terror. This cut them and caught more cancer.
body: Two UK teams ran AI inside live NHS breast screening — one in Aberdeen in 2023, one in London — and published within days of each other in March 2026. The larger study reviewed scans from 125,000 women, then ran prospectively on new ones.

Cancer detection rose from 7.54 to 9.33 cancers per 1,000 women screened. And for women coming in for their first-ever scan, recalls — the terrifying 'we need to see you again' letters — dropped 39.3% while detection rose 8.8%. Reading workload fell about a third. The AI also caught a quarter of the cancers that the old system had missed entirely between screening rounds.

The second study, GEMINI, screened 10,889 women at NHS Grampian in Aberdeen using an AI called Mia, made by Kheiron Medical Technologies. Two radiologists read every mammogram the normal way and found 106 cancers. Where Mia wanted to call a woman back and the two radiologists had not, those scans went for extra human review. That turned up 11 more cancers. Seven were invasive, and seven were under 15mm across. Eleven more on top of 106 is where the headline 10.4% comes from — note that the announcements in March 2024 said 12%, and the published figure is lower.

One of the 11 was a woman in Aberdeen the BBC named only as Barbara. Her tumour was 6mm. Because it was found that early she had an operation and five days of radiotherapy, and she told BBC technology editor Zoe Kleinman it was far less invasive than what her sister and her mother had already been through years before. She had no symptoms. Without Mia her cancer would probably have gone unfound until her next routine mammogram, three years later.

stat.l: fewer healthy women called back for a cancer scare — while 8.8% more cancers were found

why: Screening always involved a cruel trade-off: catch more cancer, or frighten fewer healthy people. AI improved both sides of it at once, in a real national programme.
caveat: Two different studies with different numbers — don't merge them. On GEMINI: three of the paper's authors worked for Kheiron and held stock options, so this is not vendor-independent. The 11 extra cancers were flagged by AI but confirmed by humans in an added review round, and four of the 11 had already been through arbitration before AI saw them, so the authors re-ran the analysis assuming only nine to check the finding held. Mia also declined to read 1,260 of the mammograms as outside its criteria. And the widely repeated line that AI cut the wait for results from 14 days to 3 is a projection, not a measured result — no such figure appears in the published paper, and we have removed it. Imperial's AI initially had a higher recall rate and its thresholds had to be adjusted.

sources.name: Nature Cancer (Mar 2026) — the GEMINI study, peer-reviewed, open access
BBC News, Zoe Kleinman (Mar 2024) — original reporting on the 11 women and Barbara

people: Dr. Patrik Bachtiger and Prof. Nicholas Peters, Imperial College London
title: The AI stethoscope worked. Four in five doctors never used it.
hook: The first national-scale randomised trial of a clinical AI tool, and the device wasn't the problem.
body: An AI stethoscope can record a patient's heart in about fifteen seconds and screen for three conditions at once. Imperial College ran it as a cluster-randomised trial across 205 London GP practices — the first trial of a clinical AI tool at this scale.
The headline result, published in The Lancet, was null. Practices given the device diagnosed no more heart failure than practices without it. Atrial fibrillation and valve disease were null too.

The reason was not the algorithm. Of 96 practices handed a device, 38 never used it at all and another 38 used it fewer than ten times a month. Six practices did the heavy lifting, and the top five produced a third of all recordings. GPs said what they needed was for it to be built into their patient record software, not handed to them as a separate gadget.

This is in the bank deliberately. It is the most useful negative result in clinical AI, and it says something no success story can: a tool that detects disease accurately still changes nothing if it sits outside the way people actually work.

stat.l: of GP practices given the AI device never used it, or barely did

why: Every argument about AI in medicine assumes the hard part is accuracy. This trial says the hard part is adoption — which is a much more tractable problem, once you admit it is the problem.
caveat: Read this as a workflow finding, not a verdict on the technology. The widely quoted 2.3x and 3.5x improvements come from an exploratory comparison of practices that did use it, which the authors themselves label non-definitive and vulnerable to selection bias. The false-positive burden was also heavy: of patients flagged for heart failure, 70% did not have it. The senior author advises the device maker, though the company funded nothing and had no access to the data.

sources.name: The Lancet (Jan 2026) — the TRICORDER trial, open access via Imperial's repository
Imperial College London — the most balanced institutional account

people: Akash Kulgod, Dognosis
title: Trained dogs in EEG helmets, read by AI, caught 9 in 10 early cancers
hook: The leading blood test catches about one Stage I cancer in six. This caught nine in ten.
body: Dogs can detect cancer by smell. The obstacle has never been the nose — it is that a tail wag is not a diagnostic output. Dognosis puts EEG helmets and sensor suits on beagles, labradors and shelter dogs so AI can read each animal's perceptual judgment as a signal, then combines at least three dogs' verdicts with a Bayesian model.

In a Phase 2 study of 3,275 participants across six hospitals in Karnataka, published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology in April 2026, it reached 90.8% sensitivity and 91.3% specificity across seven cancer groups.
The figure that matters most: it held 90.6% sensitivity for Stage I and II disease — the stage where treatment still works, and the stage where blood-based multi-cancer tests have struggled most.

stat.l: sensitivity on Stage I–II cancers, where early detection actually matters

why: Every multi-cancer screening test struggles with early-stage disease, which is the only stage worth screening for. This one didn't.
caveat: We removed a comparison to a leading blood test that we had constructed ourselves and could not stand behind — the figures were not like-for-like on stage, cancer count or study design. The real limitation is specificity: at 91.3%, about one in eleven healthy people is flagged, which at population scale means many false alarms. Seven cancer groups, one Indian state, hospital patients rather than a screening population.

sources.name: Journal of Clinical Oncology (Apr 2026) — the Phase 2 study

people: UC San Diego's ALERTCalifornia team
title: AI cameras caught 900+ California wildfires before anyone called 911
hook: With wildfire, the first fifteen minutes decide everything.
body: California wired more than 1,100 mountaintop cameras to an AI at UC San Diego that watches for smoke around the clock. Since 2023 it has spotted more than 900 fires on state lands before the first 911 call.

With wildfire, the first fifteen minutes decide everything — it's the difference between a small burn and a megafire that takes a town. In 2025 alone, the network helped CAL FIRE respond to roughly 3,600 incidents, over half flagged before any human reported them.

On 7 July 2026, three FireSat satellites launched to do the same job from orbit, able to detect a fire the size of a schoolyard — five metres by five — from space. The full constellation of 50-plus satellites will scan the entire planet every 20 minutes by 2030.

stat.l: wildfires detected by AI before the first 911 call

why: AI gave firefighters eyes that never blink — first on every ridge in California, soon over the whole planet.
caveat: The satellites launched in July 2026 need about three months of commissioning before operational data. The 2025 incident figures come from CAL FIRE via government and trade press, not a peer-reviewed study.

people: Zanskar
title: AI found geothermal heat where prospectors had failed for 17 years
hook: 280°F, at only 2,500 feet, under a valley littered with abandoned wells.
body: Geothermal energy is clean, constant and indifferent to whether the wind blows. Its problem is finding it: hidden resources give almost no surface clues, so exploration has been expensive guesswork.

Zanskar ran stochastic reservoir modelling over legacy geological data and shallow exploration wells, and pointed at Pumpernickel Valley in northern Nevada — a site drilled intermittently since the 1970s by oil and gas companies and the federal government, none of whom ever hit commercially viable temperatures. The AI also picked the drilling angles earlier attempts had missed.

In September 2025 they struck steam: about 280°F at roughly 2,500 feet, shallow enough to be commercial, with enough heat in place to support a first 20-megawatt development. The company's chief executive calls it probably one of the biggest confirmed geothermal resources of the past decade, with a plant targeted for 2028.

stat.l: at just 2,500 feet — under a valley written off since the 1970s

why: Clean firm power is the hardest gap in the energy system. AI is turning old, unread data into new energy.

sources.name: Heatmap News (Sep 2025) — 'This AI for Geothermal Startup Just Announced Its Biggest Find Yet'
MIT Technology Review (Dec 2025) — 'How AI is uncovering hidden geothermal energy resources'

caveat: Correcting our first draft: this was announced in September 2025, not December, and we could find no source for '17 years of failed attempts' — the record shows intermittent drilling since the 1970s. All temperature, depth and capacity figures originate with Zanskar; there is no third-party reservoir certification, which is why independent coverage uses the word 'claims'.

title: Europe's best school system looked at AI and decided the risk was NOT teaching it
hook: Estonia tops Europe on the PISA tests. It didn't ban chatbots — it bought them for everyone.
body: Estonia scores highest in Europe on the PISA international tests. When AI arrived, it did the opposite of most school systems: it leaned in.

Its national 'AI Leap' programme launched on 1 September 2025, giving 20,000 students in grades 10 and 11 — plus thousands of teachers — free access to education versions of leading AI tools. Teachers were trained first. In September 2026 it expands to vocational schools and new tenth-graders, about 38,000 more students, reaching roughly 58,000 by 2027.

By March 2026, 94% of participating teachers were using AI in their work. Student adoption is more gradual and honest about itself: about 7,700 of the first 20,000 had activated accounts by then, and 47% of those used it weekly.

stat.l: students getting state-provided AI tools by 2027 — in Europe's top-performing school system

why: The country with the strongest schools in Europe concluded that the danger lies in not teaching kids to use these tools. That's a powerful signal for every hesitant school board.
caveat: No learning-outcome data yet — this is a bold national bet with teacher training first, not proven results.

place: Abu Dhabi and the wider UAE
people: Alef Education; MBZUAI
title: The UAE put an AI curriculum in every public school, from kindergarten up
hook: It appointed the world's first AI minister in 2017. Now it teaches the ethics of the thing to five-year-olds.
body: Alef Education began as a trial in a single Abu Dhabi public school in 2017. By 2020 the Ministry of Education had rolled it across roughly 350 public schools nationwide; today the company reports its platforms reaching thousands of schools across the UAE, Indonesia and Morocco, with full penetration of UAE government schools from Grade 5 up, teaching Arabic, maths, science, Islamic studies, social studies and English.

The policy around it is unusually deliberate. The UAE appointed the world's first minister for artificial intelligence in 2017. From the 2025-26 academic year, AI is a required subject in every public school from kindergarten through Grade 12, delivered by around a thousand specialist teachers — with roughly a quarter of the curriculum given over to ethics.
Its dedicated AI university, MBZUAI, says about 85% of its graduates stay in the country.

stat.l: every UAE public school now teaches AI as a required subject

why: Most countries are still debating whether to allow AI in classrooms. A few decided years ago and are compounding the head start.

sources.name: UAE Ministry of Education — Alef platform in all UAE public schools
Gulf News (Aug 2025) — UAE schools to introduce AI curriculum
UNESCO Courier (Apr 2026) — 'AI goes to school in the United Arab Emirates'

caveat: School counts here are company-reported and have been inconsistently stated; the 350-school figure is a 2020 milestone, not current. MBZUAI's graduate programmes are scholarship-funded but its new undergraduate degree charges tuition.

people: Milagros Costabel, writer, blind from birth — and 750,000+ users like her
title: Born blind, she points her phone at the world — and it tells her what's there
hook: Menus, street signs, decades of family photos she'd never 'seen.' Now described in seconds, no favors asked.
body: Milagros Costabel was born completely blind. With Be My AI — the AI vision feature inside the free Be My Eyes app — she photographs anything and hears a detailed description within seconds. She reads restaurant menus by herself. She checks prices. And she finally learned what was in years of family photos sitting on her camera roll — without having to ask anyone.
She calls the independence 'strangely liberating.' That's the quiet revolution: not a lab prototype, but a free app on an ordinary phone doing what a sighted assistant used to do.

The app now serves a community of over 750,000 blind and low-vision users (the company's own figure), handling tens of millions of AI and volunteer requests a year. The AI still makes mistakes — so human volunteers remain one tap away as backup.

stat.l: blind and low-vision people using the app

why: Independence at internet scale. The gap between 'needs help' and 'doesn't' just got dramatically smaller, for free.

place: Stanford University and the Arc Institute, California
people: Brian Hie, Samuel King
title: AI wrote the genomes of viruses that never existed — and they killed bacteria antibiotics can't
hook: Sixteen working viruses, designed by a machine, that beat bacteria which had already learned to survive the natural one.
body: Bacteriophages are viruses that kill bacteria — a possible answer to antibiotic resistance. Brian Hie's team trained genome-writing AI on the DNA of two million natural phages, deliberately excluding anything that infects humans, animals or plants.

Starting from a small natural phage, the models wrote hundreds of thousands of new genomes. The team chemically built nearly 300 of them; 16 came to life as working viruses, several fitter than the natural original. Combined into one cocktail, the 16 wiped out two strains of E. coli that had already evolved resistance to the natural phage.
These are the first complete functional genomes ever written by AI. Published in Science in August 2026.

stat.l: working viruses designed by AI that beat bacteria resistant to the natural version

why: Drug-resistant infection is one of the great slow-moving health crises. This is a route to weapons bacteria have never seen.
caveat: This is openly dual-use, and the coverage is genuinely two-sided — infectious disease specialists have called it both valuable and a potential biosecurity risk. Human-infecting viral sequences were excluded from the training data by design. Nothing here has been tested in a patient. We include it because it's real and important, not because it's simple.

people: Conceivable Life Sciences; Aike Ho
title: More than thirty babies have been born from a robotic IVF line
hook: Thirty micro-adjustments a second, at thousandth-of-a-millimetre precision.
body: IVF produces a live birth about 37.5% of the time, and part of that variance is human hands doing microscopic work on a tired afternoon. Conceivable Life Sciences built AURA, a 17-foot robotic line that performs every step of embryo creation: separating sperm, fertilising eggs, freezing embryos.

It makes around thirty micro-adjustments a second at thousandth-of-a-millimetre precision, uses computer vision to find eggs in follicular fluid, and freezes embryos fast enough to cut ice-crystal damage tenfold.

The company now reports more than 30 live births and over 60 pregnancies, most at a clinic in Mexico City. One of the babies belongs to the investor who wrote Conceivable's first cheque and then enrolled in the trial herself. Co-founder Joshua Abram died of cancer weeks before the first American baby arrived.

stat.l: babies born from an AI-guided robotic IVF line

why: IVF is one of the few medical procedures where a small gain in precision converts directly into a person who exists.

sources.name: Conceivable Life Sciences — current birth figures
Bloomberg (Jan 2026) — 'Conceivable Wants Embryo-Making Robots to Transform IVF Industry'
Not Boring (Jan 2026) — summary of the Bloomberg feature

caveat: Every outcome figure is company-reported under an IRB-approved study; there is no peer-reviewed publication of the birth results and no independent audit. The investor whose child was born through it, and who supplies the most-quoted line about it, led the company's seed round.

place: Columbia University Fertility Center, New York
people: Dr. Zev Williams and Hemant Suryawanshi, Columbia University
title: The AI found two sperm in a sample humans had given up on. A baby was born.
hook: It borrowed the trick astronomers use to pick faint stars out of a dark sky.
body: About one in ten infertile men has azoospermia: no sperm can be found in his semen even under a microscope. Sometimes a handful really are there, but an embryologist has to hunt by eye for hours and usually finds nothing.

Columbia built a system called STAR that borrows from astronomy — photograph everything, then let software pick the faint signal out of the dark. It images the whole sample, uses AI to spot anything sperm-shaped, and a robot draws that droplet out through a hair-thin channel within milliseconds, with no dyes or centrifuging that would damage the cell.

One man had been trying for nearly twenty years, through several manual searches and two operations. STAR scanned 2.5 million images of his sample in about two hours and found two usable sperm. Both were injected into eggs. Two embryos formed. A pregnancy followed, and Columbia reports the couple delivered a healthy baby girl.

stat.l: found by AI in a sample that hand-searching had declared empty

why: It turns 'you will never father a biological child' into a maybe, for men whose only option was a donor. And it puts AI on a task humans are simply badly built for: staring at millions of near-identical images without blinking.
caveat: This is one patient, written up as a short research letter rather than a trial. No control group, no published success rate, no peer-reviewed comparison against a skilled embryologist. STAR exists at a single clinic and has been used on a few dozen patients, without a published breakdown of successes and failures. Some striking figures circulating elsewhere — a 30% find rate, '44 sperm in an hour' — trace only to secondary write-ups, not to any paper.

people: Timothy Gowers (Fields Medallist), Daniel Litt, Gil Kalai, Will Sawin
title: A chatbot settled a geometry question that had stood since 1946
hook: For 80 years mathematicians assumed the square grid was the best answer. It wasn't.
body: For eighty years, mathematicians assumed a square grid was the optimal arrangement of points for a problem in Paul Erdős's family of 'unit distance' questions. Everyone believed it. Nobody could prove it.

In May 2026 an OpenAI reasoning model — not a special-purpose mathematics system, a general chatbot — disproved the conjecture, finding an infinite family of arrangements that beat the grid. OpenAI quietly sent the reasoning to leading mathematicians, who checked it and wrote a companion paper. Nine of them, including the Fields Medallist Timothy Gowers.

Their reactions are the story. Gowers: no previous AI-generated proof had come close to publication standard, and he called this 'a milestone in AI mathematics.' Daniel Litt called it the one genuinely interesting result produced autonomously by AI so far. Gil Kalai: 'amazing.'
And then Will Sawin, a human, improved on the AI's construction. Which is roughly how this is supposed to work.

stat.l: that mathematicians had been stuck — settled by a general-purpose chatbot

why: This is the moment respected mathematicians stopped treating AI as a novelty in their own field. Not because it was impressive, but because it was correct.
caveat: The mathematicians themselves are precise about the limits: the broader planar problem is still open, the AI assembled existing algebraic number theory rather than inventing new concepts, and humans cleaned up the write-up. As one put it: the human still plays a vital role.

place: Nigeria — multi-site trial with Mayo Clinic
people: Dr. Demilade Adedinsewo, Mayo Clinic
title: An AI stethoscope doubled detection of pregnancy-related heart failure in Nigeria
hook: Nigeria has the world's highest rate. It usually goes unnoticed until the heart is failing.
body: Nigeria has the world's highest rate of peripartum cardiomyopathy — a dangerous weakening of the heart during or after pregnancy. It usually goes unnoticed until it's severe, because spotting it requires a cardiologist and equipment most clinics don't have.

Mayo Clinic trained an AI to detect a weak heart pump from a simple ECG trace, then loaded it into a digital stethoscope. In a randomized trial of 1,232 pregnant women and new mothers, published in Nature Medicine, AI screening found the condition in 4.1% of women versus 2.0% with usual care.
Twice as many. Each one a young mother who can start treatment before her heart fails.

stat.l: as many cases of pregnancy-related heart weakness detected (4.1% vs 2.0%)

why: This is frontier AI running on a stethoscope in clinics with no cardiologist — proof that AI can leapfrog scarce specialists exactly where mothers are most at risk.

place: Lusaka, Zambia and Chapel Hill, North Carolina
people: Jeffrey Stringer and Margaret Kasaro, University of North Carolina; University of Zambia
title: A nurse with one day of training now dates a pregnancy as well as an expert
hook: The AI was off by 3.2 days. The trained sonographer with the expensive machine was off by 3.0.
body: Knowing how many weeks along a pregnancy is decides almost everything else: when to worry, when to deliver, and whether a small baby is sick or simply early. Getting that number normally requires a trained sonographer and a costly machine — which much of the world does not have.

Researchers at the University of North Carolina and the University of Zambia built an AI that reads a 'blind sweep'. The operator simply glides a cheap handheld probe across the belly in set lines, aiming at nothing in particular, and the software works out the rest. No skill in finding the right view is required, because finding the right view is the part that takes years to learn.

They tested it on 400 pregnant women — 200 in Lusaka, 200 in Chapel Hill — with the scans performed by novices who had a single day of training. The AI's estimates were off by an average of 3.19 days. Expert sonographers using high-end machines were off by 3.03 days. A gap of about four hours, which changes nothing about anyone's care.

stat.l: the AI's average error dating a pregnancy — the expert's was 3.0

why: This takes a skill that took years to acquire and puts it on a battery-powered probe a health worker can carry to a village clinic. It closes a gap between rich and poor countries rather than widening one.
caveat: This measured accuracy, not outcomes — nobody has yet shown it saves babies' lives. It holds for the 14-to-27-week window tested, across only two sites. The company that sells the probe donated the hardware and helped load the model onto it, though the authors reported no financial conflicts.

sources.name: NEJM Evidence (2022) — the earlier model development in 4,695 women
UNC Institute for Global Health and Infectious Diseases

title: Machine translation was meant to kill translators. Their pay is 20% above the median.
hook: They have worked from machine first drafts for years. The pay went up, not down.
body: Translation was supposed to be the first profession AI destroyed, and unusually we have a long run of data — professionals have started from a machine first draft rather than a blank page for years now.

US government figures put the median wage for interpreters and translators at $59,440 in May 2024, against $49,500 across all occupations — about 20% above the median American worker. Employment grew substantially over the preceding decade and a half.

The honest update: the Bureau of Labor Statistics now projects only 2% growth for 2024-2034, slower than the 4% average, and a downgrade on its own earlier projection. Most of the roughly 7,000 annual openings are replacements rather than new posts. The profession did not collapse — but the outlook has softened, and there is reporting on translators who have lost work to AI.

stat.l: what translators earn above the median US worker

why: The one profession everyone agreed would be wiped out first is still here and still paid above average. That is worth knowing — as is the fact that its growth outlook is weakening.

sources.name: US Bureau of Labor Statistics — Interpreters and Translators
Slator (May 2025) — 'BLS Job Outlook for Translators and Interpreters Worsens'

caveat: We cut two things we could not source: a Duolingo quote about AI failing to hold the app's voice, and a claimed corroboration from the Census Bureau. Only the BLS data stands. We added the projection downgrade, because publishing this as a settled victory would be misleading.

people: Matthew Abercrombie, HALO Trust
title: AI has found 50,000 landmines in Ukraine by reading drone photos in 0.2 seconds each
hook: Analysts used to spend three to five days studying photos of a single minefield.
body: Ukraine is the most heavily mined country on Earth — roughly 17 million hectares may be contaminated. At the old pace, clearing it would take centuries.

Human analysts used to spend three to five days studying drone photos of a single minefield before clearance could even begin. Now AI does the first pass. One system has analysed nearly 3 million drone images and flagged over 50,000 landmines and explosive remnants across some 38,000 acres, checking each image in under 0.2 seconds. The UN Development Programme was an early customer. The HALO Trust, the world's largest demining charity, runs a similar programme with Amazon Web Services.
Humans still dig out every single mine by hand. The AI just tells them where to look first — which is the difference between farmland returning to farmers in years instead of decades.

stat.l: landmines and explosives detected by AI in drone imagery of Ukraine

why: Nothing about demining is fast, but the searching part just stopped being the bottleneck. That's years of a farmer's life back.
caveat: The detection counts are the company's own figures — consistent over time and backed by a UN purchase order and US Army evaluations, but not independently audited. HALO reports about 70% detection accuracy in its trials: AI narrows the search, it does not certify land as safe. No land is cleared by AI.

people: Ulysses Ecosystem Engineering
title: Robot gardeners replant the seabed 10x faster and 90% cheaper than divers
hook: Seagrass stores carbon up to 35 times faster than rainforest.
body: Seagrass meadows are one of the ocean's great carbon sinks, and we have destroyed a lot of them. Restoration meant human divers planting seeds by hand at enormous cost per hectare, which is why almost nobody did it at scale.
Ulysses builds autonomous underwater robot gardeners that plant seagrass seeds at precise seabed locations and can cover up to five hectares a day.

On an Australian restoration project the drones cut costs 90% against diver-based replanting and worked ten times faster. That is the difference between a demonstration project and something you can do to a coastline.

stat.l: than human divers, and ten times faster, on an Australian project

why: Most environmental restoration fails on cost per hectare. Change the cost per hectare and you change what is possible.

sources.name: Bloomberg (Jan 2026) — 'Underwater Drones Reveal the Ocean's Potential to Store Carbon'

caveat: All three figures are the company's own, for a single project, as reported by Bloomberg — there is no independent measurement or peer-reviewed evaluation of the restoration outcomes. We removed a widely-quoted claim that seagrass buries carbon 35 times faster than rainforest, because it is not in the source we cite and the underlying comparison is narrower than it sounds.

people: Te Hiku Media and 2,500 community volunteers
title: A Māori community built its own speech AI — and the tribe owns every voice in it
hook: 2,500 people recorded 300 hours of their language in about ten days.
body: Te Hiku Media, a small Māori-owned broadcaster, wanted to save te reo Māori — a language once punished in schools. Big tech companies wanted their archives. They said no.

Instead they ran a community campaign: over 2,500 people recorded more than 300 hours of labelled speech, over 200,000 phrases, in about ten days. With it they trained a speech-recognition model that transcribes te reo at 92% accuracy — unlocking more than 30 years of archived recordings of native speakers, many no longer living.

The data sits under a guardianship licence written on their own terms: it can only ever be used for the benefit of the Māori people. Roughly half the world's languages are endangered. A community of a few thousand, not a trillion-dollar company, showed how AI can save one.

stat.l: transcription accuracy for te reo Māori, from 300 hours volunteered in ~10 days

why: AI is usually framed as something done to communities. This is a community doing it themselves, keeping ownership, and saving a language with it.

people: Fabrizio Dell'Acqua, Karim Lakhani, Ethan Mollick and colleagues
title: One person with AI matched a two-person team without it
hook: A pre-registered trial of 791 professionals at Procter & Gamble.
body: Procter & Gamble let researchers run a pre-registered randomised trial on 791 of its own professionals, working real business problems in four conditions: alone, alone with AI, in a pair, and in a pair with AI.

A person working with AI improved solution quality by 0.37 standard deviations. A two-person team working without AI improved by 0.24. In other words one person plus AI beat — and a two-person team with AI barely exceeded — what a human pair achieved unaided.

Both AI-enabled groups also worked faster, spending 12.7% to 16.4% less time while producing longer, more detailed work. And the AI-assisted teams were about three times more likely to land a solution in the top 10% of quality. That last effect held for teams, not for individuals.

stat.l: quality gain in standard deviations: one person with AI, versus a human pair without

why: Almost all professional work is organised around how many people a task needs. This is evidence that number just changed.

sources.name: Organization Science (Jun 2026) — peer-reviewed version of record
Harvard Business School AI Institute — summary

caveat: Published in Organization Science in 2026 with 791 participants; the earlier working paper reported 776. One firm, one set of tasks, and the top-10% effect appeared only for teams — for individuals it was positive but not statistically significant.

people: Mark Jackson, living with ALS
title: No brain surgery: he controls an iPad through a stent in a blood vessel
hook: The implant rode up through his jugular vein. Apple treats his thoughts as a native input.
body: Mark Jackson has ALS and is losing his hands and voice. His brain implant — a mesh of electrodes called a Stentrode, made by Synchron — was threaded up through a blood vessel to sit over his motor cortex. No open brain surgery. No skull drilled.

In August 2025 he became the first person on Earth to control an iPad directly with brain signals using Apple's new built-in brain-interface protocol: opening apps, writing messages, navigating — no hands, no eyes, no voice required.

The significance is bigger than one demo. Apple treating brain signals as a standard input — like touch, or a mouse — means future implant users get the entire device, not one custom app. And an implant that goes in through a vein is the path to reaching millions, not dozens.

stat.l: brain surgeries required — the implant travels through the jugular vein

why: Two firsts at once: a trillion-dollar consumer company building thought-control into its products, and an implant simple enough to place without opening the skull.

people: Generate:Biomedicines
title: An AI-engineered asthma drug that needs two injections a year instead of twenty-six
hook: Same biology, redesigned to fit into a human life.
body: People with severe asthma can end up in hospital repeatedly even on the best inhalers. The add-on biologic drugs that help mean an injection every two to four weeks — forever.

Generate:Biomedicines used machine-learning models plus high-throughput lab testing to engineer an antibody that binds a key inflammation trigger very tightly and stays in the body for months. In a 96-patient early trial it was well tolerated and kept suppressing its target for at least six months.

In December 2025 the company launched two global Phase 3 trials in about 1,600 patients across more than 40 countries. Dosing: twice a year. This is the furthest an AI-engineered biologic has travelled toward approval.

stat.l: injections instead of one every two to four weeks

why: AI isn't only finding new targets — it's redesigning known biology so treatment fits a patient's life instead of ruling it.
caveat: No efficacy results yet — the Phase 3 trials are underway, and the measure that matters (fewer asthma attacks over 52 weeks) won't report for a while.

place: Princeton / DIII-D, San Diego & EPFL, Switzerland
people: Egemen Kolemen, Jaemin Seo; DeepMind–EPFL team
title: AI sees fusion plasma crashes 300 milliseconds early — and steers around them
hook: Plasma hotter than 100 million degrees, held steady by a controller that learned from every past failure.
body: Fusion reactors hold plasma hotter than 100 million degrees Celsius — and sudden 'tearing' instabilities can kill the reaction in an instant. They're one of the hardest problems between humanity and fusion power.

In a Nature study, Princeton researchers trained an AI on past experiments at the DIII-D tokamak to predict these instabilities up to 300 milliseconds before they happen — an eternity for a computer — and let it adjust the reactor in real time to dodge them. It held real, high-power plasma stable through conditions that normally cause crashes. It built on DeepMind's 2022 breakthrough with EPFL, where an AI learned to sculpt and hold plasma shapes in a real Swiss tokamak.

In October 2025, DeepMind partnered with Commonwealth Fusion Systems to run millions of simulated experiments before the SPARC reactor even switches on. These are control milestones, not net-energy milestones — but control is precisely what fusion has been missing.

stat.l: advance warning of plasma instabilities — enough for AI to prevent them

why: AI is now in fusion's control room, and the leading fusion companies are betting on it to shorten the road to the grid.

place: Rady Children's Hospital, San Diego, and four other California hospitals
people: Dr. Stephen Kingsmore, Rady Children's Institute for Genomic Medicine
title: A dying newborn's genome, decoded in days instead of weeks
hook: Standard genetic testing takes six weeks. For a baby in intensive care, that's often too late.
body: When a newborn is dying in intensive care and nobody knows why, standard genetic testing takes four to six weeks. Often the answer arrives after the baby is gone.

Rady Children's in San Diego built a pipeline that sequences a baby's whole genome and uses AI to match millions of genetic variants against the medical record, returning answers in about three days. Their world record is 19.5 hours.

California tested it on 178 critically ill babies on Medicaid. It found a diagnosis for 43% of them and changed treatment for nearly a third — avoiding 513 hospital days and 11 major surgeries, and saving the state $2.5 million net. The model has since spread to a network of more than 100 children's hospitals.

stat.l: to a genetic diagnosis instead of six weeks — record: 19.5 hours

why: For a baby in a genetic crisis, a diagnosis in days is the difference between the right treatment now and an answer at the autopsy.

sources.name: American Journal of Human Genetics (via PubMed Central)

title: AI tripwire cameras cut poaching 80% — and caught 39 poachers in a single night
hook: A ranger can't watch a thousand square kilometres of jungle. A $600 camera can.
body: Similipal is home to some of India's rarest tigers, including the black-striped melanistic ones found almost nowhere else. Rangers hid roughly 100 to 150 TrailGuard AI cameras along forest trails.

A chip inside each camera recognises humans, tigers and vehicles, and beams the photo to rangers' phones within about 40 seconds. In the first ten months, alerts led to 96 poacher arrests and 86 guns seized, and poaching incidents fell by an estimated 80%.

On 20 February 2026, the cameras spotted an armed hunting party moving at night and gave rangers their exact position. Thirty-nine poachers were arrested in one coordinated raid, along with firearms, bows and explosives.

stat.l: estimated drop in poaching incidents after AI cameras went in

why: The cheapest anti-poaching breakthrough since the radio — and it works by giving rangers information, not weapons.
caveat: The arrest and reduction figures come from Odisha forest department statements reported in Indian media — official, but not independently audited.

people: Chick-fil-A; Bay Center Foods
title: Squeezing lemons by hand cost 10,000 hours a day and a lot of fingers
hook: Nobody's calling was hand-squeezing lemons for eight hours.
body: Across all Chick-fil-A locations, squeezing lemons by hand added up to about 10,000 hours of work a day by the company's own reckoning — and a steady stream of injured fingers.

A 190,000-square-foot plant north of Los Angeles, larger than an average Costco, now squeezes up to 1.6 million pounds of lemons with hardly any human involvement, staffed by around 120 people who maintain the machines. Where employees used only about 40% of each fruit, the robots use nearly all of it.

The candid version came from the company's own supply-chain vice president, explaining why they automated at all: 'You start doing the math, and there's not going to be enough team members.' This is a labour shortage being solved, not simply a cost being cut.

stat.l: of finger-injuring work per day, eliminated

why: The jobs automation takes first are often the ones nobody wanted and everyone got hurt doing.

sources.name: Bloomberg (Jan 2025) — 'Chick-fil-A's Lemon-Squeezing Robots Are Saving 10,000 Hours of Work'
Futurism — coverage of the Bloomberg report

caveat: The 10,000-hour figure is Chick-fil-A's own, shared with Bloomberg. The 1.6-million-pound figure carries no stated time period in any source we could find.

people: Fabrizio Dell'Acqua, Ethan Mollick, Karim Lakhani and co-authors
title: Elite consultants with AI worked faster and better — and the bottom half improved most
hook: But on the task designed to be beyond the AI, they were 19 points more likely to get it wrong.
body: In a field experiment, 758 Boston Consulting Group consultants — 7% of the firm's consulting workforce — were randomly given GPT-4 or not. On 18 realistic consulting tasks within the AI's abilities, the AI users completed 12.2% more tasks, worked 25.1% faster, and produced roughly 30–34% higher-quality work.
Below-average performers improved most: about +43%, against +17% for the top performers. Even among some of the world's most credentialed knowledge workers, AI acted as a leveller.

And now the honest half. On a task deliberately designed to sit beyond the AI's abilities, the AI users were 19 percentage points more likely to get it wrong. The researchers called it the 'jagged frontier': AI is superb on one side of an invisible line and confidently useless on the other, and you have to know which side you're standing on.

stat.l: performance jump for below-average consultants (top performers gained +17%)

why: The caveat is what makes it believable. This is what real evidence looks like: a large effect, unevenly distributed, with a failure mode you need to respect.
caveat: Correcting a viral number: the peer-reviewed version reports quality gains of about 30–34%, not the '40%+' from the 2023 preprint. Always pair this study with its jagged-frontier finding.

people: Kristen Faulkner, double Olympic gold medallist and Harvard computer science graduate
title: Sports science ignores women. So an Olympic champion wrote her own.
hook: Ten hours a day at a laptop, still in cycling kit.
body: Kristen Faulkner won two gold medals at the Paris 2024 Olympics. She also has a computer science degree from Harvard — and a specific frustration: almost no sports science exists for female athletes, because the research was built overwhelmingly on men.

So in her off-season she wrote code, sometimes ten hours a day, sitting at her laptop still in cycling kit. Her system pulls together nine years of her own data — heart rate, variability, sleep, weight, power, temperature, training load, bloodwork, body scans and menstrual cycle phase — roughly 4,400 hours of training history. It builds models of her own physiology rather than showing another dashboard, so it can suggest *why* a session went badly, not just that it did.

She used AI assistants to help write and debug it, and is clear about the division of labour: she writes the architecture, defines the logic, reviews the implementation. Her own website footer describes it as vibe coded between intervals, which is more honest than most of the headlines about her.

stat.l: of her own training history, across about ten data streams, modelled on one body

why: The gap in sports science for women is real and slow to close. Here the technical skill to do something about it landed in the hands of someone with the problem.
caveat: The 'she built it' part is solid and in her own words. The 'and that's why she won' part is not, and we are not running it. Her three recent golds came at two different continental championships a month apart in two countries — widely misreported as one meet — where in two events the silver medallist was her own teammate. Her account dates the coding to after two of those wins, and she was returning from surgery, so improvement was expected anyway. She also owns the system as a product in closed beta, invests in AI companies, and speaks professionally on this story. There is no independent evaluation. To her credit she discloses the commercial interests herself, and says that when the model disagrees with her body, she trusts her body.

sources.name: Kristen Faulkner — her own account of building it
USA Cycling — Pan American track results, Santiago

people: Four paralyzed research volunteers
title: The implant that hears sentences you only imagine — protected by a thought password
hook: For people too weak to even attempt speech, AI now decodes the words they think.
body: Some people are too weak even to attempt speaking — the signal every earlier brain-computer interface relied on. So Stanford researchers went one level deeper: decoding inner speech, sentences said silently in the mind.

In a study published in Cell in August 2025, implants in four paralyzed volunteers turned imagined sentences into text from a 125,000-word vocabulary, at up to 74% accuracy and conversational speed. It's a proof of concept — less accurate than attempted-speech systems, and the researchers say so plainly.

The detail that matters for the future: because thoughts should stay private, the system only begins decoding when the user thinks a chosen password. It caught the password nearly every time. Privacy isn't an afterthought — it's being engineered in from day one.

stat.l: accuracy decoding sentences participants only imagined

why: This could reach the most paralyzed people of all — and it shows the field building mental privacy into the foundation, not bolting it on later.

people: Recursion Pharmaceuticals
title: For a disease with no treatment at all, AI pulled a shelved drug off the shelf
hook: Hundreds of precancerous polyps. No approved drug. Many patients lose their colon.
body: People with familial adenomatous polyposis grow hundreds or thousands of precancerous polyps in the colon. There is no approved drug, so many end up having the colon removed.

Recursion's AI — which analyses millions of images of diseased cells looking for patterns humans can't see — flagged that blocking a pathway called MEK should help. The company licensed a molecule Takeda had shelved and tested it. Patients' polyp burden dropped by a median of 43% in three months, and most kept the benefit for 12 weeks after stopping the drug.

Rare diseases are commercially unattractive, so nobody screens for them. AI screening is cheap enough to run anyway — which is how a molecule sitting in a corporate freezer became a treatment for people the market had written off.

stat.l: median reduction in polyp burden — in a disease with no approved treatment

why: The cheaper the search gets, the more the ignored diseases get looked at. That's the quiet revolution in rare disease.
caveat: The trial is ongoing (completion targeted 2027), and these figures come from trade-press reporting rather than a peer-reviewed publication with full statistics. The same reporting also covers an AI drug failure — Verge Genomics' ALS candidate — which is worth knowing.

place: Microsoft + Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Washington
people: Vijay Murugesan, Karl Mueller, Nathan Baker
title: AI searched 32 million materials in 80 hours and found a battery needing 70% less lithium
hook: Decades of trial-and-error, compressed into a long weekend — and it ended with a real battery.
body: Lithium is expensive, and mining it is hard on the environment. Microsoft's AI screened 32.6 million candidate battery materials — most never seen in nature — and narrowed them to 18 promising ones in 80 hours. The team says that's thousands of times faster than standard simulation.

Then scientists at the Department of Energy's Pacific Northwest National Laboratory actually made the top candidate: a solid electrolyte that swaps about 70% of the lithium for cheap, abundant sodium. Within months it was running in a working prototype battery.

It's a lab prototype, not a product on shelves — the story here is the speed. The bottleneck in materials science has always been that testing ideas takes years. This compressed the search from decades to days, and ended with an object you can hold.

stat.l: less lithium in the new electrolyte — found among 32.6M candidates in 80 hours

why: This is the template for how new energy materials will be found from now on: AI searches, humans build, months not decades.

people: Chengyu Xiao and Han Zhou, Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Yuebing Zheng and Kan Yao, UT Austin; Cheng-Wei Qiu, National University of Singapore
title: AI designed a roof coating that ran 20°C cooler than grey paint
hook: It works backwards: start from the heat behaviour you want, then design the structure.
body: Designing a material that dumps heat to the sky has always been slow trial and error — guess a recipe, make it, measure it, guess again — and it was largely stuck with flat two-dimensional shapes and a short list of ingredients.

This team built a machine learning system that runs the problem backwards. You specify the heat behaviour you want, and it designs a three-dimensional structure to deliver it. It generated more than 1,500 candidate coatings that reflect sunlight while radiating heat straight out to space.

Then they actually made them, painted them onto model buildings, and left them outside in the sun. After four hours of midday sun the coated roofs ran about 5°C cooler than white paint and 20°C cooler than grey. No power, no wiring, no moving parts — published in Nature in July 2025.

stat.l: cooler than grey paint after four hours of midday sun
