why: Cooling is among the fastest-growing uses of electricity on a warming planet, and a coating needs no electricity at all. It also shows AI compressing materials discovery from months of guesswork into days.
caveat: Tested on small model buildings, not real occupied ones, so the temperature gap is not a measured building result. The widely quoted 15,800 kilowatt-hours a year saving for a four-storey block is calculated from a model, not observed anywhere. And calling this 'paint' is loose: these are nanostructured meta-emitters, harder to make than opening a tin, with cost, durability and manufacturing at scale all unproven. Two patent applications have been filed, which the authors declare.

sources.name: Nature (Jul 2025) — 'Ultrabroadband and band-selective thermal meta-emitters by machine learning'
University of Texas at Austin — news release

title: The NHS let an AI make its own cancer decisions. It has checked 165,000 patients.
hook: The first AI trusted to work a cancer queue by itself — and a regulator signed off.
body: Fear of melanoma sends enormous numbers of people into urgent two-week cancer referrals, and the overwhelming majority turn out to be harmless moles. Dermatologists spend their days ruling things out.

DERM, an AI from a London company, examines a smartphone photo of a skin lesion taken through a small lens attachment. At more than 25 NHS sites it now discharges clearly benign cases on its own — the first AI in the NHS trusted to make an autonomous clinical decision in a cancer pathway.

By 2025 it had assessed over 165,000 NHS patients and helped find more than 15,500 cancers, ruling out melanoma with 99.8% reliability. In May 2025 the UK's health technology watchdog, NICE, backed wider NHS use.

stat.l: skin cancers found across 165,000+ NHS patients by an autonomous AI

why: This is the milestone skeptics said was a decade away: a regulator-approved AI safely working a cancer queue alone, so specialists spend their time on the patients who are actually sick.
caveat: The patient and cancer-detection counts are the company's own figures, echoed in trade press but not independently audited. The regulatory approvals are verified.

sources.name: NHS England — AI skin lesion guidance

title: An AI prospector found Zambia's biggest copper discovery in a century
hook: The clean energy transition is really a copper problem. Big new deposits had become brutally hard to find.
body: The world needs enormous amounts of copper for wires, EVs and the electrical grid, but major new deposits have become brutally hard to find. The easy ones were found generations ago.

KoBold Metals uses AI to digest old geological maps, drill logs and survey data — decades of records nobody has fully read — and predict where ore hides deep underground. At Mingomba in Zambia, its models guided drilling to a deposit the company calls the country's largest copper find in a hundred years, with ore grades around 5%, several times richer than a typical mine.

It's now a construction site, not a press release. Shaft sinking began in April 2026 on a mine costing over $2.3 billion, designed to produce about 300,000 tonnes of copper a year by the early 2030s. Zambia's state mining company holds 20%.

stat.l: since Zambia's last copper discovery of this size

why: The clean-energy transition is a metals problem before it's anything else. If AI can find world-class deposits humans walked past, the bottleneck changes shape.
caveat: 'Largest in a century' is KoBold's own characterisation, widely reported but not independently adjudicated. Mingomba sits in a historically known copper district — the AI's contribution was working out the deposit's true size and where to drill. First copper is still years away.

title: Kenyan farmers don't just chat with the AI — 70% acted on its advice within a month
hook: For 83% of them, it was the first digital farming advice they'd ever had.
body: Farm advice normally requires a human extension agent who might visit once a year, if ever. Farmer.Chat, from the nonprofit Digital Green, answers smallholder farmers' questions in their own language, drawing on a library built from thousands of farmer-made training videos.

The independent research firm 60 Decibels interviewed 450 Kenyan farmers using it in mid-2025. 70% had applied one of its recommendations on their own farm within the previous 30 days. 99% called the advice trustworthy. For 83% of them, it was the first digital farming advice they had ever received.
Women rated it higher than men did — which in agricultural extension, historically, almost never happens.

stat.l: of surveyed Kenyan farmers applied the AI's advice on their farm within 30 days

why: The gap between knowing and not knowing is the difference between a failed harvest and a fed family. An AI agronomist in your own language closes it.
caveat: This measures behaviour change, not yet yields or income.

people: Erik Brynjolfsson, Avinash Collis, Felix Eggers and colleagues, Stanford Digital Economy Lab
title: Americans captured $116 billion of value from AI. It appears in no GDP figure.
hook: Ask people what you'd have to pay them to give it up. That's the measurement.
body: How do you value something people get for free? Economists ask what you would have to pay someone to give it up for a month. Run that survey at scale and multiply by users, and you get consumer surplus — real welfare that never passes through a till and so never lands in GDP.

The Stanford Digital Economy Lab's working paper puts US consumer surplus from generative AI at $116 billion in 2025, rising to $172 billion in 2026. An earlier back-of-envelope version by two of the same authors estimated roughly $97 billion for 2024, against something like $7 billion of US revenue booked by OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic and Google combined.

The direction is the point, and the authors state it plainly: consumers capture most of the welfare gains from these tools. When people ask where AI's returns have gone, a large part of the answer is that they landed in users' hands rather than on any company's income statement.

stat.l: US consumer surplus from generative AI in 2025, rising to $172B in 2026

why: The most common argument that AI isn't paying off measures only company revenue. The value is real; it is just accruing to the people using it.

sources.name: Stanford Digital Economy Lab (Apr 2026) — 'What is Generative AI Worth?'
Stanford Digital Economy Lab — the $97bn op-ed

caveat: Both figures come from a working paper, not a peer-reviewed journal, and rest on survey-based willingness-to-accept — a legitimate but contested method. The widely-quoted '$97 billion in 2024' appeared in a newspaper opinion column, not a paper, and applies a mid-2025 survey figure to a 2024 user base.

people: Thomas Costello, Gordon Pennycook and David Rand
title: A chatbot talked people out of conspiracy theories, and it lasted two months
hook: Decades of research said facts bounce off committed believers.
body: Researchers asked 2,190 Americans to name a conspiracy theory they personally believed and to explain their evidence for it. Each then had a three-round conversation with GPT-4, which answered their specific reasons rather than delivering generic debunking.

Belief in their own chosen theory fell about 20% on average, and was still down when they were checked two months later. The effect appeared even among people whose beliefs were deeply held, and it spilled over to other conspiracy theories they had never discussed.

That was not supposed to work. Decades of research suggested facts bounce off committed believers. The apparent difference here is patience and specificity — engaging with what one person actually thinks, which no human debunker has time to do at scale.

stat.l: average fall in belief in a conspiracy theory the participant chose themselves

why: If conspiracy belief is resistant to generic facts but not to a patient, personalised conversation, then something that can hold millions of those conversations at once matters a great deal.
caveat: Read this one with a live flag attached. In June 2026 Science published an Editorial Expression of Concern after the authors self-reported inconsistencies in how participant screening was applied, plus problems in the public dataset that made some exact reported values hard to reproduce. The journal says a reanalysis matches the original in direction, significance and substantive size, and follow-up studies support the effect — but the specific 20% figure is under active review, so treat it as provisional. It also measures self-reported belief among paid online participants, not real-world behaviour.

sources.name: Retraction Watch (Jun 2026) — coverage of the Expression of Concern

people: Sarah de Lagarde, 44, City executive and mother of two
title: Run over by two Tube trains, she climbed Kilimanjaro again — with an arm that learns
hook: Sixteen electrodes read her muscles. The AI hand starts the grip before she finishes asking.
body: In September 2022, Sarah de Lagarde slipped on a rainy London Underground platform and was run over by two trains. She lost her right arm and leg. A year later she was fitted with a bionic arm driven by AI: sixteen electrodes read the signals in her remaining muscles, and the software learns her patterns — so the hand begins a grip before she has finished intending it.
She was back at her City job in four months. She hugs her daughters with both arms. And roughly two years after the accident, she summited Kilimanjaro — again.

Users like Sarah say the AI is the whole difference: a hand that predicts intent feels like a limb, not a tool. She now campaigns for platform safety and for making smart prosthetics affordable for everyone who needs one.

stat.l: from double amputation back to her full-time job

why: AI is what turns a heavy mechanical hand into something closer to a real limb — it predicts intent instead of waiting for commands.

people: César de la Fuente-Nunez, Fangping Wan, Marcelo Torres
title: AI resurrected antibiotics from the DNA of woolly mammoths
hook: They named the molecules after their sources: mammuthusin. Mylodonin. Hydrodamin.
body: César de la Fuente's lab built a deep-learning model that reads genetic sequences and predicts which protein fragments can kill bacteria. Then they pointed it at the genomes of extinct animals — what they call the 'extinctome.'

It pulled out germ-killing molecules they named after their sources: mammuthusin from the woolly mammoth, mylodonin from a giant sloth, hydrodamin from an ancient sea cow. The molecules killed drug-resistant bacteria in lab dishes and treated infections in mice about as well as a last-resort antibiotic.

The real story isn't the mammoths — it's the speed. Finding antibiotic candidates traditionally takes years. The model does it in hours, across a library of over a million genetic recipes that no human will ever read.

stat.l: to surface antibiotic candidates — work that traditionally takes up to six years

why: Antimicrobial resistance kills over four million people a year. AI turns unread genetic archives — including extinct ones — into a searchable pharmacy.
caveat: Nothing from this programme has entered human trials yet.

people: LIGO–Caltech and Google DeepMind teams
title: AI made humanity's most sensitive instrument 30–100x quieter
hook: LIGO measures ripples in space-time smaller than a proton. Its own controls were the noise.
body: LIGO detects gravitational waves — ripples in space-time from colliding black holes — by measuring changes thousands of times smaller than a proton. At the lowest frequencies, its own control systems inject tiny vibrations that drown out the signals.

In September 2025, DeepMind and LIGO published 'Deep Loop Shaping' in Science: a reinforcement-learning controller tested on the real detector in Louisiana. It cut the worst control noise 30 to 100-fold, beating targets set by the quantum limit.

Quieter detectors see farther. The teams project this could help astronomers catch hundreds more black-hole collisions per year — and observe the intermediate-mass black holes that have so far stayed hidden. AI is now improving the instruments of physics itself.

stat.l: reduction in LIGO's worst control noise, on the real detector

why: Every layer of science AI touches — the questions, the analysis, now the instruments themselves — compounds the speed of discovery.

people: Weike Zhao and colleagues, Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Xinhua Hospital
title: On the hardest rare-disease cases, an AI out-diagnosed specialists with 10+ years' experience
hook: A rare disease diagnosis commonly takes five years of referrals and wrong answers.
body: Rare diseases are hard to spot because their symptoms look like everything else. A diagnosis commonly takes five years of referrals, tests and wrong answers — what families call the diagnostic odyssey.

A Shanghai team built DeepRare, which isn't a single model but a system of agents wired to 40 specialist tools that can read genome data, structured records, clinical notes, even handwriting. They validated it on 6,401 cases with known answers, then ran a head-to-head on 163 genuinely difficult cases against five doctors who each had more than ten years of experience.

DeepRare named the right disease on its first guess 64.4% of the time, against the doctors' 54.6%. Given three guesses: 79% against 66%. And the number that makes it usable rather than just impressive — rare-disease specialists agreed with the AI's reasoning 95.4% of the time. It shows its work.

stat.l: first-guess accuracy: the AI versus doctors with 10+ years of experience

why: Five years of a child's life spent looking for a name. Tools like this are how that becomes five weeks.
caveat: Retrospective cases, not live patients, and the head-to-head sample was small at 163 cases.

title: A weed-seeing AI sprayed 5 million acres and cut herbicide use nearly in half
hook: Cameras scanning 2,500 square feet per second at 15 mph, firing only at the weeds.
body: Traditionally a farmer sprays the whole field, because you can't aim at what you can't see fast enough. That means chemical everywhere, on crop and soil alike.
A See & Spray machine rolls through at 15 mph while boom-mounted cameras scan 2,500 square feet per second. Onboard AI distinguishes crop from weed and fires individual nozzles only at the weeds.

In the 2025 season, US farmers used it across more than 5 million acres and cut non-residual herbicide use by an average of nearly 50% — about 31 million gallons of herbicide mix that never went on the ground. An independent Iowa State University study measured average product savings of 76% and about $15.70 an acre. John Deere is confident enough to charge by the acre with a money-back savings guarantee.

stat.l: of herbicide mix not sprayed on US fields in one season

why: Less chemical, same weed control, lower costs. This is what environmental progress looks like when it pays for itself — no mandate required.
caveat: The ~50% cut applies to post-emergence herbicide passes, not all farm chemicals.

sources.name: John Deere — See & Spray herbicide savings

people: Manu Chopra and Vivek Seshadri
title: Rural Indians are paid nearly 20x minimum wage to teach AI their languages
hook: The AI boom created a new export for people the global economy had ignored: their own voices.
body: AI needs data in India's hundreds of languages, and someone has to create it. The story of that work is usually about exploitation.

Karya, a Bengaluru nonprofit that calls itself the world's first ethical data company, routes it differently. Villagers record speech, transcribe and label through a smartphone app, earning about $5 an hour — nearly twenty times India's minimum wage — plus ongoing royalties when their data is resold.

By the end of 2023 it had reached over 35,000 workers across 24 states and completed more than 35 million paid tasks, with clients including Microsoft, Google and the Gates Foundation. Many of the workers are rural women earning their first independent income.
It flips the exploited-data-worker story on its head — by design, not by accident.

stat.l: India's minimum wage — hourly pay for rural workers building AI datasets

why: Who captures the value of AI is a choice, not a law of nature. This is proof the choice can go the other way.
caveat: Worker counts are self-reported in Karya's own annual report; the $5/hour figure was independently reported by TIME.

people: Neisha Cruz, Amazon
title: She picked items for five years. Now she runs robot fleets for 2.5x the pay.
hook: Amazon has more than a million robots — and says it retrained 700,000 people.
body: Neisha Cruz spent five years picking items in an Amazon warehouse in Windsor, Connecticut. She was trained to oversee robotic fleets, and now monitors them from an office in Tempe, Arizona for about two and a half times her starting pay.

Amazon has deployed more than a million robots — approaching the point of having more robots than people in its warehouses — and says it has trained over 700,000 workers worldwide for higher-paying roles that can involve robotics. Around 75% of its global deliveries are now robotics-assisted.

The number that cuts both ways: packages shipped per employee per year have risen from about 175 in 2015 to roughly 3,870, and average staff per facility is now about 670, the lowest in sixteen years. Rising output per worker is good for the worker who stays. It is also consistent with needing fewer of them.

stat.l: the pay, after five years of picking and a retraining programme

why: One named person's career is worth more than a forecast. The route from warehouse floor to robot supervisor exists and someone walked it.

sources.name: The Wall Street Journal (Jul 2025) — 'Amazon Is on the Cusp of Using More Robots Than Humans in Its Warehouses'

caveat: Every figure is Amazon's own, relayed by the Wall Street Journal, with no independent audit — and note the hedge: 700,000 trained for higher-paying jobs 'that can include' robotics is looser than retrained into robotics roles.

people: BenevolentAI research team
title: An AI picked a COVID drug in 48 hours. It became an approved treatment that cut deaths.
hook: January 2020. One question to a knowledge graph. Two years later, a WHO recommendation.
body: In late January 2020, as COVID began to spread, scientists at BenevolentAI asked their AI one question: which already-approved drug might both block the virus from entering cells and calm the deadly immune overreaction that was killing patients?

Within 48 hours it surfaced baricitinib — an arthritis pill. Then came the part AI can't do: big randomized trials in real hospitalized patients. In the COV-BARRIER trial, deaths at 28 days fell 38%, a finding backed up by the much larger RECOVERY trial. The FDA authorized it for emergency use in November 2020 and granted full approval in May 2022. The World Health Organization issued a strong recommendation.
This is the whole gauntlet: AI hypothesis, randomized trials, regulators, global guidelines, doctors' hands. The AI narrowed thousands of candidates to one. Humans proved it.

stat.l: reduction in deaths among hospitalized COVID patients

why: The clearest case of an AI-generated idea running the full course to an approved treatment — during an emergency, when speed was measured in lives.
caveat: COV-BARRIER missed its main goal (slowing disease progression); the 38% figure is the death-rate result, later confirmed by larger trials. Baricitinib was already an approved drug — the AI's contribution was spotting the new use, not inventing the molecule.

sources.name: Frontiers in Pharmacology (2021) — the method, peer reviewed

people: Pratyusha Sharma, Project CETI
title: Machine learning found a 'phonetic alphabet' hiding in whale conversation
hook: For 40 years we thought sperm whales had a few dozen calls. We weren't listening closely enough.
body: Sperm whales talk in patterns of clicks called codas. For decades, scientists believed they used only a few dozen fixed calls. Then Project CETI and MIT researchers ran machine learning over more than 8,700 recorded codas from Caribbean sperm whales.

The calls, it turns out, are built from combinable features — rhythm, tempo, subtle timing shifts, ornamental extra clicks — a combinatorial system the researchers describe as a phonetic alphabet. Follow-ups kept coming: a 2025 study found vowel-like sounds in whale codas, and in 2026 researchers published the first acoustic record of whales' distinctive calls during a birth.

To be precise about what's been found: structure, not translation. Nobody 'speaks whale' yet. But there is far more information in those clicks than anyone knew — and AI is the reason we can finally see its shape.

stat.l: whale click sequences analyzed to reveal the hidden structure

why: Understanding what whales say to each other could transform conservation — and our sense of the other minds on this planet.

people: Dr. Aaron Tierney, Kaiser Permanente Division of Research
title: 2.5 million doctor's visits, documented by AI. 16,000 hours given back.
hook: Your doctor spends up to two hours on notes for every hour with patients, then finishes at night.
body: Doctors in the US spend up to two hours on documentation for every hour with patients, then finish their charts at night — the profession calls it 'pajama time,' and it's a leading cause of burnout.

Kaiser Permanente in Northern California rolled out ambient AI scribes that listen to the visit, with patient consent, and draft the note automatically. Between October 2023 and December 2024, 7,260 physicians used it across 2,576,627 patient visits, saving an estimated 15,791 hours of typing — about 1,800 working days.
But the number that says the most: 84% of surveyed physicians said it improved their communication with patients. And 47% of patients noticed their doctor spent less time looking at a screen.

stat.l: patient visits documented by AI in 14 months at one health system

why: Burnout-driven paperwork is why your doctor stares at a screen instead of at you. This is AI quietly handing back the eye contact.

place: Global oceans — enforcement in Panama, Chile, Mexico, Ecuador, Gabon
title: AI exposed the hidden fishing fleet — three quarters of it was invisible
hook: Boats that break the rules just switch off their trackers and vanish. Satellites don't care.
body: Most industrial fishing boats that break the rules do something simple: they switch off their trackers and disappear from public view.

Global Fishing Watch trained AI on radar and optical satellite imagery to spot the ships anyway. Its findings, published in Nature, revealed that roughly three quarters of the world's industrial fishing vessels had been invisible to public tracking systems. An entire shadow fleet, mapped for the first time.

The map is free for any coast guard on Earth. In 2025, its analysts completed over 40,000 vessel reviews that contributed to more than 400 sanctions and penalties against illegal operators. Off Chile it flagged 43 boats fishing before the season opened, leading to 21 fines and a measurable change in fleet behaviour. In Panama its reports became primary evidence against longliners near a protected ridge.

stat.l: sanctions and penalties against illegal fishing vessels in one year

why: You can't police what you can't see, and the ocean was mostly unseen. Now every country can watch its own waters, rich or poor.

sources.name: Global Fishing Watch — Dark Vessels research

people: US Treasury, Bureau of the Fiscal Service, Office of Payment Integrity
title: Machine learning clawed back $1 billion in stolen Treasury cheques
hook: 1.4 billion payments a year. Find the bad one.
body: The US Treasury sends out roughly 1.4 billion payments a year, worth more than $6.9 trillion. That makes it one of the largest fraud targets on earth, and the difficulty is not subtlety but scale: finding a stolen cheque among a billion legitimate ones, fast enough to get the money back before it is gone.
Treasury's Office of Payment Integrity put machine learning on the problem. In the year to September 2024, that work recovered $1 billion in cheque fraud.

It sat inside a wider $4 billion of fraud and improper payments prevented and recovered that year, up from $652.7 million the year before. But only the $1 billion is the AI number — the rest came from expanded risk screening, prioritising high-risk transactions and payment scheduling. Anyone reporting '$4 billion recovered by AI' has misread the release.

stat.l: in Treasury cheque fraud recovered using machine learning in a single year

why: Public money returned to taxpayers, documented in an official government release rather than a vendor case study. It is one of the clearest examples anywhere of machine learning paying for itself in government.
caveat: Be precise about which number belongs to the AI: Treasury attributes only the $1 billion cheque-fraud recovery to machine learning, not the $4 billion total. A larger figure also circulates — $11.7 billion prevented, detected and recovered in fiscal 2025 — with no machine-learning breakdown given. And these are agency self-reported figures for money 'prevented and recovered', not independently audited, and prevented-loss estimates always rest on assumptions about what would otherwise have been paid.

sources.name: US Department of the Treasury (Oct 2024) — official press release
Bureau of the Fiscal Service — Do Not Pay programme figures

title: India's farmers now fix stalled benefit payments by talking to an AI in 11 languages
hook: A government office that speaks your language at midnight.
body: India's PM-KISAN scheme sends small farmers about ₹6,000 a year in income support. When a payment stalled, fixing it used to mean paperwork, queues, or a trip to a distant office — often in a language you don't read.

Kisan e-Mitra, an AI chatbot built with the nonprofit Wadhwani AI and plugged into India's national language platform, lets farmers ask by voice or text in 11 Indian languages, 24 hours a day. By July 2025 it had handled over 5 million farmer grievances and queries across all 28 states.
For a farmer with limited literacy and no English, a government that answers in your own language at midnight is the difference between getting your money and giving up on it.

stat.l: farmer grievances handled in 11 languages, around the clock

why: Most government help fails at the last mile — language, literacy, distance. This is AI dissolving that barrier at national scale.
caveat: Volume figures are programme-reported; there's no independent evaluation of resolution quality yet.

people: Hillary Vipond, Complexity Science Hub and LSE
title: Victorian bootmaking was mechanised. The bootmakers kept their jobs.
hook: 170 million census records, read one worker at a time.
body: We argue about technological unemployment with almost no good historical data, because old statistics are too coarse to see individual workers. Hillary Vipond rebuilt the mechanisation of English bootmaking from more than 170 million individual British census records between 1851 and 1911, resolving them down to specific tasks — about 1.3 million bootmakers within that dataset.

152,000 artisanal jobs disappeared as skills became obsolete. 144,000 new jobs emerged. Roughly a wash — but the detail is what matters: incumbent bootmakers were rarely displaced. Adoption was slow enough, and demand persistent enough, that people already in the trade largely worked until they retired.

What vanished was the entrance. In her words, the decline was driven by young men no longer entering the artisanal trade. Slow adoption and steady demand shielded the people already inside, while the opportunities disappeared for anyone trying to get in.

stat.l: artisanal jobs lost versus new jobs created — but incumbents kept theirs

why: This is a far more precise warning than 'the robots took our jobs' — and it points at exactly who to help: not incumbents, but the people trying to start.

sources.name: Vipond (Nov 2025) — 'Technological Unemployment in Victorian Britain: Young Workers and the Collapse of Entry'
LSE Research Online — the underlying PhD thesis

caveat: A November 2025 working paper, not yet peer-reviewed. Note that an earlier 2020 version of this project circulated with different headline figures, so cite the current paper.

people: Prof. Masato Sakai, Yamagata University + IBM Research
title: Humans took a century to find 430 Nazca figures. AI found 303 more in six months.
hook: Two-thousand-year-old desert drawings, invisible to the naked eye, flagged by a model and confirmed on foot.
body: The giant desert drawings of Nazca, Peru — birds, cats, human-like figures scratched into the ground 2,000 years ago — are so faint that a century of archaeology had found 430 of them.

A Yamagata University team working with IBM trained an AI to scan high-resolution aerial imagery of the entire desert and flag likely geoglyphs. Following the AI's leads on foot for just six months, they confirmed 303 brand-new figures — nearly doubling the known total in a single field season, roughly a 16-fold speed-up in discovery.

The finds, published in PNAS, even revealed a pattern humans had missed: the small figures cluster along ancient footpaths. They were made to be seen by travelers — a 2,000-year-old audience, finally getting counted.

stat.l: new geoglyphs found in 6 months — vs 430 in the previous century

why: Archaeology was limited by how much ground human eyes could search. That limit just disappeared.

place: Worldwide — trials across the US, Europe and Asia
title: AI watching colonoscopies cut missed pre-cancerous growths by half
hook: Tired human eyes miss about a quarter of polyps. The AI never blinks.
body: Colonoscopies prevent colon cancer by finding and removing polyps before they turn deadly. But tired human eyes miss roughly a quarter of them — and every missed polyp is a cancer risk left behind.

AI systems now watch the live video feed and draw a box around anything suspicious. A meta-analysis of 28 randomized trials covering 23,861 patients found AI-assisted colonoscopy raised the detection rate of pre-cancerous polyps by 20% and cut the miss rate by 55%.
The first such device was authorized by the FDA in 2021. It's now standard equipment in thousands of endoscopy suites — one of those AI deployments that became invisible because it just works.

stat.l: reduction in missed pre-cancerous polyps

why: Every 1% increase in polyp detection is linked to a measurable drop in later colon cancer. A second pair of eyes that never gets tired makes an already life-saving procedure better.
caveat: An honest wrinkle: a 2025 observational study suggested endoscopists' unassisted detection skills may dip after routine AI use. It doesn't undo the trial evidence, but it's a real question about how to deploy these tools.

people: Joshua Blumenstock (UC Berkeley); Dean Karlan and Chris Udry (Northwestern)
title: Togo used AI on satellite photos to find its poorest citizens — and paid them
hook: The hardest problem in aid isn't money. It's knowing who needs it.
body: When COVID lockdowns hit Togo, the government had no reliable list of who was poorest. Many of its citizens had never appeared in any registry at all — invisible to the state that wanted to help them.

Economists trained machine learning on satellite images — roof materials, road quality — and anonymised mobile phone records to estimate poverty person by person. The Novissi programme then sent mobile-money payments of around $20 a month directly to 154,238 of the poorest people. No paperwork, no travel, no office.

Research published in Nature found this reached the truly poor far better than the practical alternatives, cutting exclusion errors sharply compared to simply targeting the poorest districts. It was the first time a country targeted national emergency aid this way.

stat.l: of Togo's poorest citizens found by machine learning and paid directly

why: An algorithm found people the census had missed. That's a permanent upgrade to what a poor government can do for its own citizens.
caveat: A 2020–21 story, kept because it's the canonical proof. ML targeting still makes individual errors, and the researchers themselves flag the data-privacy questions it raises.

place: Austin, Texas — expanding to Chicago, Atlanta, Charlotte, Raleigh, California
people: MacKenzie Price, co-founder
title: The school where AI teaches academics in two hours a day is going to ~50 campuses
hook: Mornings for mastery. Afternoons for everything school never had time for.
body: At Alpha School, students do all core academics in about two hours a day using AI-personalised learning apps. Adults act as motivators and coaches rather than lecturers. Afternoons go to projects, workshops and life skills.

The school's published results on NWEA MAP — a standard national assessment — show students scoring around the 99th percentile in most grades and subjects. Families are voting with their feet: in August 2026 Alpha announced plans to grow from about a dozen campuses to roughly 50.

Read it as an experiment, not a proof. But it's a live demonstration that mastery-paced AI learning can compress the school day dramatically — and it's now being stress-tested at fifty locations at once.

stat.l: of AI-guided academics per day, with school-reported scores near the 99th percentile

why: Even discounting heavily for a selective, affluent intake, the structural claim is interesting: if mastery learning works, most of the school day is scheduling, not teaching.
caveat: Be sceptical here in a way the school isn't. The test results are Alpha's own data on a selective ~$40,000-a-year student body — real tests, but no independent audit and no randomized trial. The 'learning 2.6x faster' figure is a marketing claim. What IS independently confirmed: the model, the tuition, and the expansion.

title: The one job AI really did take — and taking it was a mercy
hook: Reviewing the worst material on the internet used to be a human career.
body: Content moderation means sitting at a desk and looking at the most violent, abusive and traumatising material people upload, for eight hours a day. It has produced documented PTSD, lawsuits and settlements. It is a job that damages the people who do it.
At Facebook and Instagram, 94% and 98% of moderation decisions respectively are now made by machines.
This belongs in a collection of good news precisely because it is displacement. Not every job is worth preserving. Some work should be given to something that cannot be harmed by it.

stat.l: of Facebook and Instagram moderation decisions now made by machines

why: An honest optimism has to include the cases where automation removed human beings from work — and be glad about it.

people: Dr. Michael Abràmoff, University of Iowa
title: In 2015 the FDA had cleared 6 AI medical devices. By the end of 2025: 1,451.
hook: The AI doctor's visit isn't coming. It's already quietly inside your scans.
body: In April 2018 the FDA did something it had never done: it authorized an AI to make a diagnosis entirely on its own. IDx-DR screened eye photos for diabetic retinopathy with no specialist involved, after a 900-patient trial showed 87% sensitivity. Its creator, retina surgeon Michael Abràmoff, had worked on the problem for over 20 years.

That single approval opened the gates. The FDA's official list of AI-enabled medical devices reached 1,451 by the end of 2025 — 295 authorized in 2025 alone, against 6 in the whole of 2015. They span radiology, cardiology and neurology.

Each of those cleared the same evidence bar as any other medical device. Which means the AI doctor's visit isn't a future event — for most Americans it's already quietly part of their scans, their ECGs, and their eye exams.

stat.l: FDA-authorized AI medical devices, 2015 vs end of 2025

why: This is the answer to 'but is any of it actually approved?' More than fourteen hundred times over, by the world's strictest regulator.

title: Google gave away its eye-scan AI to screen 6 million people for preventable blindness
hook: Diabetes quietly destroys the retina. Caught early, the blindness is preventable. There aren't enough eye doctors.
body: Diabetes can quietly destroy the retina. Caught early, the resulting blindness is largely preventable — but there are nowhere near enough eye specialists to screen everyone who needs it. Roughly 100 million people worldwide have diabetic retinopathy and most don't know it.
Google spent a decade building and field-testing ARDA, an AI that grades retina photos in seconds, trained on over 100,000 scans and validated in peer-reviewed studies in both countries.

In October 2024 it licensed the technology to three partners — two in India, one in Thailand — to deliver 6 million free screenings over ten years in underserved communities, working with Thailand's health ministry. A nurse with a camera can now do what used to require a specialist.

stat.l: free AI eye screenings committed for underserved patients

why: Unglamorous, enormous, and exactly the kind of good AI is built for: giving people in poor districts the same standard of screening as people in rich ones.
caveat: The 6 million is a forward commitment now being rolled out, not screenings already completed.
